A number of five figures at the left side indicates the location of the key word
in the basic texts. In the case of the SV, the HB and the VN, the first three figures
indicate the page number, and the last two indicate the line number (for example,
SV16026=SV 160,26; HB02314=HB 23,14; VN06110=VN 61,10). In the case of the
PV and the NB, the second figure indicates the chapter number and the last three
figures indicate the karika or sutra number (for example, PV02232=PV, the
Pramanasiddhi-chapter v.232; NB03015=NB, the Pararthanumana-chapter sutra 15.
In the case of the SP, the last two figures indicate the karika number (for example,
SP00015=SP, v.15).

children.translated_text: 3. In this database, sentences are artificially divided into word-units, although they involve a phonetic fusion or union in the basic texts. Further, compound words are divided into their shortest constitutive elements (we use a hyphen to indicate that hyphenated elements originally form a compound word) with the following exceptions:

children.text:
3.1. The prefixes a-, dur-, nih- remain undivided, irrespective of attachment to
words or compound words.
children.translated_text: 3.1. The prefixes a-, dur-, niḥ- remain undivided, irrespective of attachment to words or compound words.

children.text:
3.2. Suffixes making an adverb, for example -vat, -vasa, are divided. But suffixes
making a possessive adjective, for example -vat, -mat, remain undivided, and terms
such as a numeral+ -dha/-vidha/-prakara remain also undivided.
children.translated_text: 3.2. Suffixes making an adverb, for example -vat, -vaśa, are divided. But suffixes making a possessive adjective, for example -vat, -mat, remain undivided, and terms such as a numeral + -dhā/-vidhā/-prakāra remain also undivided.

children.text:
3.3. Compound words with the suffixes -ta/-tva or -bhava/-bhuta fundamentally
remain undivided. For example: karyakaranabhava/-bhuta/-ta.
children.translated_text: 3.3. Compound words with the suffixes -tā/-tva or -bhāva/-bhūta fundamentally remain undivided. For example: kāryakāraṇabhāva/-bhūta/-tā.

children.text:
3.4. Compound words with evam-, tat-, tatha-, para-, yatha-, su-, sva- in the
wordhead fundamentally remain undivided. For example: evamjatiya, tadutpatti,
tathakrta, paratantra, yathartha, yathasvam, sujnanatva, svabhava.
children.translated_text: 3.4. Compound words with evam-, tat-, tathā-, para-, yathā-, su-, sva- in the word-head fundamentally remain undivided. For example: evaṃjātīya, tadutpatti, tathākṛta, paratantra, yathārtha, yathāsvam, sujñānatva, svabhāva.

children.text:
3.5. Some compound words which are regarded as terminology remain also
undivided. For example: agnihotra, ayogavyavaccheda, arthapatti, padartha,
paramartha, prasajyapratisedha, viruddhavyabhicarin, samanantarapratyaya,
samtanaparinama, samanyalaksana, svabhavapratibandha.
children.translated_text: 3.5. Some compound words which are regarded as terminology remain also undivided. For example: agnihotra, ayogavyavaccheda, arthāpatti, padārtha, paramārtha, prasajyapratiṣedha, viruddhavyabhicārin, samanantarapratyaya, saṃtānapariṇāma, sāmānyalakṣaṇa, svabhāvapratibandha.

children.text:
4. Those terms whose wordhead is subject to the Sandhi rules (for example, -d
dhetu-) are cited in their original form (for example, -d *hetu-) for the sake of
using this database to make an KWIC index.
children.translated_text: 4. Those terms whose word-head is subject to the <s>sandhi</s> rules (for example, -d dhetu-) are cited in their original form (for example, -d *hetu-) for the sake of using this database to make a KWIC index.

children.text: 00101 oṃ namo buddhāya /
children.translated_text: <s>Oṃ</s>, homage to the <s>Buddha</s>!

children.text: 00102 vidhūta-kalpanā-jāla-gambhīra-udāra-mūrtaye /
children.translated_text: To the one whose form is profound and noble, with the net of conceptual constructions dispelled,

children.text: 00103 namaḥ samantabhadrāya samanta-spharaṇa-tviṣe //
children.translated_text: Homage to <s>Samantabhadra</s>, whose radiance pervades all directions! //

children.text: 00104 prāyaḥ prākṛta-saktir apratibala-prajño janaḥ kevalaṃ /
children.translated_text: For the most part, people are attached to the ordinary, with feeble intelligence;

children.text: 00105 na anarthy eva subhāṣitaiḥ parigato vidveṣṭy api īrṣyā-malaiḥ //
children.translated_text: not that good speech is purposeless, but [those] defiled by the stains of jealousy hate [it] even so. //

children.text: 00106 tena ayaṃ na para-upakāra iti naś cintā api cetaś ciraṃ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, this [work] is not for the benefit of others—such is our thought, yet the mind for a long time

children.text: 00107 sūkta-abhyāsa-vivardhita-vyasanam ity atra anubaddha-spṛham //
children.translated_text: has been addicted through habitual practice of well-spoken [teachings], and thus remains attached to this [endeavor]. //

children.text: 00108 artha-anartha-vivecanasya anumāna-āśrayatvāt tad-vipratipattes tad-vyavasthāpanāya
children.translated_text: Since inference is the basis for discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful, and since there is disagreement about that, in order to establish it,
he states:

children.text: 00110 pakṣa-dharmas tad-aṃśena vyāpto hetus tridhā eva saḥ /
children.translated_text: The property of the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis-subject), pervaded by a portion of that—the <s>hetu</s> (logical reason) is exactly threefold.

children.text: 00111 avinābhāva-niyamād hetv-ābhāsās tato apare //1//
children.translated_text: Due to the restriction of invariable concomitance, the remaining ones are <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (pseudo-reasons). //1//

children.translated_text:
The effect, being invariably accompanied by the cause through whatever essential natures—of those [natures alone] it is not established without—[it is] a <s>hetu</s>.
Due to the restriction of being an effect of that, [it is a reason] only through those properties without which it does not exist. If [one objects that] there would be an unwanted consequence of the producer-produced relationship with [only] a part—no, because in the apprehension of the specific product in question, the qualifications of the <s>liṅga</s> (logical mark) are generalities.

children.text: 00401 svabhāve bhāvo api bhāva-mātra-anurodhini //2//
children.translated_text: When there is the intention to speak of an undifferentiated generality, it is not accepted because of deviation.

The <s>pakṣa</s> is the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer). [This is] by metaphorical extension of the whole to the part. If [one objects that] there is no metaphorical extension due to the absence of purpose—no, because [the statement] is intended to negate the <s>dharma</s> (property) of every <s>dharmin</s>; because it is a part of that, it is for the sake of cognizing the <s>dharma</s> of a <s>dharmin</s> fit for such metaphorical extension. And thus the exclusion of visual perceptibility and so forth [is achieved]. Even by the mention of <s>dharma</s>, if the <s>dharmin</s>-basis is established, [then] by the capacity of the mention of <s>dharmin</s>, through proximity, the <s>sādhya-dharmin</s> (subject to be proved) is established—if [one objects] thus—no, because the <s>dharmin</s> of the example also has proximity. By the pervasion with a portion of that, since existence is established in the <s>dharmin</s> of the example, through the mention of <s>dharmin</s>, the <s>sādhya-dharmin</s> is delimited. The statement regarding what is already established may be suspected to be for the purpose of restriction—that existence belongs only to what is homogeneous—even when this is established, like the statement of non-existence regarding the exclusion of the heterogeneous in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s>. And the mention of <s>pakṣa</s> is for the sake of avoiding the complexity of cognition when the meaning is [already] obtained through [logical] capacity. If [one objects that] because the <s>pakṣa</s> has the property [in question], the qualifier depending on that does not recur elsewhere, and thus there would be uncommonness—no, because [we] qualify by <s>ayogavyavaccheda</s> (exclusion of what is not connected). Just as "<s>Caitra</s> is an archer"—not by <s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s> (exclusion of other connections)—just as "<s>Pārtha</s> is an archer"—this we shall raise [later].
A portion of that is a property of that—according to the intention of the speaker, not a part of that—because the word <s>pakṣa</s> does not denote the aggregate. Pervasion is precisely the presence of the pervader there, or the presence of the pervaded only there. By this, the positive and negative [concomitances] are said to be ascertained by their respective <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid cognition), and also the property of the <s>pakṣa</s>. These three types of <s>hetus</s> are characterized as <s>kārya</s> (effect), <s>svabhāva</s> (essential nature), and <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension). For example: "There is fire here, because of smoke"; "This is a tree, because it is a <s>śiṃśapā</s>"; "In a particular place, there is no pot, because of the non-apprehension of what fulfills the conditions of apprehension." If it existed, it would only fulfill the conditions of apprehension, not otherwise. Therefore, [the qualification] "fulfilling the conditions of apprehension of the existent" is stated. Among these, two establish a positive entity, and one is a reason for negation. For when there is <s>svabhāvapratibandha</s> (essential connection), one thing does not deviate from another. And that [connection is] due to being of that nature. If [one objects that] when there is identity of nature, there is no distinction between what is to be proved and the prover—no, because of the postulation of a distinction of properties—this we shall explain. And thus he states: "This entire practice of inference and what is to be inferred operates through a distinction of <s>dharma</s> and <s>dharmin</s> superimposed upon cognition." The distinction as <s>dharma</s> and <s>dharmin</s> is made by the form of cognition, not by the object [itself]. Because independent conceptual distinctions have no basis in real objects, from a domain constructed by them, the cognition of objects would be nothing but the grasping of non-objects. Even of the effect, there is <s>svabhāvapratibandha</s>—because of the arising from what has that nature.
These two [types of reasons] give rise to the cognition of what is to be inferred; since they do not directly arise [from the object], although they do not reflect that [object], because they arise from that, they are not deviating from it—and thus are <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), just like perception. For even perception's validity consists precisely in non-deviation from the object. In its absence, what will come into being would be a deception regarding that. And what other non-deviation of another [cognition] is there besides arising from that? Because for things whose natures are not dependent [on each other], there is no restriction of co-occurrence. If [one argues that] because the effect is an indicator due to arising from that, then the indicator-indicated relationship [holds] in every respect, because the producer-produced relationship [holds] in every respect—no, because in the absence of that, there is no restriction of arising from that [in every respect]. Therefore:

children.translated_text:
In the case of essential nature, an existent entity [is a <s>hetu</s>] only insofar as it follows from mere existence. //2//
<s>Hetu</s> is to be supplied. For identity of nature belongs to a thing only insofar as it follows from that alone, and does not depend on anything else—because there is no restriction that what was non-existent in the presence of that should subsequently come into existence, [and] because causes deviate from their effects.
The non-operation of <s>pramāṇas</s>—

children.translated_text: The establishment and non-establishment of contrary effects, and the establishment and non-establishment of the reason—

children.text: 00508 dṛśya-ātmanor abhāva-artha-anupalabdhiś caturvidhā //4//
children.translated_text: The non-apprehension of visible [entities] and self-nature is fourfold in meaning as [establishing] absence. //4//

<s>Anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension) is fruitful as non-operation in the absence [of the object], and its fruit is the negation of cognition, language, and conventional practice of the existent. Because these [cognitions] are preceded by apprehension, this form is the same for both the reason establishing non-existence and the reason establishing existence. For indeed, existence is apprehension itself, characterized by fitness for [producing] objective [cognition], or the operation of cognition based upon that. From that [arises] the operation of cognition, language, and conventional practice of the existent. And the non-existence of non-existents is non-apprehension.
Some [non-apprehension] whose fruit is the cognition of non-existence, with reference to a distinction of reasons— //3//

00525 tadā abhāvo api iti / iyaṃ pratiṣedha-viṣaya-anupalabdhiḥ prayoga-
00601 bhedena caturdhā bhavati / viruddha-siddhyā yathā na śīta-sparśo
00602 atra agneḥ / etena vyāpaka-viruddha-siddhir uktā veditavyā yathā
00603 na tuṣāra-sparśo atra agneḥ / viruddha-kārya-siddhyā yathā na śīta-
00604 sparśo atra dhūmāt / hetv-asiddhyā yathā na atra dhūmo anagneḥ /
00605 svabhāva-asiddhyā yathā na atra dhūmo anupalabdheḥ / etena vyāpaka-
00606 svabhāva-asiddher uktā yathā na atra śiṃśapā vṛkṣā-abhāvāt /
00607 sarvatra ca asyām abhāva-sādhanyām anupalabdhau dṛśya-ātmanām eva
00608 teṣāṃ tad-viruddhānāṃ ca siddhir asiddhiś ca veditavyā / anyeṣām
00609 abhāva-virodha-asiddheḥ / yadi viruddha-kārya-upalabdhyā apy abhāva-
00610 siddhiḥ tat-kāraṇa-upalabdhyā kiṃ na sidhyati /
children.translated_text: becomes fourfold by variation of application. [First,] by the establishment of the contradictory—as, 'there is no cold touch here, because of fire.' By this, the establishment of what contradicts the pervader should be understood as stated—as, 'there is no touch of frost here, because of fire.' [Second,] by the establishment of the contradictory effect—as, 'there is no cold touch here, because of smoke.' [Third,] by the non-establishment of the reason—as, 'there is no smoke here, because of the absence of fire.' [Fourth,] by the non-establishment of essential nature—as, 'there is no smoke here, because of non-perception.' By this, the non-establishment of the pervading essential nature is stated—as, 'there is no <s>śiṃśapā</s> tree here, because of the absence of trees.' And in all cases of this non-perception which establishes absence, the establishment and non-establishment of those [entities] and their contradictories should be understood only for those whose essential nature is perceptible. Because the absence and incompatibility of others is not established. If absence is established even by the perception of the contradictory effect,

children.text: 00611 tad-viruddha-nimittasya yā upalabdhiḥ prayujyate /
children.translated_text: why is it not established by the perception of its cause?

children.text: 00612 nimittayor viruddhatva-abhāve sā vyabhicāriṇī //5//
children.translated_text: The perception that is applied of the cause of something contradictory to that—in the absence of contradiction between the two causes, that [inference] is inconclusive. //5//

Whatever negation there is, all of it belongs to <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception). For it can be made twofold: [negation] of something either by a positive statement or by a prohibition. In a positive statement, either something contradictory is established or something non-contradictory. In the case of establishing something non-contradictory, since there is no incompatibility of co-existence, there is no negation. Even in the case of something contradictory, without the absence of non-perception, the incompatibility is not apprehended. For the ascertainment of incompatibility is [possible only] because of the non-existence of something that has unlimited causes in the presence of another; and that [ascertainment] is [dependent] on non-perception. Or, incompatibility is characterized by the mutual exclusion of perception—like permanence and impermanence. There too, by the perception of one, what is stated is precisely the non-perception of the other. Otherwise, since the non-existence would be unestablished due to the perception of the unnegated [entity]. When one proves the absence of another by the negation of one, non-perception is already established, since negation itself has the nature of non-perception. Therein also, in the negation of another entity, [it may be] of cause and effect, or of experience. Since experience is unobstructed therein, whence comes [the conclusion] that in its absence something else should not exist? Even in the non-perception of the effect, it is not necessarily the case that causes possess that [effect], so whence its absence? Therefore, it is only the non-perception of the cause that indicates absence. As for <s>svabhāva-anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception of essential nature), that is itself non-existence. Therein, only the subject is established. Even in this, when one states the absence of the pervaded through the non-perception of the pervading property, that too is an absence. This non-perception pertaining to the object of negation

children.text:
00613 yathā na śīta-sparśo atra kāṣṭhād iti / nimittayoḥ punar virodhe
00614 gamikā eva yathā na asya roma-harṣa-ādi-viśeṣāḥ santi saṃnihita-dahana-
00615 viśeṣatvāt etena tat kāryād api tad-viruddha-kārya-abhāva-gatir
00616 uktā veditavyā yathā na roma-harṣa-ādi-viśeṣa-yukta-puruṣavān ayaṃ
00617 pradeśo dhūmāt / iyaṃ ca hetv-asiddhyā eva tad-viruddha-siddhiḥ
00618 prāg eva nirdiṣṭā iti iyaṃ prayoga-bhedād aṣṭadhā-anupalabdhiḥ / tatra
00619 yā iyaṃ viruddha-kārya-upalabdhir uktā tatra
children.translated_text: regarding this perception of the contradictory effect that was stated,

children.text: 00620 iṣṭaṃ viruddha-kārye api deśa-kāla-ādy-apekṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: consideration of place, time, and other [factors] is accepted even in the case of the contradictory effect;

children.text: 00621 anyathā vyabhicāri syād bhasmā iva aśīta-sādhane //6//
children.translated_text: otherwise it would be inconclusive, like ashes in proving the absence of cold. //6//

For instance, 'there is no cold touch here, because of wood'—this is [inconclusive]. However, when there is contradiction between the two causes, it is indeed indicative—as, 'this [person] does not have horripilation and such distinctive [signs], because of the proximity of a particular fire.' By this, the ascertainment of the absence of the contradictory effect from that effect is also stated and should be understood—as, 'this place does not have a person with horripilation and such distinctive [signs], because of smoke.' And this establishment of what contradicts that, through the non-establishment of the reason, has already been indicated earlier. Thus, this non-perception is eightfold by variation of application. Therein,

children.text: 00622 yas tarhi samagreṇa hetunā kārya-utpādo anumīyate sa kathaṃ
children.translated_text: Now, the production of an effect that is inferred from a complete cause—how

children.text: 00623 trividhe hetāv antarbhavati /
children.translated_text: does it fall within the threefold [classification of] reasons?

children.text: 00624 hetunā yaḥ samagreṇa kārya-utpādo anumīyate /
children.translated_text: The production of an effect that is inferred from a complete cause—

children.text: 00625 artha-antara-anapekṣatvāt sa svabhāvo anuvarṇitaḥ //7//
children.translated_text: since it does not depend on anything else, it has been described as [belonging to] essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>). //7//

children.text:
00626 asāv api yathā asaṃnihitān na anyam apekṣata iti tan-mātra-anubandhī
00627 svabhāvo bhāvasya / tatra hi kevalaṃ samagrāt kāraṇāt kārya-utpatti-
00628 sambhavo anumīyate samagrāṇāṃ kārya-utpādana-yogyatā-anumānāt /
00629 yogyatā ca sāmagrī-mātra-anubandhinī iti svabhāva-bhūtā eva anumīyate /
children.translated_text: And since the capability is connected solely with the aggregate, what is inferred is indeed of the nature of <s>svabhāva</s> (essential nature).

children.text: 00701 kiṃ punaḥ kāraṇaṃ sāmagryāḥ kāryam eva na anumīyate /
children.translated_text: But then, what is the reason that the effect itself of the aggregate is not inferred?

children.text: 00703 sāmagrī-phala-śaktīnāṃ pariṇāma-anubandhini /
children.translated_text: Of the aggregate, result, and capacities, which follow upon transformation—

children.text: 00704 anaikāntikatā kārye pratibandhasya sambhavāt //8//
children.translated_text: there is inconclusiveness regarding the effect, because of the possibility of obstruction. //8//

That too, just as [an entity] that does not depend on another not present [in the causal aggregate]—[its] essential nature follows solely from that [aggregate]. For therein, merely the possibility of the production of the effect from the complete cause is inferred, since it is an inference of the capability of the complete [causes] to produce the effect.

children.text:
00705 na hi samagrāṇi ity eva kāraṇa-dravyāṇi sva-kāryaṃ janayanti sāmagrī-
00706 janmanāṃ śaktīnāṃ pariṇāma-apekṣatvāt kārya-utpādasya / atra
00707 antare ca pratibandha-sambhavān na kārya-anumānam / yogyatāyās
00708 tu dravya-antara-anapekṣatvān na virudhyate anumānam / uttarottara-
00709 śakti-pariṇāmena kārya-utpādana-samarthā iyaṃ kāraṇa-sāmagrī
00710 śakti-pariṇāma-pratyayasya anyasya apekṣaṇīyasya abhāvād iti / pūrva-
00711 sajāti-mātra-hetutvāt śakti-prasūteḥ sāmagryā yogyatā ananya-apekṣiṇī
00712 ity ucyate / yā tarhy akāryakāraṇabhūtena anyena rasa-ādinā rūpa-
00713 ādi-gatiḥ sā katham / sā api
00714 eka-sāmagry-adhīnasya rūpa-āder asato gatiḥ /
children.translated_text: the cognition of color and the like, which are non-existent [and] dependent on a single aggregate—

children.text: 00715 hetu-dharma-anumānena dhūma-indhana-vikāra-vat //9//
children.translated_text: [is] through inference of a property of the cause, like the transformation of fuel [inferred from] smoke. //9//

For the causal substances do not produce their effect merely because they are complete, since the production of the effect depends on the transformation of the capacities born of the aggregate. And because of the possibility of obstruction in the interval, the effect cannot be inferred. But since the capability does not depend on another substance, the inference is not contradicted. [One infers:] 'This causal aggregate is capable of producing the effect through the transformation of successive capacities, because of the absence of any other condition to be expected for the transformation of capacities.' Since the generation of capacity arises from merely the preceding homogeneous [cause], the capability of the aggregate, not depending on anything else, is stated [to be inferable]. Now, as for the cognition of color and such from something else—like taste—which is not a cause-and-effect relation, how [is that]? That too—

children.text:
00716 tatra hetur eva tathābhūto anumīyate / pravṛtta-śakti-rūpa-upādāna-
00717 kāraṇa-sahakāri-pratyayo hi rasa-hetū rasaṃ janayati / indhana-vikāra-
00718 viśeṣa-upādāna-hetu-sahakāri-pratyaya-agni-dhūma-janana-vat / tathā
00719 hi /
00720 śakti-pravṛttyā /
00721 sva-kāraṇasya phala-utpādanaṃ praty ābhimukhyena
00801 na vinā rasaḥ sa eva anya-kāraṇam /
00802 rūpa-upādāna-hetūnāṃ pravṛtti-kāraṇam / sā api rasa-upādāna-kāraṇa-pravṛttī
00803 rūpa-upādāna-kāraṇa-pravṛtti-sahakāriṇī / tasmād yathābhūtād heto
00804 rasa utpannas tathābhūtam anumāpayan rūpam anumāpayati
00805 ity /
00806 tatra api
00807 atīta-ekaikālānāṃ gatis /
00808 na anāgatānāṃ vyabhicārāt
children.translated_text: but not of future ones, because of deviation
[from the rule].

children.text: 00810 tasmād iyam
children.translated_text: Therefore this

children.text: 00811 kārya-liṅgajā //10//
children.translated_text: [inference] is born from the mark of the effect. //10//

Therein, it is precisely the cause in such a state that is inferred. For the auxiliary condition that is the cause of taste, having the form of an active capacity [and] the material cause, produces the taste—like the production of smoke by fire, which is the auxiliary condition having [as its material cause] a particular transformation of fuel [as] the material cause. Thus: through the activation of capacity—the orientation of its own cause toward producing the effect—without that, there is no taste; that itself is the other cause, the cause of the activation of the material causes of color. And that activation of the material cause of taste is the co-operative condition for the activation of the material cause of color. Therefore, the taste produced from the cause in such a state, by indicating such a cause, indicates the color. And therein too, the cognition of those [properties] whose individual moments are past [is possible],

children.text:
00812 tena na anyo hetur gamako asti / apratibaddha-svabhāvasya avinābhāva-
00813 niyama-abhāvāt / etena pipīlika-utsaraṇa-matsya-vikāra-āder
00814 varṣa-ādy-anumānam uktam / tatra api bhūta-pariṇāma eva varṣa-hetuḥ
00815 pipīlika-ādi saṃkṣobha-ādi-hetur iti /
children.translated_text: and the cause of the agitation and the like of ants and so forth.

children.text: 00816 hetunā tv asamagreṇa yat kāryam anumīyate /
children.translated_text: But that effect which is inferred from an incomplete cause—

children.text: 00817 śeṣavat tad asāmarthyād dehād rāga-anumāna-vat //11//
children.translated_text: that, like the <s>śeṣavat</s> (residual inference), due to incapability, is like the inference of passion from the body. //11//

Therefore, there is no other indicative reason. Because there is no invariable concomitance for something whose essential nature is not restricted. By this, the inference of rain and the like from the swarming of ants, the behavior of fish, and so forth is explained. There too, precisely the transformation of elements is the cause of rain,

children.text:
00818 samagrāṇy eva hi kāraṇāni yogyatām apy anumāpayanty asamagrasya
00819 ekānta-asāmarthyāt / yathā deha-indriya-buddhibhyo rāga-ādy-anumānam /
00820 ātma-ātmīya-abhiniveśa-pūrvakā hi rāga-ādayo ayoniśo-manaskāra-
00821 pūrvakatvāt sarva-doṣa-utpatteḥ / deha-ādīnāṃ hetutve api
00822 na kevalānāṃ sāmarthyam asti iti / vipakṣa-vṛtter adṛṣṭāv api
00823 śeṣavad-anumānāt saṃśayaḥ / tathā
00901 vipakṣe adṛṣṭi-mātreṇa kārya-sāmānya-darśanāt /
children.translated_text: merely by non-observation in dissimilar instances, due to the observation of the general [class of] effects,

children.text: 00902 hetu-jñānaṃ pramāṇa-ābhaṃ vacanād rāgita-ādi-vat //12//
children.translated_text: the knowledge of the reason is pseudo-valid, like [the inference of] passion and the like from speech, based on [mere] testimony. //12//

For only complete causes indicate capability as well, since an incomplete [cause] has absolutely no capacity. Just as the inference of passion and the like from body, sense organs, and intellect. For passion and the like are preceded by attachment to self and what belongs to self, because all afflictions arise from <s>ayoniśo-manaskāra</s> (improper mental attention). Even though the body and the like are causes, they alone do not have the capacity. Even when non-occurrence in the dissimilar instances is not observed, there is doubt because of <s>śeṣavat</s> inference. Thus—

children.text:
00903 na hi rāga-ādīnām eva kāryaṃ spandana-vacana-ādayaḥ vaktukāmatā-
00904 sāmānya-hetutvāt / sa eva rāga iti cet iṣṭatvān na kiṃcid bādhitaṃ
00905 syāt / nitya-sukha-ātma-ātmīya-darśana-ākṣiptaṃ sāsrava-dharma-viṣayaṃ
00906 cetaso abhiṣvaṅgaṃ rāgam āhuḥ / na evaṃ karuṇā-ādayo anyathā
00907 api sambhavād iti nivedayiṣyāmaḥ / atra yathā rakto bravīti
00908 tathā virakto api iti vacana-mātrād apratipattiḥ / na api viśeṣāt /
00909 abhiprāyasya durbodhatvāt / vyavahāra-saṃkareṇa sarveṣāṃ vyabhicārāt /
00910 prayojana-abhāvād avyāhāra iti cet na parārthatvāt /
00911 na yukto vīta-rāgatvād iti cet na karuṇā api vṛtteḥ / sa eva
00912 rāga iti cet / iṣṭam / aviparyāsa-samudbhavān na doṣaḥ / asaty
00913 apy ātma-grahe duḥkha-viśeṣa-darśana-mātreṇa abhyāsa-bala-utpādinī
00914 bhavaty eva karuṇā / tathā hi / sattva-dharma-ādy-ālambanā maitry-ādaya
00915 iṣyante / etāś ca sajātīya-abhyāsa-vṛttayo na rāga-apekṣiṇyaḥ /
00916 na evaṃ rāga-ādayo viparyāsa-abhāve abhāvāt / kāruṇikasya api
00917 niṣphala ārambho aviparyāsād iti cet / na / parārthasya eva
00918 phalatvena iṣṭatvāt / icchā-lakṣaṇatvāt phalasya / sarvathā abhūta-
00919 asamāropān nirdoṣaḥ / tad-anyena doṣavattva-sādhane na kiṃcid
00920 aniṣṭam / vaktary ātmani rāga-ādi-darśanena anyatra tad-anumāne
00921 atiprasaṅgaḥ / vyabhicārāt / ananya-anumāne iha avyabhicāra iti
01001 ko niścayaḥ / karaṇa-guṇa-vaktukāmate hi vacanam anumāpayet /
01002 rāga-utpādana-yogyatā-rahite vacana-adarśanāt tad-anumāne
01003 atiprasaṅgaḥ uktaḥ / rāgasya anupayoge kathaṃ tac-śaktir upayujyate /
01004 śakty-upayoge hi sa eva upayuktaḥ syāt tac ca na asti ity uktam /
01005 tasmān nāntarīyakam eva kāryaṃ kāraṇam anumāpayati tat-
01006 pratibandhāt na anyad vipakṣe adarśane api / sarva-darśino hi darśana-
01007 vyāvṛttiḥ sarvatra abhāvaṃ gamayet / kvacit tathā dṛṣṭānām
01008 api deśa-kāla-saṃskāra-bhedena anyathā adarśanād / yathā āmalakyaḥ
01009 kṣīra-avasekena madhura-phalā bhavanti / na ca evaṃ bahulaṃ dṛśyante /
01010 tena evaṃ syād yuktaṃ vaktum mādṛśo vaktā rāgī iti
01011 rāga-utpatti-pratyaya-viśeṣeṇa ātma-darśana-ayoniśo-manaskāreṇa yogāt /
01012 tadā apy apārthako vacana-udāhāraḥ / tasmād vipakṣe adṛṣṭir ahetuḥ /
01013 na ca adarśana-mātreṇa vipakṣe avyabhicāritā /
children.translated_text: And mere non-observation in the dissimilar instance does not [establish] non-deviation [of the reason],

children.text: 01014 sambhāvya-vyabhicāratvāt sthālī-taṇḍula-pāka-vat //13//
children.translated_text: because of the possibility of deviation, like the cooking of rice in a pot. //13//

For trembling, speech, and such are not exclusively the effects of passion and the like, since the desire to speak is a general cause. If [one says] 'that itself is passion'—since that is accepted [by you], nothing would be refuted. They call passion the mind's attachment toward the objects of <s>sāsrava dharma</s> (defiled phenomena), which is impelled by the perception of self, permanent happiness, and what belongs to self. Compassion and the like are not like this, since they can arise otherwise too—this we shall explain. Here, just as one who is passionate speaks, so too does one who is dispassionate—hence from mere speech, there is no ascertainment. Nor from any distinguishing feature, because the intention is difficult to discern. Because of the confusion of conventional usage, there is deviation in all cases. If [one objects that] there would be no utterance due to the absence of purpose—no, because it is for the benefit of others. If [one says] it is improper due to freedom from passion—no, because compassion too motivates action. If [one says] that itself is passion—accepted. Since it arises from non-error, there is no fault. Even without grasping a self, compassion arises merely from the perception of particular suffering, generated by the force of habituation. For <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) and the like are accepted as having sentient beings and <s>dharma</s> and the like as their objects. And these, being activities of homogeneous practice, do not depend on passion. Passion and the like are not like this, because they are absent in the absence of error. If [one objects that] even for a compassionate one, the undertaking is fruitless because of non-error—no, because the benefit of others itself is accepted as the fruit, since fruit has the character of desire. Since there is no superimposition of what is unreal in any way, [the compassionate one] is faultless. In proving faultiness by something other than that, nothing undesirable [follows]. In inferring passion and the like in the speaker himself [and then extending it] elsewhere, there is overextension, because of deviation. In the inference of nothing else, what certainty is there of non-deviation here? For speech may indicate the [speaker's] qualities and desire to speak. Since speech is not observed in one devoid of the capability to produce passion, the overextension in inferring that [passion] has been stated. If passion is of no use, how is its capacity used? For if the capacity were used, that [passion] itself would be used—and that is not the case, as stated. Therefore, only an indispensable effect indicates the cause, because of its restriction to that [cause], and nothing else—even when non-observation in the dissimilar instance [obtains]. For the exclusion from observation by one who sees all would indicate absence everywhere. Even for those observed somewhere in a particular way, there is non-observation in a different form due to differences in place, time, and conditioning—just as <s>āmalakī</s> (gooseberry) fruits become sweet by being watered with milk. And this is not commonly observed. Therefore, it would be proper to say thus: 'A speaker like me is passionate'—because of the connection with the particular condition for the arising of passion, namely the perception of self and improper mental attention. Even then, the example of speech is pointless. Therefore, mere non-observation in the dissimilar instance is not a [valid] reason.

children.text:
01015 na hi bahulaṃ pakva-darśane api sthāly-antargamana-mātreṇa pākaḥ
01016 sidhyati / vyabhicāra-darśanāt / evaṃ tu syād evaṃ svabhāvā
01017 etat-samāna-pāka-hetavaḥ pakvā iti / anyathā tu śeṣavad etad anumānaṃ
01018 vyabhicāri / kiṃ punar etac śeṣavat /
01019 yasya adarśana-mātreṇa vyatirekaḥ pradarśyate /
children.translated_text: That whose negative concomitance is demonstrated merely by non-observation—

children.text: 01020 tasya saṃśaya-hetutvāc śeṣavat tad udāhṛtam //14//
children.translated_text: since it is a cause of doubt, it is called <s>śeṣavat</s> (residual). //14//

For even though cooking is frequently observed, mere entry into a pot does not establish cooking, because deviation is observed. Rather, it would be [correct to say]: 'Those having such a nature, being causes of cooking similar to this, are cooked.' Otherwise, this inference would be inconclusive, like <s>śeṣavat</s>. But what then is this <s>śeṣavat</s>?

children.text:
01021 sa tasya vyatireko na niścita iti vipakṣe vṛttir āśaṅkyeta / vyatireka-
01022 sādhanasya adarśana-mātrasya saṃśaya-hetutvāt / na sarva-anupalabdhir
01023 gamikā / tasmād eka-nivṛttyā anya-nivṛttim icchatā tayoḥ
01024 kaścit svabhāvapratibandho apy eṣṭavyaḥ / anyathā agamako
01025 hetuḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: would be non-indicative.

children.text: 01026 hetos triṣu api rūpeṣu niścayas tena varṇitaḥ /
children.translated_text: The ascertainment regarding all three forms of the reason has thus been described,

children.text: 01027 asiddha-viparīta-artha-vyabhicāri-vipakṣataḥ //15//
children.translated_text: in contrast to the unestablished, the one with a contrary meaning, and the inconclusive. //15//

Its negative concomitance is not ascertained, so occurrence in the dissimilar instance may be suspected—because the mere non-observation that proves the negative concomitance is a cause of doubt. Not every non-perception is indicative. Therefore, by one who wishes to establish the cessation of one thing through the cessation of another, some essential-nature restriction between the two must also be accepted; otherwise, the reason

children.text:
01028 na hy asati pratibandhe anvaya-vyatireka-niścayo asti / tena tam
01101 eva darśayan niścayam āha / tatra anvayasya niścayena viruddha-
01102 tat pakṣyāṇāṃ nirāsaḥ / vyatirekasya anaikāntikasya tat-pakṣasya ca
01103 śeṣavad-ādeḥ / dvayor ity eka-siddha-pratiṣedhaḥ / prasiddha-vacanena
01104 sandigdhayoḥ śeṣavad-asādhāraṇayoḥ sapakṣa-vipakṣayor
01105 api / anyathā hy asati pratibandhe adarśana-mātreṇa vyatireke /
01106 vyabhicāri-vipakṣeṇa vaidharmya-vacanaṃ ca yat /
01107 yad āha / eṣa tāvan nyāyo yad ubhayaṃ vaktavyam viruddha- anaikāntika-
01108 pratipakṣeṇa iti / vaidharmya-vacanam anaikāntika-pratipakṣeṇa /
01110 yady adṛṣṭi-phalaṃ tac ca /
children.translated_text: If that [dissimilarity statement] has non-observation as its result—

children.text: 01111 yadi tena vipakṣe adarśanaṃ khyāpyate /
children.translated_text: if by that, non-observation in the dissimilar instance is proclaimed—

children.text: 01112 tad anukte api gamyate //16//
children.translated_text: that is understood even without being stated. //16//

For without a necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>), there is no certainty of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). Therefore, showing that very certainty, he states: By the certainty of positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), the exclusion of the contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>) and those belonging to its class [is established]. By [the certainty of] negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), [the exclusion] of the inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) and its class, such as the "remainder" (<s>śeṣavat</s>) and so on. "Of both" means the negation of [fallacies] established by either one alone. By the word "established" (<s>prasiddha</s>), [also] of the doubtful ones—the "remainder" and the "uncommon" (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>)—in both the similar and dissimilar instances. For otherwise, without a necessary connection, merely through non-observation of negative concomitance— "And the statement of dissimilarity with an inconclusive contrary instance"— As he says: This is the principle that both must be stated, as a counter to the contradictory and inconclusive—the statement of dissimilarity is the counter to the inconclusive.

children.text:
01113 na hi tasya prāg darśana-bhrāntir yā vacanena nivartyeta / smṛtir
01201 vāca-adarśane kriyata iti cet / darśanaṃ khalv apratīyamānam
01202 anaṅgam iti yuktaṃ tatra smaraṇa-ādhānam / adarśanaṃ tu darśana-
01203 abhāvaḥ / sa darśanena bādhyate / tad-abhāve tu siddha eva ity apārthakaṃ
01204 tat-siddhaye vacanaṃ / na vai anupalambhamānasya
01205 tāvatā na asti iti bhavati tad-arthaṃ vacanam iti cet /
children.translated_text: it does not follow that "it does not exist" just from that much—if the statement is for that purpose,

children.text: 01206 na ca na asti iti vacanāt tan na asty eva yathā yadi /
children.translated_text: nor does it not exist merely because of the statement "it does not exist"; if

children.text: 01207 na asti sa khyāpyate nyāyas tadā na asti iti gamyate //17//
children.translated_text: that principle—"it does not exist"—is proclaimed, then "it does not exist" is [already] understood. //17//

For there is no prior error of observation on his part that would be removed by a statement. If it be said that recollection is produced regarding non-observation—indeed, observation that is not being cognized is irrelevant, so it is proper to establish recollection in that case. But non-observation is the absence of observation. That is contradicted by observation. In its absence, however, [non-observation] is already established—therefore a statement for establishing it is pointless. Surely for one who does not perceive [something],

children.text:
01208 yady anupalabhamāno na asti iti na pratyeti vacanād api na eva pratyeṣyati /
01209 tad api hy anupalambham eva khyāpayati / na ca eka-anupalambho
01210 anya-abhāvaṃ sādhayaty atiprasaṅgāt / na ca tena
01211 na asti iti vacanāt tathā bhavaty atiprasaṅgāt / tat kathaṃ vaidharmya-vacanena
01212 anaikāntika-parihāraḥ / tasmād vyāvṛttim icchatā
01213 tatra nyāyo vaktavyaḥ yato asya vyāvṛttam iti bhavati /
01214 nanu tad-abhāve anupalambhāt siddhā vyāvṛttiḥ /
01215 yady adṛṣṭyā nivṛttiḥ syāc śeṣavad vyabhicāri kim /
01216 yathā pakvāny etāni phalāny evaṃ-rasāni vā rūpa-aviśeṣād eka-śākhā-
01217 prabhavatvād vā upayukta-vad iti / atra api vivakṣita-aśeṣa-pakṣīkaraṇe
01218 hetoḥ sādhya-abhāve anupalambho asti iti kathaṃ vyabhicāraḥ /
01219 pratyakṣa-bādhā-āśaṅkā vyabhicāra ity eke / na / pakṣīkṛta-
01220 viṣaye abhāvāt / kadācid bhaved iti cet / tathā śaṅkāyām atiprasaṅgaḥ /
01221 anyatra apy abhāva-niyama-abhāvāt / vṛttaṃ pramāṇaṃ bādhakam /
01222 avṛtta-bādhane sarvatra anāśvāsaḥ / vyatirekas tu siddha
01223 eva sādhanam iti tathā abhāva-niścayam apekṣate / anupalambhāt tu
01224 kvacid abhāva-siddhāv apy apratibaddhasya tad-abhāve sarvatra
01225 abhāva-asiddheḥ saṃśayād avyatireko vyabhicāraḥ śeṣavataḥ /
01226 kiṃ ca /
01301 vyatireky api hetuḥ syān /
01302 na idaṃ nirātmakaṃ jīvaccharīram aprāṇa-ādimattva-prasaṅgād iti /
01303 nirātmakeṣu ghaṭa-ādiṣu dṛṣṭeṣu prāṇa-ādy-adarśanāt tan-nivṛtty-
01304 ātma-gatiḥ syāt / adṛśya-anupalambhād abhāva-asiddhau ghaṭa-ādīnāṃ
01305 nairātmya-asiddheḥ prāṇa-āder anivṛttiḥ / abhyupagamāt siddham
01306 iti cet / katham idānīm ātma-siddhiḥ / parasya apy apramāṇikā
01307 kathaṃ nairātmya-siddhiḥ / abhyupagamena ca sātmaka-anātmakau
01308 vibhajya tatra abhāvena gamakatvaṃ kathayatā āgamikatvam
01309 ātmani pratipannaṃ syāt / na anumeyatvam / tasmād adarśane apy
01310 ātmano-nivṛtty-asiddheḥ / tan-nivṛttau kvacin nivṛttāv api prāṇa-ādīnām
01311 apratibandhāt / sarvatra nivṛtty-asiddher agamakatvam /
01312 yā apy asiddhi-yojanā tathā sapakṣe sann asann ity evam-ādiṣv api
01313 yathāyogam udāharyam ity evam-ādikā / sā api
01314 na vācyā asiddhi-yojanā //18//
children.translated_text: If one who does not perceive [something] does not cognize that "it does not exist," he will not cognize it even from a statement either. For that [statement] too merely proclaims non-perception. And one non-perception does not establish the absence of another, because of over-extension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>). Nor does it become so merely from the statement "it does not exist," because of over-extension. Then how is the inconclusive [fallacy] remedied by a statement of dissimilarity? Therefore, one who wishes to establish exclusion must state the principle [of necessary connection] there, whereby [one knows] that this has been excluded. [Objection:] But exclusion is established by non-perception in the absence of that. If cessation were [established] merely by non-observation, how could the "remainder" (<s>śeṣavat</s>) be inconclusive? For example: "These fruits are ripe, being of such taste, because of no difference in color, or because of originating from the same branch, like those already consumed." Here too, when the intended [property] is made to belong entirely to the thesis, there is non-perception of the reason in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s> (property to be proved)—so how is there inconclusiveness? Some say the suspicion of contradiction by perception constitutes inconclusiveness. No—because [such contradiction] is absent in the subject that has been made part of the thesis. If [it be said] it might occur sometimes—then with such suspicion there would be over-extension, since the restriction of absence is not established elsewhere either. An [already] occurred <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) is the contradicting [evidence]. If something that has not occurred could contradict, there would be no confidence anywhere. But negative concomitance, being itself the means of proof, thus requires certainty of absence [in the dissimilar instance]. However, from non-perception, even if absence is established somewhere, since the absence of that which is not necessarily connected is not established everywhere due to its absence [in the dissimilar instance], the doubt [constitutes] non-exclusion, which is the inconclusiveness of the "remainder." Moreover—a reason that has negative concomitance could also [be inconclusive]: "This living body is not without a self, because otherwise it would absurdly lack vital breath and the like." Since in selfless things like pots, vital breath and the like are not observed, the understanding of the self would come from their cessation. But since absence is not established due to non-perception of the imperceptible, and since the selflessness of pots and the like is not established, vital breath and the like are not negated. If it be said that it is established by acceptance—then how now is the self established? For the other party too, how is selflessness established without valid means? And by one who, having divided [things] into those with a self and those without by acceptance, and declaring inferability through absence in the latter, the self would be accepted on the basis of scripture (<s>āgama</s>), not inferability. Therefore, even with non-observation, since the cessation of the self is not established—and even if there were cessation somewhere, since vital breath and the like are not necessarily connected [with it]—since cessation everywhere is not established, [the reason] is non-probative. As for the formulation of non-establishment applied also in [examples like] "present in the similar instance, absent or present" and so on, as appropriate—that formulation of non-establishment also need not be stated. //18//

children.text:
01315 anupalambha eva saṃśayāt / upalambhe tad-abhāvāt / anupalambhāc
01316 ca vyatireka iti saṃśayito anivāryaḥ syāt / yathāyoga-vacanāt
01317 anivārita eva iti cet / na / ya eva tu ubhaya-niścita-vācī ity ādi-vacanāt /
01318 tena anupalambhe api saṃśayād anivṛttiṃ manyamānaḥ tat-pratiṣedham
01319 āha / kiṃ ca /
01401 viśeṣasya vyavaccheda-hetutā syād adarśanāt /
01402 śrāvaṇatvasya api nitya-anityayor adarśanād vyāvṛttir iti tad-vyavaccheda-
01403 hetutā syāt / na hi tad-vyāvṛtter anyad vyavacchedanam /
01404 avyavacchedas tu kutaścid vyāvṛtter eva aniścayāt / yo hi yatra
01405 na asti iti niścitaḥ sa bhavaṃs tad-abhāvaṃ kathaṃ na gamayet /
01406 pramāṇa-antara-bādhā cen /
01407 atha api syād ubhaya-vyavacchede pramāṇa-antaraṃ bādhakam asti /
01408 anyonya-vyavaccheda-rūpāṇām eka-vyavacchedena anya-vidhānād
01409 apratiṣedhaḥ / vidhi-pratiṣedhayor virodhāt /
01410 na idānīṃ nāstitā adṛśaḥ //19//
children.translated_text: Non-perception itself [involves] doubt. In [the case of] perception, due to its absence. And since negative concomitance is [established] from non-perception, what is doubted cannot be removed. If it be said that from the phrase "as appropriate" it is indeed not removed—no, because of the statement "that which expresses certainty of both" and so forth. Therefore, one who thinks that there is no exclusion even in non-perception, due to doubt—he states the refutation of that. Moreover:

children.text:
01411 na evam adarśanaṃ pramāṇaṃ bādhā-asambhavāt /
01412 tathā anyatra api sambhāvyaṃ pramāṇa-antara-bādhanam /
01413 lakṣaṇa-yukte bādhā-asambhave tal-lakṣaṇam eva dūṣitaṃ syād iti
01414 sarvatra anāśvāsaḥ / anumāna-viṣaye api pratyakṣa-anumāna-virodha-
01415 darśanād anāśvāsa-prasaṅga iti cet / na / yathokte asambhavāt /
01416 sambhavinaś ca atal-lakṣaṇatvāt / viruddhāvyabhicāry-avacanam iti
01417 cet / anumāna-viṣaye avacanād iṣṭam / viṣayaṃ ca asya nivedayiṣyāmaḥ /
01418 kiṃ ca /
children.translated_text: Moreover—

children.text: 01419 dṛṣṭā ayuktir adṛṣṭeś ca syāt sparśasya avirodhinī //20//
children.translated_text: The observed impropriety and that of the unobserved would be non-contradictory with regard to touch. //20//

Non-observation [cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge] because the impossibility of contradiction [by other means]. Likewise, the contradiction by another means of knowledge should be considered possible elsewhere too. If contradiction is impossible when the defining characteristics are met, then the very defining characteristic would be vitiated—hence no confidence anywhere. If it be said that there would be a similar lack of confidence in the domain of inference, since contradiction between perception and inference is observed—no, because [such contradiction] is impossible as stated. And because what is possible does not have those defining characteristics. If it be said that there is no statement of the contradictory-inconclusive—[we reply:] this is as desired, since there is no statement in the domain of inference. And we shall indicate its domain.

children.text:
01420 yadi hy anupalambhena abhāvaḥ sidhyet / yad āha / yady adarśana-
01421 mātreṇa dṛṣṭebhyaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ kriyate / na ca so api yukta
01501 iti / katham ayuktaḥ / anupalambhād abhāva-siddheḥ / nanu upalabdhi-
01502 lakṣaṇa-prāpteḥ sparśasya yukta eva pratiṣedhaḥ / na yuktaḥ /
01503 dṛśya-tat-svabhāva-viṣaya-mātra-apratiṣedhāt / pṛthivy-ādi sāmānyena
01504 gṛhītvā ayaṃ pratiṣedham āha / tatra ca tūla-upala-pallava-
01505 ādiṣu tad-bhāve api sparśa-bheda-darśanāt asya api kvacid viśeṣe
01506 sambhava-āśaṅkayā bhavitavyam iti sarvatra adarśana-mātreṇa ayuktaḥ
01507 pratiṣedha iti / evam ācāryīyaḥ kaścid anupalambhād abhāvaṃ
01508 bruvāṇa upālabdhaḥ / api ca /
01509 deśa-ādi-bhedād dṛśyante bhinnā dravyeṣu śaktayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Due to differences of place and the like, different powers are seen in substances;

children.text: 01510 tatra eka-dṛṣṭyā na anyatra yuktas tad-bhāva-niścayaḥ //21//
children.translated_text: therefore, from observation in one [instance], the certainty of its presence elsewhere is not proper. //21//

If absence were established by non-perception—as he states: "If negation from observed [things] is made merely by non-observation"—"nor is even that proper." How is it improper? Because absence is established by non-perception. But surely the negation of touch is proper since it meets the conditions for perception (<s>upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti</s>). [Reply:] It is not proper, because only what is perceptible and of that nature is not negated [by non-perception alone]. Taking earth and the like in general, he states this negation. But there, since differences of touch are observed in cotton, stones, sprouts, and the like even when [earth] is present, one must suspect the possibility [of different touch] in some particular case here too—therefore negation merely from non-observation everywhere is improper. Thus a certain follower of the teacher (<s>ācārya</s>), asserting absence from non-perception, was criticized. Furthermore—

children.text:
01511 yadi kathaṃcid vipakṣe adarśana-mātreṇa apratibaddhasya api tad-
01512 avyabhicāraḥ / kvacid deśe kānicid dravyāṇi kathaṃcid dṛṣṭāni
01513 punar anyathā anyatra dṛśyante / yathā kāścid oṣadhayaḥ kṣetra-
01514 viśeṣe viśiṣṭa-rasa-vīrya-vipākā bhavanti / na anyatra / tathā kāla-
01515 saṃskāra-bhedāt / na ca tad-deśais tathā dṛṣṭā iti sarvās tattvena
01516 tathābhūtāḥ sidhyanti / guṇa-antarāṇāṃ kāraṇa-antara-apekṣatvāt /
01517 viśeṣa-hetv-abhāve tu syād anumānam / yathā adṛṣṭa-kartṛkam api
01518 vākyaṃ puruṣa-saṃskāra-pūrvakam iti / vākyeṣu viśeṣa-abhāvāt /
01519 sarva-prakārāṇāṃ puruṣaiḥ karaṇasya darśanāt / na evam asambhavad-
01520 viśeṣa-hetavaḥ puruṣā yena vacana-ādeḥ kiṃcin-mātra-sādharmyāt
01521 sarva-ākāra-sāmyam anumīyeta / sarva-guṇeṣu viśeṣa-darśanāt /
01522 saṃskāra-bhedena viśeṣa-pratipatteḥ / tadvad anyasya api sambhavād /
01523 asambhava-anumāne ca bādhaka-hetv-abhāvāt vairāgya-adṛṣṭeḥ
01524 adṛṣṭena ca bādhyabādhakabhāva-asiddheḥ / rāga-ādy-avyabhicāri-
01525 kārya-abhāvāt / sambhave api viśeṣāṇāṃ draṣṭum aśakyatvāt /
01601 tādṛśāṃ ca apratikṣepa-arthatvāt / na evaṃ vākyāni dṛśya-viśeṣatvāt /
01602 adṛśyatve apy adṛṣṭa-viśeṣāṇāṃ vijātīyatva-upagama-virodhāt / tad-
01603 viśeṣāṇām anyatra api śakya-kriyatvāt / pratyakṣāṇāṃ śabdānām
01604 apratyakṣa-svabhāva-abhāvāt / bhrānti-nimitta-abhāvāt / bādhaka-abhāvād
01605 bhrānty-asiddheḥ / puruṣeṣu viśeṣa-darśanasya bādhakatvād
01606 asamānam / parabhāva-bhūtasya ca vākya-viśeṣasya atad-viśeṣatvāt /
01607 tad abhinna-svabhāvānāṃ sarveṣāṃ puruṣa-kriyā na vā kasyacit /
children.translated_text: Therefore, either the action of a person [pertains to] all those of undifferentiated nature, or to none whatsoever.

children.text: 01608 kiṃ ca /
children.translated_text: Moreover—

children.text: 01609 ātma-mṛc-cetanā-ādīnāṃ yo abhāvasya aprasādhakaḥ /
children.translated_text: That very non-perception which does not establish the absence of self, clay-consciousness, and the like—

children.text: 01610 sa eva anupalambhaḥ kiṃ hetv-abhāvasya sādhakaḥ //22//
children.translated_text: how can it establish the absence of a cause? //22//

If somehow, merely by non-observation in the dissimilar instance, non-deviation is [established] even for something not necessarily connected— [consider that] certain substances observed in a certain way in a certain place are seen differently elsewhere. Just as certain herbs have distinctive taste, potency, and post-digestive effect in a particular region, but not elsewhere. Likewise due to differences of time and processing. And it cannot be established that because they are observed thus in those regions, all are truly of that nature—because other qualities depend on other causes. But when there is an absence of a cause for distinction, inference would be valid—as, for example, even a sentence whose author is unknown presupposes human composition—because there is no distinction among sentences and because all types are seen to be produced by persons. But persons are not [such that] impossible distinguishing causes [are absent], whereby from mere partial similarity of speech and the like, complete identity in all respects could be inferred—because distinction is observed in all qualities, because particular [qualities] are apprehended through differences of conditioning, and because such [conditioning] is possible for others too. And in inferring impossibility, because there is no contradicting reason, because of the non-observation of detachment (<s>vairāgya</s>), and because the contradicting-contradicted relationship is not established through the unobserved. Because of the absence of effects that invariably accompany desire and the like. Even if distinctions were possible, because of their unobservability. And because [non-perception of invisible things] does not serve to negate such [distinctions]. Sentences are not like this, because their distinctions are observable. Even if unobservable, because accepting the different nature of unobserved distinctions contradicts [their being of a different class]. Because the distinctive features of those [sentences] can be produced elsewhere too. Because perceptible words do not lack an imperceptible nature. Because there is no cause for error. Because absence is not established due to the absence of a contradicting [cognition]. Because the observation of distinction among persons serves as a contradicting [cognition], [the cases are] not equivalent. And because the particular sentence, which belongs to another's existence, does not have the distinctive features of that [inference].

children.text:
01611 anupalambhaṃ ca asya pramāṇayata ātma-vādo nirālambaḥ syāt /
01612 apratyakṣatvād ātmanas tat-kārya-asiddheḥ / indriya-ādīnāṃ tu
01613 vijñāna-kāryasya kādācitkatvāt sāpekṣya-siddhyā prasiddhir ucyate /
01614 kim apy asya kāraṇam asti iti / ca tv evaṃbhūtam iti /
01615 na evaṃ sukha-ādi-kāryaṃ prasādhitaṃ kaṃcid arthaṃ puṣṇāti /
01616 yena kenacit kāraṇavattva-abhyupagamāt / tathā ca anupalambha
01617 eva ātmanaḥ syāt / taṃ tena pratyācakṣāṇaḥ kim iti prativyūḍho
01618 anupalambhasya asādhanatvād iti / katham asādhanaṃ vyatirekaṃ
01619 sādhayet / mṛdaḥ khalv api kaścic caitanyam anupalabhyamānam
01620 api icchann adarśanād vacana-āder vyāvṛttim āha / dadhy-ādikaṃ
01621 ca aparaḥ kṣīra-ādiṣv apara-artheṣu saṃghātatva-adarśanād vyatirekam /
01622 ko hy atra niyamaḥ saṃhatair avaśyaṃ parārthair bhavitavyam iti /
01623 asty eva upalambho dadhy-ādīnāṃ kṣīra-ādiṣv anumānam /
01624 aśaktād anutpatteḥ / atha kā iyaṃ śaktiḥ sa eva bhāvaḥ
01625 uta anyad eva kiṃcit / sa eva cet tathā eva upalabhyeta viśeṣa-abhāvāt /
01626 anyac cet katham anya-bhāve tad asti / upacāra-mātraṃ tu syād
01627 ity ayam eṣāṃ paraspara-vyāghātaḥ /
01628 tasmāt tan-mātra-sambandhaḥ svabhāvo bhāvam eva vā /
01629 nivartayet /
01630 yathā vṛkṣaḥ śiṃśapāṃ / śākhā-ādimad-viśeṣasya eva kasyacit tathā-
01701 prasiddheḥ sa tasya svabhāvaḥ / svaṃ ca svabhāvaṃ parityajya
01702 kathaṃ bhāvo bhavet / svabhāvasya eva bhāvatvād iti tasya svabhāvapratibandhād
01703 avyabhicāraḥ /
children.translated_text: its invariable [absence]. //

children.text: 01704 kāraṇaṃ vā kāryam avyabhicārataḥ //23//
children.translated_text: Or a cause [negates] an effect, through non-deviation. //23//

And if one accepts non-perception as a valid means for this, the doctrine of the self (<s>ātmavāda</s>) would be without foundation—because the self is not perceptible and its effects are not established. But for the senses and the like, since the effect of consciousness is occasional, [their causal status] is said to be established through the establishment of their dependence [on conditions]—[one concludes] that it has some cause. But it is not [established] that it is of this [particular] nature. Thus, the established effect of pleasure and the like does not support any [particular] object, because causal status is accepted for just anything. And so there would be mere non-perception of the self. One who rejects that [non-perception] by means of it [i.e., non-perception]—how can he be refuted [by saying] that non-perception is non-probative? How can something non-probative establish negative concomitance? For someone, wishing [to establish] consciousness even of clay, though not perceived, asserts exclusion from speech and the like due to non-observation. And another [asserts] the negative concomitance of curds and the like from milk and the like, from non-observation of composition in other objects. For what rule is there that what is composed must necessarily serve another's purpose? There is indeed perception of curds and the like—[namely] inference [of them] in milk and the like—because [effects] do not arise from what lacks the capacity. Now what is this capacity? Is it the very nature [of the thing] or something else entirely? If it is the very nature, then it should be perceived in just that way, since there is no difference. If it is something else, how does it exist when the other thing exists? It would be mere figurative usage—this is the mutual contradiction among these [positions]. Therefore, only the connection with that alone—[namely] the intrinsic nature—would negate [the existence of] a thing, or [would negate]

Because:
The identity of nature and the causal relation are made known in the example, for one who does not know that.
They are made known—
For in the example, the identity of nature of the <s>sādhya-dharma</s> (property to be proved) is made known through its invariable connection with that alone, as being of that nature. The <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) is shown by means of the example that whatever produces an entity that is <s>kṛtaka</s> (produced), that produces an entity that is <s>anitya</s> (impermanent). Otherwise, since from the existence of one property there would be no restriction that another [property] must also exist, there would be the suspicion that the proving property deviates from the property to be proved. And by that <s>pramāṇa</s>, the invariable connection of the <s>sādhya-dharma</s> with that alone is made known. What is produced is produced from its own cause alone, and being thus produced, it is perishable—having the property of lasting only a moment. Because its being of that nature is negated from anything else. Or the causal relation is demonstrated by means of the example that [the effect] exists only when that [cause] exists. When, for another object, it is well-known that in the identity of nature or in the causal relation, in the absence of impermanence, producedness does not exist, and in the absence of fire, [there is no] smoke. For that [property] is either its essential nature or its cause. How could it exist without its own essential nature or cause?

children.translated_text: For those two [types of reasons], when ceasing, cause the cessation of what is essentially connected with them. Therefore, even one who wishes to prove the negation of some object should declare the cessation of the <s>hetu</s> or of a pervader of its essential nature as the logical reason. For without [essential] connection, how could the cessation of one establish the cessation of another?

children.text: 02003 yukta-upalabhasya tasya ca anupalambhanam //29//
children.translated_text: And the non-apprehension of that which fulfills the conditions of apprehension— //29//

As he stated: "Or by <s>arthāpatti</s>, through the demonstration of both by [stating] either one." Even there, considering that the demonstration of identity of nature and causal relation is by means of the example, he states that by <s>arthāpatti</s>, through stating one, the second is established. For when it is said "whatever is produced is impermanent," in the absence of any other meaning, it is clear that this is its essential nature, connected with that alone, seen by <s>pramāṇa</s>, due to the restriction of being of that nature. For one who knows that identity of nature, by <s>arthāpatti</s>, [the thought] "in the absence of impermanence, producedness does not exist" arises. For in the absence of an essential nature, there cannot be existence, due to non-difference. Otherwise, "it exists in the presence of that" would not hold at all. Likewise, when it is said "in its absence, it does not exist"—from that very [statement], one who knows the identity of nature [understands]: "For this is its essential nature, because of which in its absence it does not exist; otherwise there would be no logical connection." Thus, through the cognition of the identity of nature in each case, the recollection of positive concomitance arises. Likewise, when it is said "where there is smoke, there is fire"—smoke is an effect of fire, because of which fire necessarily exists [where there is] smoke. Otherwise, since there would be no restriction of invariable connection for a different thing, the entity would be independent. Therefore, even in the absence of that [cause], due to the completeness of its own nature, there would be no absence. But in the case of an effect, the cause necessarily exists. For this is precisely the causality of the cause—that in the presence of another thing, it contributes its own nature. And the effect too exists only in the presence of that [cause], and that [relation] exists in smoke. Therefore, for one who knows through positive concomitance that smoke is an effect [of fire], the cognition of negative concomitance—that in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist—arises from the meaning. Likewise, when it is said "in the absence of fire, there is no smoke," [the cognition] that fire necessarily exists [where there is] smoke—the cognition of positive concomitance arises from the meaning. For otherwise, in the absence of what would it not exist? Now, even in the absence of the property of being an effect of either permanent or impermanent things, auditory cognition does not exist in their absence. Indeed, it is not the case that it does not exist—because of doubt about [whether it arises] from precisely those [causes]. Otherwise, from what is ascertained as absent, how could there be doubt through the consideration of its being of that nature? Rather, it is only said "it does not exist" because there is no ascertainment of its existence. But when the causal relation between fire and smoke is not demonstrated by means of an example, then "where there is smoke, there is fire" would simply not hold, due to the absence of [essential] connection. How then could the establishment of negative concomitance—"in the absence of fire, there is no smoke"—arise from the meaning? Likewise, since the absence is not established through dissimilarity, the recollection of positive concomitance [would not arise]. Therefore, by means of the example, precisely this <s>svabhāvapratibandha</s> as described above is demonstrated—for the purpose of establishing [the existence of] the other when one is present, because of its impossibility in the absence of that.
Therefore, the absence of the essential nature of the <s>hetu</s> is also a <s>hetu</s> for the negation of something.

Thus [are] the intervening verses. Moreover:
For a property caused by something else would be entirely different. For when that [first thing] has come into being, [a property that is] not yet come into being, or one having a different cause, is not logically [its] essential nature. Indeed, this alone is the distinction or the cause of distinction among entities: the superimposition of contradictory properties and the difference of causes. If these two are not differentiators, then nothing would be different from anything, and the whole [universe] would be one substance. And then there would be simultaneous origination and destruction, and the utility of everything for everything. Otherwise, [the predicate] "is one" would simply not apply—or it would be [merely] a different name, since there would be a different meaning while accepting the difference of meaning, because it is so designated. Now, even if [impermanence is] not caused by something else, in the time of the entity's existence, impermanence—since it has not [separately] arisen—is equally not of that nature. But indeed there is no other [thing] called "impermanence" that would arise later. For that very entity, having the property of lasting [only] a moment, is impermanence. Even though the designation differs, we shall explain the reason as [the relation of] <s>dharmin</s> and <s>dharma</s>. But again, even one of dull intellect who sees this momentary-duration nature, this essential nature, as arising from its own cause alone, being deceived by the apprehension of existence, suspecting its continued existence at all times, does not ascertain [its impermanence]—or being deceived by the arising of a similar successor. From the ascertainment of those who observe the final moment: afterward, through non-apprehension of it, from the cognition that it has not persisted, the time of ascertainment [arrives], and then impermanence is established. Just as, even though the capacity to produce an effect belongs to the nature of the cause, for one who has not seen that effect, even upon seeing the cause, when the nature [of the causal relation] is not cognized, from seeing the effect, that cognition [arises]. Otherwise, impermanence would be an entirely different thing—if it were caused by something else or by nothing at all. And then the entity would not possess it, because of its non-utility. Or if there were utility, then it itself, being its own essential nature, would be impermanence—so what [need] for another? Or for one whose essential nature is unchanging, even when connected with something else, the existence of that nature would not arise. And that [impermanence], arising from something else, would be either a different property, a cause, or an effect. Because what has no cause-and-effect [relation] has no connection. In that case, inferring the entity would be impossible. Therefore:
