children.translated_text: Even one who thinks: 'How can there be a single expression for many without an undifferentiated object, since they are unequal, since an expression occurring in one does not generate cognition in another, since there would be over-extension if cognition arose without proximity, since assigning one word to those [many] would be futile without assignment to a single object, and since in the separate assignment of those having different natures, the divisions of what is thus enjoined would not be known?'—even for him, the word must be assigned by the world as 'there is one [thing],' or else that one [thing] makes this expression resonate through the power of the real entity itself. This is not so. Rather, certain words are assigned to certain [objects] for some purpose. If many [things] are useful in a single [context], that [group] must necessarily be enjoined there. In enjoining them separately one by one, there would be excessive cumbersomeness. Nor is it possible to enjoin its unique form that belongs to nothing else. Nor would this effort have any result. Rather, by this [single word], those objects that are fit [for that purpose] are to be enjoined. Whether they are enjoined by one word or by many—that is the freedom of the speaker. Thus this single expression, operating among many through the speaker's intention, does not deserve reproach. Nor is it incapable of operating [thus], because it is subject to volition. For if the user's volition [were lacking], how would it operate even in a single [case]? And given volition, who can prevent it [from operating] even among many? If [one says] it does not operate because of the absence of purpose—the purpose has been stated. The cognition from a single [word] among different [things] is due to the difference of purpose from what does not [serve that purpose]—that has been stated. But not because of oneness of nature. Since things whose natures are fixed each in its own way do not partake of each other's form—how could a word based on oneness of nature apply to different [things]?—this was stated before. But the exclusion from what does not [serve] that purpose is not contradicted among different [things]—so let that very identity of meaning be the cause for identity of words. Therefore, these [things] are said to be 'serving that purpose' and hence different from those not serving that purpose. But their production of that effect is nothing other than their difference from what is other than that. Just as in [the case of] the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention—or in [the case of] self, sense organ, mind, object, and the contact of those—[all of which] produce a single effect of visual cognition, when it is possible to enjoin by the generality of that effect 'whence visual cognition?', someone would assign a conventional expression for the sake of convenience of transaction—whether 'yara' or 'śasa' [as the name of] the cause of visual cognition—in order that all those causes of that [cognition] be apprehended at once. And there is no pervading form here—merely, those entities, by virtue of serving that purpose, are different from those not serving that purpose, so their very difference is their non-difference. And all words of this kind—for aggregates, continua, and particular states—those that collectively produce some single effect, since there is no distinction among them with respect to that [effect], the specific enjoining [of each] would be pointless; so for the purpose of apprehending all at once, the world assigns a single word to them, such as 'pot.' And those too, even though there is no distinction [between them and] their own kind or others, since they differ from those others by virtue of being components serving that purpose, they are apprehended without distinction from that [identity], because of [their] non-difference. Therein, 'the color and the like of the pot' also [means]: the colors and the like are of the nature of the pot, that is, colors and the like are capable of the particular effect of holding water and so on. Known by the name of accomplishing a general effect, they are known by the words 'color' and the like; qualified by the particular of being known by the name of accomplishing a particular effect, they are thus spoken of. But there is no other substance here with the characteristics described, because of the non-perception of such [a substance]. Even the singular number is for the purpose of indicating its single power, or is dependent on convention. Likewise, those that are particular causes and effects, [and] accomplish or are accomplished as some one [result], are also spoken of by words like 'rice' and the like, for which conventions have been established for the purpose of single apprehension—this should be stated as before. And those that are useful individually or collectively in some [context] are proclaimed by words denoting particular states, at once, for the purpose of apprehension—'having resistance' or 'having obstruction' and the like—by the generality of difference from what is other than that. Just as those [things] that produce a single effect, when being enjoined by that effect, are conventionally designated by words like 'pot' and the like, by [their] difference from what is other than that—so too with respect to causation, many [things are designated] by one [word] for the purpose of conventional practice alone. For example, <s>Śābaleya</s>, <s>Bāhuleya</s>, 'sound [produced] immediately after effort,' 'manufactured,' and so on. Likewise, through the negation of the effect of that [production]: 'not visual,' 'sound,' 'impermanent,' 'not-self,' and so on. Through the negation of the cause of that [production] too: 'ownerless,' 'empty,' and so on. Thus, other [cases] too should be stated as appropriate. In the case of words like 'empty,' 'impermanent,' and the like, the desired aspect is superimposed in cognition according to the hypothesis, and the designation is made through the exclusion of that [superimposed aspect]—because the operation of the cognition and the desire [underlying it] is shown by the division [of aspects]; for all word-meaning [works this way]. [Objections such as] 'the fault of the absence of a counter-thesis' and the like are agitations of the dull-witted and should be disregarded. Now: even though many [things], having a single occurrence, may have a single expression—

children.text: 07014 pravisarpataḥ /
children.translated_text: Since a permanent [entity] cannot be benefited, there is no container.

children.text: 07015 śaktis tad-deśa-jananaṃ kuṇḍa-āder badara-ādiṣu //144//

not only are things producing a single effect spoken of by a single word because of non-distinction from what is other than that, but even many [things] with a single occurrence might be spoken of by a single word—what contradiction would there be? It has been stated in response: because of the absence of what is accepted as perceivable—in [the case of] non-perception, or if [it were] perceivable, [then] designations, recognitions, and the like that are based on the perception of that would not occur—and so forth. Moreover: occurrence, containment, manifestation—[none of] these is reasonable in that [universal]. //143//

children.translated_text: because it persists even in the absence of that [substrate], due to its permanence.

children.text: 07130 sā apy ayuktā eva bheda-abheda-vivecane //145//
children.translated_text: That [persistence] too is not tenable when difference and non-difference are examined. //145//

The state of producing effects in the same location, for a heavy substance whose nature is to produce effects in different locations, is caused by the substrate. Therefore, the pot, cooperating with the preceding moment of that [substance], generating the effect of the jujube-fruit in that very [location], is called a substrate. Otherwise, even [the expression] 'the jujube-fruits are in this pot' would not be [possible]. This designation is not made on the basis of [the pot's] benefit [to the fruits]. What then? On the basis of contact. But is that contact of those two alone? Because it is produced from those two, or because of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>)? Does it inhere in only one, or is it produced [by both]? Due to its incapacity— what is incapable separately is of the same nature even when combined—therefore, since it does not benefit, it would not be [a substrate] through contact. [Objection:] The capacity [arises] from the origination of a distinction through the assistance of something other than that when combined. [Reply:] What is this benefit of those that have the nature of not producing and producing? Because its own nature, being already established, is not an effect; and because even in the production of another's nature, there is no benefit there—in both cases, since the agent is ineffective and thus non-beneficial—this has been essentially stated. Therefore, all relationships among real things are established through the cause-effect relation, in accordance with the differentiation of the specific utility of the producer alone. Thus, even the substrate-status of pots and the like in relation to jujube-fruits and the like is nothing but the capacity to generate. That too is not possible here [for the universal]—for this substrate-status, characterized by a specific mode of generation, is not possible for the universal in relation to the substrate of the universal, because it [the universal] is unproduced,

children.translated_text: That which, in order to be fit for producing cognition, conforms to another in itself—

children.text: 07215 tad vyaṅgyaṃ yogyatāyāś ca kāraṇam kārakaṃ matam //146//
children.translated_text: that is what is to be manifested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>); and the cause of that fitness is considered the producer (<s>kāraka</s>). //146//

Let the persistence of the universal be caused by the substrate. That [persistence] would either be different from or non-different from the universal. If it is different, the substrate produces precisely that [persistence], and it [persistence] is unconnected with the universal—so what use is the substrate to the universal? Or if [persistence is] connected [to the universal], the nature of that connection must be stated. If [it is said that] the making of persistence [is the connection]—the same absurd consequence and infinite regress [apply] there too. Therefore, since the benefit cannot be ascertained—'this is its persistence'—there is no cognition [of such a relationship]. If [the benefit is] generation—then what use is a substrate that is required but does not benefit? For dependence (<s>apekṣā</s>) means necessary connection with that, and that is not tenable for a universal that admits no additional qualification—[it would] simply generate [on its own]. [Reply:] There is no other cause of persistence. Or, if persistence is non-different from the universal, that [persistence] is just its own nature. And that is eternally existent—therefore its persistence is not produced by anything. Therefore there is no substrate for the universal; hence its occurrence is not the state of being a substratum. But again, even though the universal exists, since the unmanifested [universal] is made the cause of cognition by the particular (<s>vyakti</s>), its manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>) in that [particular] could be its occurrence. It is not reasonable for it to be so, because:

children.text: 07217 prāg eva asya ca yogyatve tad-apekṣā na yujyate /
children.translated_text: And if it already has that fitness prior [to manifestation], dependence on that [manifestor] is not tenable;

children.translated_text: for the universal, which cannot be modified—whence would that [fitness come] to the possessor of the universal? //147//

children.translated_text: Unlike collyrium and the like, the particular does not condition the sense-faculty;

children.text: 07321 pratipatter abhinnatvāt tad-bhāva-abhāva-kālayoḥ //148//
children.translated_text: because there is no difference in cognition between the times of its presence and absence. //148//

There is indeed no difference between a producer (<s>kāraka</s>) and a manifestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>). One who, being capable of producing cognition of its own object, generates another entity that requires a homogeneous material cause or does not require one—is called a manifestor. But elsewhere, when the capacity to generate cognition is not drawn out by what is to be produced, the status of producer [arises] merely through generation. For if one from whom [something] obtains the fitness to produce cognition were not its producer—[then] that fitness, being intrinsic to its nature, already exists beforehand, and it would not depend on him for generating cognition. And if this [fitness] belongs to another, the same absurd consequence as with persistence [arises]—namely, that [universal] comes from that [other] in exactly the same way. Therefore the manifestor neither produces that [universal] nor anything else—and [to say that] what is ineffective is depended upon is contradictory. [Objection:] But smoke and the like, though not producers, are manifestors because they are effects. [Reply:] True, they are manifestors, but fire does not depend on smoke to generate cognition in itself—because fire of such a nature is not directly a non-producer. Rather, cognition arises there solely through the power of the material cause, not through the power of the object, since [cognition] exists even in its absence—indirectly, following the logical mark. Nor do cognitions that appear with the general characteristic (<s>sāmānya-lakṣaṇa</s>) have a proximate object or arise from the power of the object—this has been explained and will be explained further. Therefore, those objects that directly generate cognition through [their] utility and depend on another [factor] for that—they necessarily obtain their own nature from that [factor]. And this obtaining of nature is not possible for the permanent universal from anything whatsoever. Therefore it cannot be manifested by anything. [Objection:] We do not call the obtaining of fitness by the universal its 'manifestation.' What then? Its inherence in its own substrate. For it, inhering in its own substrate, is a cause of cognition in itself or elsewhere. [Reply:] It has been stated regarding this: what is this inherence characterized as the substrate-superstratum relation between the unproduced and the producer? [The universal's] inherence with the particular is merely born [of convention]—no other distinction [exists]. Therefore, as before, even afterward it would not be a cause of cognition. If the cause of cognition is inherence alone, even other things that inhere in their own substrates would absurdly become visible. Therefore, manifestor-status is nothing but being a cause of cognition. And that is equally [applicable] to lamps and the like—hence the same absurd consequence [follows]. Therefore, neither the state of being a substratum nor manifestation is the occurrence of the universal [in particulars]. Since [it has] no occurrence, it is not a cause of cognition in multiple [instances]. For this very reason:

children.translated_text: If the manifestor of universals is held to possess universality,

children.text: 07421 prāpto gotva-ādinā tadvān pradīpa-ādiḥ prakāśakaḥ //149//
children.translated_text: then, being pervaded by cow-ness and the like, lamps and such would be manifestors [of those universals]. //149//

The sense-faculty, conditioned by collyrium and the like, achieves some enhancement in cognition—because of the difference between clear and unclear [perception]. And because what does not produce that [enhancement] does not condition for that. But the particular does not condition the sense-faculty in this way, because there is no difference in cognition between the times when [the universal] is present and absent. A conditioning of the object, however, even without a difference in the sense-faculty, could be beneficial by conferring a distinction on that [sense-faculty]. Not a conditioning of the sense-faculty. [Objection:] It is beneficial because it confers the power of seeing what was previously unseen. [Reply:] How can [something that] makes visible a supersensory object not produce a difference in cognition? And if [it were] restricted to one [universal], it would not make visible other universals. And if, through the particular's conditioning of the sense-faculty, in seeing that [universal], there were sometimes uncertainty regarding the universals to be manifested by it—or certainty of [only] one—[this would be] because there is no distinction in those [universals] for that [particular] which is undivided. Whether or not the particular conditions the sense-faculty—since the universal has the nature of generating cognition, it would generate cognition without depending on the conditioning of the sense-faculty, due to not departing from its own nature. [Objection:] It is merely incapable [on its own], because it requires the cooperation of a conditioned sense-faculty. [Reply:] What is this purpose of cooperation for one that admits no additional qualification? For impermanent entities would depend on cooperating conditions because they obtain a distinguished self [through them]. For the self that produces them comes into being precisely then from that [condition]—thus their mutual dependence on each other is nothing but being produced. But the permanent universal, not obtaining anything from another, being eternally of that nature—why does it depend on the sense-faculty? For its [capacity] when alone, which is not of that nature—how can the conditioning of the sense-faculty by the particular [bring about] something that would [otherwise] come about [only] in some way? Even [the claim] that the universal, cooperating with that [conditioned sense-faculty], is a cause of cognition—would amount to saying that the universal is indirectly an effect of the particular. Moreover:

children.translated_text: For those who hold that the universal, whether different from or non-different from the particular, exists—

children.text: 07511 teṣāṃ vyaktiṣv apūrvāsu kathaṃ sāmānya-buddhayaḥ //150//
children.translated_text: how do cognitions of the universal [arise] regarding previously unseen particulars? //150//

For whoever is a cause of cognition having a certain object is a manifestor of that. Lamps and the like also have the status of being causes of cognition of cow-ness and the like—because the eye, which requires the conditioning of light, apprehends objects. Therefore lamps and the like would possess cow-ness and the like. For there is no other manifestation of the particular besides being a cause of cognition—because no additional qualification can be conferred on the nature of the universal. [Objection:] Inherence is manifestation. [Reply:] The answer to this has been stated—because inherence is not tenable for it. For merely the inherence of this [universal] with the particular has arisen—no other distinction whatsoever. Therefore, as before, even afterward it would not be a cause of cognition. If the cause of cognition is inherence alone, other things that inhere in their own substrates would also absurdly become visible. Therefore, manifestor-status is nothing but being a cause of cognition. And that is equally [applicable] to lamps and the like—hence the same absurd consequence. Therefore, neither the state of being a substratum nor manifestation is the occurrence of the universal. Since [it has] no occurrence, it is not a cause of cognition in multiple [instances]. For this very reason:

children.translated_text: [For what] exists—

children.text: 07520 ananyatve anvaya-abhāvād anyatve apy anapāśrayāt //151//
children.translated_text: if non-different, because of the absence of positive concomitance; if different, because of the absence of a substrate. //151//

The word 'tu' [in the verse] has the sense of emphasis: '[a universal that] indeed exists.' For an existing entity, when generating a cognition elsewhere that imitates its own form through its own capacity, depends on a connection with that [other instance]. Otherwise there would be over-extension. And that [connection] is not possible for the existing universal, on either the identity or difference position. Because what is seen in one [instance] cannot possibly be seen in another.

children.translated_text: is not possible. For an essential nature does not transgress either identity or otherness in relation to [other] essential natures. Because form, being not of that nature, does not transgress otherness. For this alone is the otherness of form—that it is not that, just like another aspect, due to non-distinction. And if the form of the universal is non-other [from the individual], then it would be that very [individual]. If it is not of that nature, there would be the unwanted consequence of otherness, like another real thing. And the self of one individual does not enter into another individual, because of the unwanted consequence of becoming that other individual. Therefore, there cannot be a following cognition from a universal that is non-different [from individuals]. Nor [can there be] from one that is different, because it has no locus anywhere, and because any other relation such as that between what is manifested and what manifests it, not being assisted by anything, is absent due to the lack of [essential] connection. And because, even without connection, there would be the unwanted consequence of the arising of cognition [from anything]. Therefore, this [person] who, from seeing one thing, wishes for the cognition that occurs in one [instance] to occur elsewhere—he does not transcend identity and otherness—hence this is not reasonable. Therefore, this cognition of uniform aspect in objects is nothing but an error arising from the latent impression of conceptual construction. The difference of entities and the nature of [that] latent impression are the basis of it—this has been thoroughly examined. But how then do words like 'effect of <s>pradhāna</s>' (primordial matter), '<s>Īśvara</s>' (Lord), and so forth operate without distinction upon entities that are different and not of that nature? Those too, because the stream of consciousness is furnished with latent impressions deposited according to convention, in all perceptions of objects, without regard to their difference, through determination as such, operate—having arisen from conceptual construction that is the product of the power of apprehension—through the exclusion constructed by what is not of that nature, in the object as it appears in conceptual cognition. For in those [entities] that are not of that nature, there is no universal whatsoever, either separate or non-separate. But through the construction of being of that nature, the difference from what is other than that would be according to the intention of the cognizer. [Objection:] Why not [accept] the universal itself on the basis of that intention? [Reply:] Because there, difference must necessarily be accepted since it is indispensable. That very [difference] suffices for the function of the universal—hence the postulation of a universal is purposeless. If the cognition of a universal arises whether or not entities exist, then this [cognition] is not meaningful—it is merely a distortion—and we have no concern with determining its object. Its non-deception regarding some real thing, due to the [essential] connection of cause-and-effect relation, is not because of the inclusion of what is grasped as being of that nature—it exists even when [the object] is not of that nature, like perception—this we shall explain, and have explained. But its domain being the object of difference is frequent, due to the power of seeing different objects and the determination of existence in them. Because the construction of such existence [occurs] only elsewhere. Moreover, the one who constructs the universal as a different entity would construct it either as residing only in its own substrate, or as omnipresent like space and so forth. If it resides only in its own substrate, then when pots and so forth arise in places devoid of pot-hood and so forth, how could there be the universal, which exists in substances in different locations? Because that [universal] does not go to a substance about to arise from the previous substance—

children.translated_text: For one existing elsewhere, when there is arising in another place from that,

children.text: 07809 svasmād acalataḥ sthānād vṛttir ity atiyuktimat //153//
children.translated_text: the occurrence [of a thing] without moving from its own place is exceedingly unreasonable. //153//

because of the acceptance of non-activity. For it is not reasonable that an entity existing in one substance, without moving from that, should be connected with an entity in a different location that does not pervade the interval between the two. That [universal] was not there before, and exists afterward—
and it has not arisen there and has not come from anywhere—who is capable of bearing this burden of contradiction, other than through dullness? Moreover,
it is not like a thing with parts—
it does not abandon its previous substrate—
[which is] in a different location from the location [of the entity] about to arise; and it exists in both [locations]—
oh, what an unbroken chain of calamities! //152//
For the connection of two entities in different locations could be twofold: through having the nature of many parts, by means of parts belonging to each other, through connection with those—like light, a rope, a bamboo, a stick, and so forth. For without having parts, the simultaneous connection of something with [entities in] different locations is not reasonable, because of the absence of its second self. And for what has a single self, because it has the form of what is connected to and exists in that location; otherwise, there would be no connection with that. The placing of one supported thing there—and at that very time, its non-placement there by that very self—because of the contradiction of one thing being both placed and not-placed there, this is not reasonable. [Objection:] Its self is established in all forms, everywhere, at all times. [Reply:] Then the cognition based on the observation of its essential nature would be of all forms everywhere. And thus one would cognize even a cow as 'horse.' Because of the connection through substance-hood in which the horse-[universal] is established, and because of the cognition of that nature—there would be such a determination; and because there is no absence of unseen aspects in that one [universal]. Therefore, what has no parts is not placed simultaneously in multiple locations. But if it abandons its previous substrate, it could exist in a different location. But that is not accepted.

children.translated_text: And does it pervade whatever is in that place? Even this is most wondrous! //154//

Thus [are] the intervening verses. But for one whose universal is omnipresent—even for that [view]:
If in one place the [universal] is manifest, then, since it is omnipresent due to non-difference from that manifestation—
if the <s>jāti</s> (class/universal) [were manifest], it would be seen everywhere.
[Objection:] There is no manifestation of the permanent <s>jāti</s>—this has been rejected. Therefore, being permanent, independent of any external assistance, whether seen or not seen at some point, [it abides] in that essential nature, because it is established in that nature. Because another essential nature does not arise from anywhere. Even accepting

children.translated_text: For if it were to depend on individuals—

07925 iti cet /
children.translated_text: if [one says]—

children.text: 07926 na jātiḥ karma-saṃśrayāt //157//
children.translated_text: <s>jāti</s> is not [the cause], because of its dependence on action. //157//

Even one who would respond that the universal, whose cognition depends on the conjunction of its substrate with the sense faculty, is not seen in places devoid of a substrate—even for that [person], there does exist the conjunction of the substrate, sense faculty, and assistance, and therefore one who sees that should see [the universal] as it is. For when the [individual] is seen, it is not reasonable that what belongs to it would be unseen. It is also wrong [to say] that the non-seeing of the universal in places devoid of manifestors is because the universal is manifested by individuals. Because the manifestor-manifested relationship of that nature does not exist there. For the manifestor, like a lamp and so forth, [which] is a cause of the cognition of another through its own cognition, does not show what it manifests in a place devoid of its own form. But the individual is not like that—because of the reverse [relation]. For how could it both be the manifestor of the universal, and be visible through the cognition of that [universal]? And it would be entailed that precisely that [individual] is what is manifested, like a lamp and a pot. Because it is somehow invisible without the cognition of that [universal]. Moreover, what impossible thing did this [person] consider that he adopted the universals-doctrine with so much effort? Because a following cognition regarding individuals that are mutually exclusive is not reasonable from a distinct universal. How then—
How, regarding cooks and so forth, without an undifferentiated object, does a word [function]?
In cooks, reciters, and so forth, even though they do not follow each other, there is a recurrent application of words and cognitions: 'cook,' 'reciter.' For there is no other single undifferentiated thing in them by which, being different, they would be cognized as such. [Objection:] There is the action (<s>karma</s>). [Reply:] Then let that cognition belong to the individuals themselves—what need is there now for action or anything else? [Objection:] What is different cannot be the cause of an undifferentiated cognition—therefore a single universal is accepted. [Reply:] If that too—action, though different—produces an undifferentiated cognition, then what offense have the individuals committed that they are not accepted [as doing] so? Because they have a single form. [Objection:] The cognition of distinction 'this belongs to that' and the cognition possessing the specific form of non-that would not arise. [Reply:] It has been stated here how distinction and specific cognitions [arise] from the discrimination from other things in each case. Therefore, like the individual,
because of difference, the action is not the cause of this—
of the undifferentiated cognition of cook and so forth. [Objection:] The <s>jāti</s> of action is the cause due to non-difference,

children.text:
08001 na hy artha-antara-sambandhinī jātir artha-antare pratyaya-hetur
08002 gotvam iva karka-ādiṣu / pācaka-karmasu ca karma-jātir na ca tāni
08003 karmāṇi pācaka-śabdena abhidhīyante / kiṃ tarhi / tat-karma-āśrayo
08004 dravyam / tasya karma-sāmānyasya
08005 śruty-antara-nimittatvāt /
08006 ca pākaḥ pāka iti hi tataḥ syān na punaḥ pācaka iti / tasya karma-
08007 nimittatve proktam / kiṃ ca
08008 sthity-abhāvāc ca karmaṇaḥ /
08009 na hy anityaṃ karma sarvadā asti / tasya ca pratyayasya karma-nimittatve
08010 niruddhe karmaṇi na pācaka ity ucyeta / pacata eva karma-
08011 sadbhāvāt / tata eva
08012 asambandhān na sāmānyaṃ na ayuktam śabda-kāraṇam //158//
children.translated_text:
For a <s>jāti</s> belonging to one thing is not the cause of cognition regarding another thing—like cow-hood in relation to mules and so forth. And in the actions of cooking, there is the <s>jāti</s> of action, but those actions are not denoted by the word 'cook.' Rather, [what is denoted is] the substance that is the substrate of that action. Of that action-universal—
because it is the cause of a different expression—
there would be 'cooking, cooking' from that, but not 'cook.' [This is] stated because [the word] is occasioned by action. Moreover—
because of the non-permanence of action—
for impermanent action does not exist at all times. And if that cognition were occasioned by action, then when action has ceased, one would not be called 'cook'—[only] while actually cooking, because action exists [only then]. From that very [consideration]—
because of non-connection, the universal is not an unreasonable cause of the word. //158//

children.text:
08013 atiprasaṅgāt /
08014 vinaṣṭe hi karmaṇi tat sāmānyaṃ na karmaṇi na kartari iti sambaddha-
08015 sambandhe apy asya na asti ity asambandhān na śabda-jñāna-
08016 hetuḥ / anyathā hy atiprasaṅgaḥ syāt / atītam anāgataṃ vā
08017 nimittīkṛtya tayoḥ pravṛttir iti cet /

08102 karma-nimittam / anyac ca vyakty-ādikaṃ na iṣṭam ity
08103 animitte te syātām / tathā ca na jāti-siddhis tasyā jñāna-abhidhānayoḥ /

08105 na karma na sāmānyam iti cet
08106 na ca śaktir ananvayāt //159//
children.translated_text:
Because of over-extension.
For when the action has perished, that universal [of action] is neither in the action nor in the agent—thus even in its connection with what is connected [to action], it does not exist—hence, because of non-connection, it is not the cause of word and cognition. For otherwise there would be over-extension. [Objection:] Past or future [action] being taken as the occasion, their operation [of words would proceed]. [Reply:]
Even action, when non-existent, is not the occasion of cognition and designation.
Of those—
because the consequence of being without occasion [would follow].
For what is non-existent, being without characterization, how could it be an occasion? Because reality has the character of causal efficacy. That [action], having the form of what has ceased or not yet arrived—past and future action as the occasion—moreover, individuals and so forth are not accepted [by the opponent]—hence those two [cognition and designation] would be without occasion. And thus the establishment of <s>jāti</s> [would not follow], since it is not accepted as the occasion of cognition and designation.
[Objection:] Capacity (<s>śakti</s>) is the occasion of words like 'cook' and so forth, not action, not universal. [Reply:]—
Nor is capacity [the cause], because of non-following. //159//

children.text:
08107 na hi śaktir nāma kiṃcid anyad eva pācaka-ādīnām / tasyā eva
08108 pācaka-ādy-arthakriyā-upayogena dravyasya anupayogitva-prasaṅgāt / tasyāṃ
08109 tasya upayoga iti cet kim idānīṃ śaktyā / śakty-upayogāya
08110 śakty-antarasya vyatirekiṇo abhyupagame atiprasaṅgād dravyam
08111 eva upayujyata iti vācyam / tasya upayoge śaktāv arthakriyāyām
08112 eva upayujyata iti kiṃ na iṣyata iti kim antarāle anarthikayā śaktyā /
08113 tasmāc śaktir iti dravyam eva tat-kāryaṃ tac ca na anveti iti / tato
08114 anvayī śabdo na syāt /
children.translated_text: there would be no following word.

children.text: 08115 sāmānyaṃ pācakatva-ādi yadi prāg eva tad bhavet /
children.translated_text: If the universal such as 'cook-hood' and so forth already existed beforehand—

children.text: 08116 vyaktaṃ sattā-ādi-van no cen na paścād aviśeṣataḥ //160//
children.translated_text: it would be manifest, like existence (<s>sattā</s>) and so forth; if not, then it would not [be manifest] afterward either, because of non-distinction. //160//

For capacity is not something entirely other than cooks and so forth. Because [if it were], there would be the unwanted consequence that the substance itself would be useless for the practical effect of cooking and so forth [attributed to] cooks. [Objection:] The substance has a use in that capacity. [Reply:] Then what need for capacity? If a separate capacity distinct [from the substance] were accepted for the purpose of the use of capacity, there would be over-extension—hence it should be said that the substance itself is used. If there is use of the substance, since it is used for the practical effect which is [its] capacity—why is that not accepted? What need then for the intervening and purposeless capacity? Therefore, capacity is just the substance itself—and that does not follow [across instances]—hence

children.text:
08117 atha api pācakatvam iti sāmānyam eva kiṃcid bhavet / saty arthe
08118 tat-samavāyasya akādācitkatvāt sattā-ādi-vat / prāg eva vyaktaṃ
08119 syāt / yāvanti hi sāmānyāny arthe samavāya-dharmāṇi tāni saha
08120 utpādena asya samavayanti iti samayaḥ / tad-vyatikrame tasya
08121 paścād apy aviśeṣān na tat-samavāyaḥ syāt / tat-sambandhi-svabhāva-
08122 vaiguṇyād hi sa tasya prāṅ na āsīt tatra eva ca asya svabhāve
children.translated_text: and for this [object], whose nature remains the same, that it should subsequently come into being

children.text: 08123 sthitasya paścād bhavati iti duranvayam etat /
children.translated_text: there [in that same nature]—this is difficult to follow.

children.text: 08124 kriyā-upakāra-apekṣasya vyañjakatve avikāriṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: For one who requires the assistance of action to be a manifester, being unchanging,

children.text: 08125 na apekṣa-atiśaye apy asya kṣaṇikatvāt kriyā kutaḥ //161//
children.translated_text: even if there were a surplus of dependence, whence would there be action, since [the universal] is momentary? //161//

Even if 'being a cook' were some kind of universal—since, when the object exists, its inherence is not occasional (like existence and so forth), it would already be manifest. For the agreement is that however many universals are inherence-properties in the object, they inhere together with the origination of this [object]. If that [rule] is violated, since there is no distinction even afterward, there would be no inherence of that [universal]. For the reason it did not previously exist in that [object] is the deficiency of the nature related to that—

children.text:
08126 karma-upakāram apekṣya pācakatvaṃ dravyeṇa vyajyata iti cet /
08201 sthira-svabhāvasya anatiśayād aviśeṣa-ādhāyini kā apekṣā / atiśaye
08202 vā kṣaṇikatvāt karmaṇaḥ pratikṣaṇaṃ svabhāva-bhūtasya anyānyasya
08203 atiśayasya utpattes tad api kṣaṇikaṃ syāt / tataḥ sva-utpatti-sthāna-vināśinaḥ
08204 kriyā kutaḥ yad-apekṣaṃ vyañjakaṃ syāt / kathaṃ
08205 tarhi idānīm asty abhinne vastuni jñāna-śabdayor anvayinor vṛttiḥ /
08206 yathā pācaka-ādiṣu / nanu tad eva idaṃ cintyate kathaṃ teṣv
08207 api iti / cintitam etad yathā na teṣu sambhavati / tat kim idānīm
08208 animitte te syātām / na animitte / kiṃ tarhi / na bāhya-tattva-nimitte /
08209 yathāsvaṃ vāsanā-prabodhād vikalpa-utpattiḥ / tataḥ śabdāḥ /
08210 na punar vikalpa-abhidhānayor vastu-sattā samāśraya ity ukta-prāyam
08211 etat / yathāsvaṃ samaya-vāsanā-vaśād virodhi-rūpa-samāveśena
08212 aparāpara-darśane apy anvayinos tayor darśanāt / na ca tatra
08213 tan-nibandhanaḥ kaścit svabhāvo asti paraspara-virodhinor yugapad
08214 ekatra samāveśa-ayogāt / aniyamena tarhi syāt / na hy animittaṃ
08215 bhavat kvacid bhavati kvacin na bhavati iti niyamam
08216 arhati / na khalu vai tad animittaṃ vāsanā-viśeṣa-nimittatvāt /
08217 bāhyaṃ tu tathābhūtaṃ dṛśyaṃ na asti iti brūmaḥ / na ca asati tasmin
08218 na bhavitavyam / supta-taimirika-upalabdheṣv artheṣv abhāveṣu
08219 samaya-vāsanā-āropita-rūpa-viśeṣeṣu ca tathā vikalpa-utpatteḥ / na
08220 ca te asatsu utpadyanta iti sarvatra sarva-ākāraḥ / vibhāge na eva tathā-upalabdhānāṃ
08221 vikalpanāt / uktaṃ ca atra kiṃcid asmābhiḥ prakṛtyā
08222 api kecid eka-jñāna-kāryāḥ svabhāva-bhedād iti / api ca /
08223 tulye bhede yayā jātiḥ pratyāsattyā prasarpati /
children.translated_text: That proximity by which a universal (<s>jāti</s>) extends to some [cases] where the difference is equal

children.text: 08224 kvacin na anyatra sa eva astu śabda-jñāna-nibandhanam //162//
children.translated_text: but not to others—let that very [proximity] be the basis of word and cognition. //162//

[Objection:] The 'being a cook' is manifested by the substance depending on the assistance of action. [Reply:] For what has an unchanging nature, since there is no surplus [of capacity], what dependence is there that does not confer any distinction? Or if there is a surplus—since action is momentary, because at each moment a different surplus, which is of the nature [of the object], arises—that [surplus] too would be momentary. Then whence would there be action for what perishes at the very place of its origination, [an action] depending on which [the universal] would be a manifester? But how then is there the operation of cognition and word, which are co-extensive, in an undifferentiated real thing—as in 'cook' and so forth? [Objection:] But this is exactly what is being considered—how [does it work] even in those [cases]? [Reply:] This has been considered—how it is not possible in those [cases]. [Objection:] Then would those two [cognition and word] be without a cause? [Reply:] Not without a cause. [Objection:] Then what? [Reply:] Not with an external reality as their cause. Conceptual construction arises from the awakening of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) according to their own [nature]. From that, words [arise]. But the existence of a real thing is not the basis for conceptual construction and designation—this has been mostly stated. Because of the perception of those two [cognition and word] as co-extensive even in the observation of different things, through the influence of convention-impressions according to their own [nature], by the inclusion of a form that is contradictory [to what is actually there]. And there is no nature based on that [co-extension], because mutually contradictory [properties] cannot be included simultaneously in one [thing]. [Objection:] Then it would occur without restriction. [Reply:] For what occurs without a cause does not merit the restriction that it occurs somewhere and not elsewhere. [Reply:] Indeed, it is not without a cause, because it is caused by specific <s>vāsanās</s>. But we say there is no external visible [reality] of such a nature. And it does not follow that without that [external reality], it should not arise—because conceptual construction arises [even] regarding objects perceived by the sleeping and those with eye diseases, which are non-existent, and regarding form-distinctions superimposed by convention-impressions. And they do not arise regarding non-existents in the sense that [they would arise] in all forms everywhere, because of the conceptual construction of distinctions not thus perceived. And here something has been stated by us: 'Some, even by their nature, are the causes of a single cognition, because of the difference of essential nature.' Moreover:

children.text: 08225 ity antaraślokaḥ /
children.translated_text: This is an intervening verse.

children.text: 08226 na nivṛttiṃ vihāya asti yadi bhāva-anvayo aparaḥ /
children.translated_text: If there is no positive concomitance of entities other than [their] negation,

children.text: 08227 ekasya kāryam anyasya na syād atyanta-bhedataḥ //163//
children.translated_text: the effect of one would not be [the effect] of another, due to absolute difference. //163//

children.text:
08228 yady ete bhāvā vyāvṛttiṃ muktvā svabhāvena kenacid anvayinā
08301 śūnyāḥ / na eṣāṃ bahūnām ekaṃ kāryaṃ syāt / yo hi tasya svabhāvo
08302 janakaḥ / na hi so anyasya asti / yo asti sa na janako vyatirekas ya
08303 niḥsvabhāvatvāt / yaj-janakaṃ tad eva vastu taj-janakaṃ
08304 ca aparatra na asti iti na aparaṃ janayet / sa hi tasya svabhāvo yo janakaḥ
08305 so anyasya api yadi syāt / sa tena svabhāvena tato abhinnaḥ
08306 syād iti asti svabhāva-anvayaḥ /
children.translated_text: and so there would be a positive concomitance of nature.

children.text: 08307 yady ekātmatayā anekaḥ kāryasya ekasya kārakaḥ /
children.translated_text: If many are the producers of one effect due to being of one nature,

children.text: 08308 ātmā ekatra api so asti iti vyarthāḥ syuḥ sahakāriṇaḥ //164//
children.translated_text: that nature exists even in one [of them] alone—so the cooperating causes would be purposeless. //164//

If these entities, apart from exclusion, are devoid of any nature that is positively concomitant—then for these many [entities], there would not be a single effect. For the nature of that [one entity] that produces [the effect]—that is not [the nature] of another. What exists [in the other] is not the producer; [its] exclusion, having no nature, [cannot produce]. What produces—that very real thing is the producer of that; and that producer does not exist elsewhere—so it would not produce another. For the nature of that [one entity] which is the producer—if that were also [the nature] of the other, then it would be undifferentiated from that by that nature,

children.text:
08309 yady eka-svabhāvatvād aneka ekasya kārakaḥ sa teṣām abhinnaḥ
08310 svabhāvaḥ / eka-saṃnidhāne apy asti iti / avaikalyāt kāraṇasya eko
08311 api janakaḥ syāt / yasmāt /
08312 na apaity abhinnaṃ tad-rūpaṃ viśeṣāḥ khalv apāyinaḥ /
08313 na hi tasya abhinna-svabhāvasya artha-antare viśeṣo asti / viśeṣo abheda-
08314 hāneḥ / sa ca tatra apy asti iti na eka-sthitāv api tasya apāyo asti / ye
08315 viśeṣās teṣāṃ saha-sthiti-niyama-abhāvāt syād apāyaḥ / na ca te
08316 janakā iṣṭāḥ / sahakāriṇām eka-svabhāvatayā janakatva-abhyupagamāt /
08317 tato janakasya sthānāt / asthāyinaś ca ajanakatvād
08318 eka-sthitāv api kārya-utpattiḥ syāt / na ca bhavati / ataḥ
08319 eka-apāye phala-abhāvād viśeṣebhyas tad-udbhavaḥ //165//
children.translated_text: If, due to being of one essential nature, many are the producers of one [effect], then their undifferentiated nature—since it exists even in the proximity of one alone—due to the non-deficiency of the cause, even one would be a producer. Because: The undifferentiated form does not depart; the particulars indeed are what depart. For of that which has an undifferentiated nature, there is no particular in another object—the particular [would entail] the loss of non-difference. And that [undifferentiated nature] exists there too—so even when only one is present, there is no departure of it. The particulars—since there is no restriction of their co-existence [with the effect]—there may be departure. But they are not accepted as producers, because the cooperating causes are accepted as producers due to being of one essential nature. Therefore, since the producer remains, and since what does not remain is not a producer, there would be the production of the effect even when only one is present. But that does not happen. Therefore: Since in the absence of one [particular], there is no effect, its arising is from the particulars. //165//

children.text:
08320 tat-kāryam aneka-sahakāri-sādhāraṇam eka-viśeṣa-apāye api na bhavati /
08321 punar apy avikaleṣu sarveṣu viśeṣeṣu bhavati / na tv avikale
08322 apy abhinne rūpe / kāryaṃ hi kutaścid bhāva-dharmi yan na bhavati
08323 tat tasya eva vaikalyāt / na ca abhinnasya rūpasya eka-sthitāv
08324 api vaikalyam asti / avikale api tasminn abhavat tasya ajanaka-ātmatāṃ
08325 sūcayati / yat-sākalya-vaikalyābhyāṃ ca kāryaṃ bhāva-abhāva-vat
08401 tata eva utpattiḥ / tasmin sati niyamena bhavatas tad-anyasmād utpatti-
08402 kalpanāyām atiprasaṅgāt / tasmād viśeṣā eva janakā na
08403 sāmānyaṃ / tatas ta eva vastu / yasmāt /
08404 sa pāramārthiko bhāvo ya eva arthakriyā-kṣamaḥ /
08405 idam eva hi vastv-avastunor lakṣaṇaṃ yad arthakriyā-yogyatā ayogyatā
08406 ca iti vakṣyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: as we shall state.

children.text: 08407 sa ca /
children.translated_text: And that [real entity]:

children.text: 08408 arthakriyā-yogyo arthaḥ
children.translated_text: The object capable of causal function

children.text: 08409 na anveti yo anveti na tasmāt kārya-sambhavaḥ //166//
children.translated_text: does not positively follow [another]; what does positively follow—from that, the arising of an effect is impossible. //166//

That effect, which is common to many cooperating causes, does not occur even when one particular is absent; it occurs again when all particulars are complete—but not when the undifferentiated form is complete [by itself]. For an effect that has the property of existing from some [causes] but does not exist [from others]—that [non-existence] is due to the deficiency of that very [particular cause]. And for the undifferentiated form, even when only one [entity] is present, there is no deficiency. That it did not occur even when that [undifferentiated form] was complete indicates its nature as a non-producer. And that by whose completeness and deficiency the effect is present or absent, like being or non-being—from that alone is the origination. Since when that is present, [the effect] necessarily exists, the supposition of origination from something other than that would lead to overextension. Therefore, the particulars alone are the producers, not the universal. Therefore, they alone are real things. Because: That which is a real entity in the ultimate sense is precisely what is capable of causal function (<s>arthakriyā</s>). For this alone is the definition of a real thing and a non-real-thing—capability and incapability of causal function,

children.text:
08410 tasmāt sarvaṃ sāmānyam anarthakriyā-yogyatvād avastu / vastu
08411 tu viśeṣa eva tata eva tan-niṣpatteḥ / svabhāva-ananvayāt tarhy
08412 ekasya janakaṃ rūpam anyasya na asti ity ajanakaḥ syāt / janakatve
08413 vā bheda-aviśeṣāt sarvo janakaḥ syāt / na etad asti / yasmāt /
08414 tena ātmanā hi bhede api hetuḥ kaścin na ca aparaḥ /
08415 svabhāvo ayam /
08416 ekasya janakād ātmano bhidyamānāḥ sarve samaṃ janakā na vā
08417 aviśeṣe kaścid iti syād etad yady eṣāṃ na viśeṣaḥ sambhavet / tato bheda-
08418 api kutaścid ātma-atiśayāt kaścij janako na aparaḥ / sa hi
08419 tasya svabhāvo na aparasya / na hi svabhāvā bhāvānāṃ paryanuyogam
08420 arhanti kim agnir dahaty uṣṇo vā na udakam iti / etāvat tu
08421 syāt kuto ayaṃ svabhāva iti / nirhetukatve anapekṣiṇo niyama-abhāvena
08422 atiprasaṅgāt / tasmāt svabhāvo asya sva-hetor ity ucyate /
08423 tasya api taj-janana-ātmatā tad-anyasmād ity anādir hetu-paraṃparā
08501 bhinnānāṃ hi kaścid hetur na anyaḥ svabhāvād ity atra na kiṃcid
children.translated_text: For some [entity] is the cause of different [things] and not another, [due to its] essential nature—in this, nothing

children.text: 08502 bādhakam /
children.translated_text: is contradictory.

children.text: 08503 abhede tu syātāṃ nāśa-udbhavau sakṛt //167//
children.translated_text: But if there were non-difference, destruction and origination would occur simultaneously. //167//

Therefore, every universal, being incapable of causal function, is a non-real-thing. But the real thing is precisely the particular, because of the accomplishment [of the effect] from that alone. [Objection:] If then, due to the non-positive-concomitance of essential nature, the form that produces one [effect] does not exist in another, then [each] would be a non-producer. Or, if [each is] a producer, then due to the non-distinction of difference, all would be producers. [Reply:] This is not so. Because: For even in difference, some [entity] by that very nature is a cause, but another is not. This is its essential nature. From among those differing from the nature that produces one, all would equally be producers or not—[one might think] this would be so if there were no distinction among them. But from the distinction, even though different from some [other nature], due to a surplus of its own nature, some one [entity] is a producer, and another is not. For that is the essential nature of this [one], not of the other. For the essential natures of entities do not warrant the cross-examination: 'Why does fire burn and is hot but not water?' But this much may be [asked]: 'Whence is this essential nature?' If it were causeless, then since what is independent has no restriction, there would be overextension. Therefore, its essential nature is said to be from its own cause. And the nature of that [cause] too, being of the nature of producing that [effect] rather than something else—[this constitutes] a beginningless chain of causes.

children.text:
08504 abhedāt / svabhāvena eva viśvasya svātma-vad vibhāga-utpatti-sthiti-
08505 nirodha-ādayo na syuḥ tathā upalakṣaṇād abhedasya / idam eva hi
08506 bheda-abheda-lakṣaṇam eka-ākārasya api vyatireko avyatirekaś ca /
08507 virodhinor ekātmany asambhavāt /
08508 bhedo api tena na evaṃ ced /
08509 na vai sarva-ākāra-avyatirekaṃ brūmo yena evaṃ syāt / kaścid asya ātmā
08510 bhinno na anya iti bhedān na sahotpatty-ādayaḥ / evaṃ tarhi
08511 ya ekasmin vinaśyati /
08512 tiṣṭhaty ātmā na tasya /
08513 bhedaḥ / sthāna-asthānayor ekātma-āśrayatve ko anyo dharmo bhedaka
08514 iti nānātvam eva kvacin na syāt / sarva-ākāra-viveka avivekinor vā arthayor
08515 abhyupagamān nāma kevalaṃ na iṣṭaṃ syān na vastv
08516 ity uktam / tad ime na ekayogakṣemā bhāvāḥ bhinnā eva
08517 ato na syāt sāmānya-bheda-dhīḥ //168//
children.translated_text: Due to non-difference. If all things were undifferentiated in essential nature, just like one's own self, there would be no separate origination, duration, cessation, and so forth of the universe—due to the characterization of non-difference by such [simultaneous] marks. For this indeed is the definition of difference and non-difference: the exclusion or non-exclusion even of what has a single form. Because contradictory [properties] are impossible in a single nature. [Objection:] Difference too would then not be thus [possible]. [Reply:] We do not say there is non-exclusion in all aspects, by which it would be thus. Some nature of this [entity] is different, and no other—therefore, because of the differences, there is no simultaneous origination and so forth. [Objection:] Then, the nature that perishes in one—

children.text:
08518 tad idam artha-antaram anāyattam ajanyatvād asya idaṃ sāmānyaṃ
08519 bhedo vā iti vyapadeśaṃ na arhati / anyāpohe apy eṣa tulyaḥ prasaṅga
08520 iti cet / na tulyaḥ / yataḥ /
08521 nivṛtter niḥsvabhāvatvān na sthāna-asthāna-kalpanā /
08522 na hy anyāpoho nāma kiṃcit tasya ca svabhāva-anuṣaṅgiṇyaḥ
children.translated_text: difference. [Reply:] If abiding and non-abiding depend on the same nature, what other property is the differentiator?—thus diversity would not exist in some [cases]. Or, from the acceptance of two things that are either completely discriminated or completely undiscriminated in all aspects, it is merely the designation that would not be accepted, not the real thing—as has been stated. Therefore, these entities, not sharing the same fortune, are indeed different.

children.text: 08523 svabhāva-sthiti-pracyuti-kalpanā na kalpante /
children.translated_text: Therefore, there would not be a cognition of universal and difference. //168//

children.text: 08524 upaplavaś ca sāmānya-dhiyas tena apy adūṣaṇā //169//
children.translated_text: [Objection:] This being something other, not dependent [on the entity], since it is unproduced [by it], it does not warrant the designation 'this is a universal' or 'a difference.' If the same absurd consequence [applies] even in the case of exclusion of others—[Reply:] No, it is not the same. Because: Since negation has no nature, there is no supposition of abiding and non-abiding.
[another] nature remains; that is not its

children.text:
08525 nirviṣayam eva khalv idaṃ mithyā-jñānaṃ yad anekatra eka-ākāram
08601 iti na tad-viṣayasya abhāvāt sthitir asthitir vā / yat punar etad uktaṃ
08602 taj-janako hi sa tasya svabhāvaḥ
08603 yat tasya janakaṃ rūpaṃ tato anyo janakaḥ katham /
08604 tatra na brūmo anyasya taj-janakaṃ rūpaṃ na asti iti / kiṃ tarhi /
08605 yad ekasya taj-janakaṃ tad anyasya na ity anyo api svarūpeṇa eva
08606 janako na pararūpeṇa atattvāt / te yathāsvaṃ bhinnāś ca taj-janakāś
08607 ca svabhāvena iti ko atra virodhaḥ / eka-rūpa-vikalas tad-rūpo
08608 na syāt na atat-kāryaḥ / tena eva ca tat-kāryaṃ kartavyam iti ko
08609 atra nyāyaḥ / api ca /
08610 bhinnā viśeṣā janakā /
08611 ity uktam / na ca te viśeṣās tena ātmanā parasparam anuyanti /
08612 yad ekasya janakaṃ rūpam anyasya tan na asti / na ca tāvatā
08613 ajanakāḥ /
children.translated_text: are not applicable [to it].

children.text: 08614 apy abhedo api teṣu cet //170//
children.translated_text: And the distortion of the cognition of universals is not vitiated by that either. //169//
For the exclusion of others is not some [real] thing, and the suppositions of abiding and departure of essential nature that pertain to essential nature

children.text:
08615 syād etat satyaṃ viśeṣā janakāḥ na punas teṣāṃ viśiṣṭam eva
08616 rūpaṃ kiṃ tv abhinnam api tad-eka-śakti-yogāj janakāḥ /
08617 tena te ajanakāḥ proktāḥ /
08618 saty api sāmānye rūpe na tena te janakās tasya anapāyād eka-sthitāv
08619 api kārya-utpatti-prasaṅgād ity uktaṃ prāk / kiṃ ca /
08620 pratibhāso api bhedakaḥ /
08621 ananya-bhāk /
08622 utpatti-sthiti-vināśa-ādi-bhedaś na ity api-śabdāt / yo ayam abhinnān
08623 sarva-arthān manyate tasya ayam artheṣu buddhi-pratibhāsa-bhedo
08624 viruddha-dharma-adhyāsaś ca na syāt / sati vā tasminn abhede api
08625 na kaścid bhedaḥ syāt / tathā ca ayaṃ pravibhāgo na syād ekātma-vat /
08626 tasmād ayaṃ bhinna-pratibhāsa-ādir viśeṣa eva / na ca atra aparam
08627 abhinnaṃ pratibhāsaṃ paśyāmo yad-balena abheda-pratītiḥ
08628 syāt / ato viśeṣa eva /
08701 sa eva arthas tasya vyāvṛttayo apare //170//
children.translated_text: For this erroneous cognition, whose object is precisely nothing [real]—the single form in many [things]—since there is no object of it, there is neither abiding nor non-abiding. As for what was stated— 'For the nature of that which produces is its essential nature; the form that produces that—how could another be a producer?'— here we do not say that the form that produces for one does not exist for the other. Rather: what produces for one does not [produce] for the other—thus the other too is a producer by its own form alone, not by the form of another, because it is not that [other]. They, being respectively different and producers of that by their essential nature—what contradiction is there? What lacks the form of one would not be of that form, nor the effect of what is not that. And that effect of that [form] must be produced by that very [form]—what principle [would require otherwise]? Moreover: The different particulars are the producers— as has been stated. And those particulars do not follow each other by that very nature. The form that produces for one does not exist for the other. But that does not make them

children.text: 08702 tat-kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ ca uktaṃ tat svalakṣaṇam iṣyate /
children.translated_text: non-producers.

children.text: 08703 tat-tyāga-āpti-phalāḥ sarvāḥ puruṣāṇāṃ pravṛttayaḥ //172//
children.translated_text: That which is called the effect and cause of that is accepted as the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular); all the activities of persons have as their fruit the avoidance and attainment of that. //172//

children.text:
08704 yad arthakriyākāri tad eva vastv ity uktam / sa ca viśeṣa eva /
08705 yat punar etat sāmānyaṃ nāma tat tasya eva aparasmād bhedaḥ /
08706 na hi tasya arthatve dṛśyasya rūpa-anupalakṣaṇaṃ yuktam / tad-
08707 upalakṣaṇa-kṛtatvād bhedeṣv abhinna-pratyayasya / api ca /
08708 yathā abheda-aviśeṣe api na sarvaṃ sarva-sādhanam /
children.translated_text: Just as, even without any distinction of non-difference, not everything is the means of accomplishing everything,

children.text: 08709 tathā bheda-aviśeṣe api na sarvaṃ sarva-sādhanam //173//
children.translated_text: so too, even without any distinction of difference, not everything is the means of accomplishing everything. //173//

It was stated that what performs efficacious action is alone a real thing. And that is only the particular. What is called 'universal' is nothing but that [particular's] difference from another. For it is not reasonable that, in the case of something real, the perceptible form should not be perceived—because the undifferentiated cognition in [different] instances is caused precisely by the perception of that [form]. Moreover:

children.text:
08710 yad uktam / kathaṃ taj-janaka-svabhāvād bhinno asya janakaḥ
08711 syāt / janakatve vā aviśeṣāt sarvo janakaḥ syād iti / uktam
08712 atra / yady aviśeṣaḥ syāt syād etad iti / yathā ca asya svayam
08713 abheda-vādino abheda-aviśeṣe api na sarvaḥ sarvasya janaka iti tathā
08714 bheda-aviśeṣe api bhaviṣyati / athavā /
08715 bhede hi kārakaṃ kiṃcid vastu-dharmatayā bhavet /
children.translated_text: In [the case of] difference, something may be an agent by virtue of the nature of reality;

children.text: 08716 abhede tu virudhyete tasya ekasya kriyā-akriye //174//
children.translated_text: but in [the case of] non-difference, action and non-action of that single [entity] are contradictory. //174//

It was objected: how could what is different from the nature that produces that be its producer? Or, if it is a producer, since there is no distinction, everything would be a producer. The response has been stated: if there were no distinction, this would follow. And just as for this proponent of non-difference himself, even without any distinction of non-difference, not everything is the producer of everything—so too it will be [the case] even without distinction of difference. Or alternatively:

children.text:
08717 bheda-mātra-aviśeṣe api sva-hetu-pratyaya-niyamita-svabhāvatvāt kecid
08718 eva kārakāḥ syuḥ na anye atat-svabhāvatvād ity atra na eva kiṃcid
08719 viruddham asti / ekatve tu tasya tatra eva tathā kārakatvam akārakatvaṃ
08720 ca iti vyāhatam etat /
08721 bhedo apy asty akriyātaś cen na kuryuḥ sahakāriṇaḥ /
08722 na vai sarva-ākāra-avivekaṃ brūmo bhedasya api bhāvāt / tasmāt
08723 kaścid akārako api iti / tathā api kathaṃcid bhedāt sahakāriṇo
08724 akārakāḥ syuḥ /
children.translated_text: be non-agents?

children.text: 08725 paryāyeṇa atha kartṛtvaṃ sa kiṃ tasya eva vastunaḥ //175//
children.translated_text: Or, if [you say] agency [belongs to them] in turn—does that [belong to] that very real thing? //175//

Even without any distinction in mere difference, since [each thing's] nature is determined by its own causes and conditions, only certain [things] would be agents, not others—because they do not have that nature—and there is nothing contradictory in this. But in [the case of] oneness, that it should be an agent there in that way and also a non-agent—this is contradictory. [Objection:] 'There is also difference from non-action'—we are not saying there is no distinction in any aspect [of difference], since difference too exists. Therefore, some [thing] may be a non-agent too. Even so, how would the co-operative conditions, through some kind of difference,

children.text:
08726 atha api syān na eva kaścid akārako asti / sarveṣāṃ sarvatra paryāyeṇa
08727 upayogāt / śakter vā vipariṇatāyās tan-niveśinyā rūpa-antareṇa
08728 upayogāt / sa eva khalv ayaṃ paryāyo bheda-āśraya ekasya katham /
08801 pariṇāmo vā avyatirekiṇyāḥ / viśeṣe vā kathaṃcid ekatva-
08802 hānir iti yat kiṃcid etat / kiṃ ca /
08803 atyanta-bheda-abhedau ca syātāṃ tadvati vastuni /
children.translated_text: And would there be absolute difference and non-difference in a real thing that possesses that [universal],

children.text: 08804 anyonyaṃ vā tayor bhedaḥ sadṛśa-asadṛśa-ātmanoḥ //176//
children.translated_text: or mutual difference between the two—[the one] similar and [the other] dissimilar in nature? //176//

Even if one might say there is nothing whatsoever that is a non-agent, because of the usefulness of all [things] everywhere in turn, or because of the usefulness of the capacity in a different form when it has been transformed and settled [in a new state]—indeed, this very alternation, which depends on difference, how [can it belong] to one [thing]? Or the transformation of [a capacity] that is non-distinct [from the entity]? Or somehow, in [accepting] a particular [form], there would be the loss of oneness—so all this amounts to nothing. Moreover:

children.text:
08805 bhāvāś ced abhinnena ātmanā svātmabhūtena bhedinas tadvantaḥ
08806 syuḥ tad-abhinna-svabhāva-ātmatvād bhedasya api kutaḥ parasparaṃ
08807 bhedaḥ / atha na sa tasya samāna ātmā / tathā sati tadātmanā
08808 tena api na yuktaṃ tathā bhavitum / tathā abhāve hy atad-
08809 dharmā syāt / na hy ayaṃ pravṛtti-nivṛttimān svabhāva eko yuktaḥ /
08810 na sarvātmanā abheda eva /
08811 tayor api bhaved bhedo yadi /
08812 na hi kvacid asya ekāntiko bhedo abhedo vā vivekena vyavasthāpanāt /
children.translated_text: Even if there were difference between those two—for there is no absolute difference or non-difference for it anywhere, since [the division into] universal and particular is established by discrimination—

children.text: 08813 sāmānyaṃ viśeṣa iti /
children.translated_text: as 'universal' and 'particular'—

children.text: 08814 yena ātmanā tayoḥ /
children.translated_text: by which nature of those two—

children.text: 08815 bhedaḥ sāmānyam ity etad yadi bhedas tadātmanā //177//
children.translated_text: if difference—that 'this is the universal'—if the difference is through that nature, //177//

If entities were possessors of that [universal] through an undifferentiated nature that is essential to them, then since difference too would be of a nature identical with that undifferentiated nature, whence would there be mutual difference? Or if that [universal] is not identical in nature to it—in that case, it would not be reasonable for [the entity] to be so [i.e., of that nature] through that nature. For in the absence of being so, it would not have its properties. For it is not reasonable that this nature should be one, [yet] possessed of both activity and non-activity. [And it is] not non-difference in every respect.

children.text:
08816 bheda eva /
08817 yadi sāmānya-viśeṣayor yam ātmānam āśritya sāmānyaṃ viśeṣa
08818 iti sthitis tena ātmanā bhedas tadā bheda eva / yasmāt tau hi
08819 tayoḥ svātmānau tau ced vyatirekiṇau vyatireka eva sāmānya-
08820 viśeṣayoḥ svabhāva-bhedāt / svabhāvo hi bhāva iti /
08821 tathā ca syān niḥsāmānyaviśeṣatā /
children.translated_text: And thus there would be the absence of the universal-particular [relationship];

children.text: 08822 bheda-sāmānyayor yadvad ghaṭa-ādīnāṃ parasparam //178//
children.translated_text: as between the universal 'difference' and [things like] a pot and the like—[they are simply distinct] from each other. //178//

then it is difference alone. If the nature through which the universal and the particular are established as 'universal' and 'particular'—if through that nature there is difference, then it is difference alone. For those [natures] are the essential natures of those two; if those are distinct, then there is simply distinction of the universal and the particular, because of the difference of essential nature. For the essential nature is the entity.

children.text:
08823 vyatireke ca bheda-sāmānyayor na bhedaḥ sāmānyān na sāmānyaṃ
08824 bheda-vat sambandha-abhāvāt parasparaṃ ghaṭa-ādi-vad
08825 ity uktam / api ca /
08826 yam ātmānaṃ puraskṛtya puruṣo ayaṃ pravartate /
children.translated_text: The nature with reference to which this person acts,

children.text: 08827 tat-sādhya-phala-vāñchāvān bheda-abhedau tad-āśrayau //179//
children.translated_text: desiring the fruit to be accomplished by that—both difference and non-difference depend on that. //179//

And in the distinctness of the universal 'difference' and [things like pots], difference is not [derived] from the universal, nor is the universal [related to] difference—like pots and the like in relation to each other, because of the absence of mutual connection—this has been stated. Moreover:

children.text:
08828 cintyete svātmanā bhedo vyāvṛttyā ca samānatā /
08901 asty eva vastu na anveti pravṛtty-ādi-prasaṅgataḥ //180 /
08902 sarva eva gaur aśvād bhinno abhinno vā iti bhedam abhedaṃ vā
08903 pṛcchan viśeṣam eva bhāvasya svabhāva-ākhyam adhikṛtya pravartate /
08904 sa eva hi tathā ucyate / dravyatva-ādayas tu na tatra śabda-coditāḥ
08905 yathāsvaṃ pṛthag-abhidhānāt / arthasya tad-avyabhicārāt
08906 tato gatiḥ syāt / nirloṭhitaṃ ca etad ācāryeṇa / tad ayaṃ gava-ādi-śabda-
08907 pratyupasthāpitam arthaṃ bhinnam abhinnaṃ vā pṛcchann
08908 artha-antara-upakṣepeṇa tatra kim iti dvi-mukha-buddhiḥ kriyate /
08909 tasmād yo asya ātmā ananya-sādhāraṇo yaṃ puraskṛtya puruṣo
08910 viśiṣṭa-arthakriyā-arthī pravartate yathā gor vāha-doha-ādau na anya-
08911 sambhavino arthasya yathā yuddha-praveśe sa eva svabhāvo
08912 yathāsvaṃ śabda-codito na dravyatva-ādi sāmānyam / tac-codanayā
08913 tadā prāptum anabhipretatvāt / gava-ādi-samāveśāt tad ātmabhūtānāṃ
08914 ca ananvayena tatra anubhaya-rūpatvāt / tam eva ca ayaṃ bhāvaṃ
08915 prakāraiḥ paryanuyuṅkte / tasya bhede dravyatva-ādy-abhedo
08916 asya abādhaka eva / sarvatra svabhāvena bhedasya abhyupagamāt
08917 sāmānyasya ca vyāvṛtti-lakṣaṇasya svabhāva-bhūtasya ca sāmānyasya
08918 abhede apy uktam / svātmanā eva abhede tu tat-svabhāva-nibandhana-
08919 arthakriyā-arthī samaṃ dvayor api pravarteta / eko api
08920 tām arthakriyāṃ tat-svabhāvatvād eva karoti / tad-anyasya api
08921 tat tulyam iti so api kiṃ na karoti /
children.translated_text: the same [reasoning] applies—so why does it not perform [that action]?

children.text: 08922 etena eva yad ahrīkāḥ kiṃ apy aślīlam ākulam /
children.translated_text: By this very [argument], whatever shameless, somewhat indecent and confused [talk]

children.text: 08923 pralapanti pratikṣiptaṃ tad apy ekānta-sambhavāt //181//
children.translated_text: they babble—that too is refuted, because of absolute [difference]. //181//

One inquires whether difference is through its own nature and sameness through exclusion. A real thing does exist [and] does not pervade [other things]—because of the consequence of activity and the like. //180// Anyone who asks whether everything—[e.g.,] all cows—is different from or identical to a horse, acts with reference to the particular itself, called the 'own nature' of the entity. For that alone is spoken of thus. But 'substancehood' and the like are not prompted by the word therein, since each has its own separate designation. Since the object is invariably [connected] with that [i.e., substancehood], understanding [of it] would [come] from that. And this has been thoroughly examined by the <s>Ācārya</s> (teacher). So this person, asking whether the object presented by the words 'cow' and the like is different or identical—creating a two-directional cognition by raising another entity with respect to that—[should understand:] therefore, that nature of it which is unique, with reference to which a person desiring a specific efficacious action acts—as in [the case of] a cow for drawing and milking, and not an action belonging to another thing, as in entering battle—that very own nature, prompted by the respective word, [is the meaning], not the universal 'substancehood' and the like. Because at that time there is no desire to attain [the universal] through its prompting. Because of its inclusion in cows and the like, and because those having [the universal] as their nature do not persist [across instances], there is no participation in both forms there. And this very entity is investigated by him through [various] modes. If there is difference of that [entity], the non-difference of 'substancehood' and the like does not contradict it at all—because difference through own nature is accepted everywhere, and because it has already been stated regarding the non-difference of the universal characterized by exclusion and the universal that is essential nature. But when there is non-difference through own nature itself, one desiring efficacious action grounded in that nature would equally engage in both [cases]. Even one [thing] performs that efficacious action precisely because it has that nature—of what is other than that,

08924 yad ayam ahrīkaḥ syād uṣṭro dadhi syān na iti kim apy aślīlam
08925 ayuktam aheya-upādeyam apariniṣṭhānād ākulaṃ pralapanti / tad
08926 apy anena nirastaṃ svabhāvena ekānta-bhedāt / tad-anvaye vā /
08927 sarvasya ubhaya-rūpatve tad-viśeṣa-nirākṛteḥ /
children.translated_text: if everything had both forms, since the specific distinction of that would be eliminated,

children.text: 08928 codito dadhi khādeti kim uṣṭraṃ na abhidhāvati //182//
children.translated_text: when told 'eat the curd,' why would one not run toward the camel? //182//

This shameless [talk]—'a camel might be curd, or not'—whatever somewhat indecent, unreasonable, [concerning what is] neither to be avoided nor adopted, confused [talk] they babble, due to non-conclusiveness—that too is refuted by this [argument], because of absolute difference of nature. Or, if [there were] persistence [of identity]:

children.text:
09001 tathā hy uṣṭro api syād dadhi na api sa eva uṣṭraḥ ye na anyo api syād
09002 uṣṭraḥ / tathā dadhy api syād uṣṭraḥ na api tad eva dadhi yena anyad
09003 api syād dadhi / tad anayor ekasya api kasyacit tad-rūpa-abhāvasya
09004 abhāvāt svarūpasya vā atad-bhāvinaḥ sva-niyatasya abhāvāt
09005 na kaścid viśeṣa iti / dadhi khādeti codita uṣṭram api khādet /
09006 atha asty atiśayaḥ kaścid yena bhedena vartate /
children.translated_text: But if there is some special distinction by virtue of which difference obtains—

children.text: 09007 sa eva dadhi so anyatra na asti ity anubhayaṃ param //183//
children.translated_text: that alone is the curd; that does not exist elsewhere—therefore [there is] neither both [forms] ultimately. //183//

For thus a camel too would be curd, and yet that very camel would not be [only] a camel, since another too would be a camel. Likewise, curd too would be a camel, and yet that very curd would not be [only] curd, since another too would be curd. Therefore, since there is no absence of that form in either of the two, or no absence of [their] own form—which does not become that other [form] and is restricted to itself—there is no distinction whatsoever. So, when told 'eat the curd,' one would eat the camel too.

children.text:
09008 atha anayoḥ kaścid atiśayo asti yena ayaṃ tathā coditaḥ kṣīra-vikāra
09009 eva pravartate na anyatra / sa eva atiśayo arthakriyā-arthi-pravṛtti-viṣayo
09010 dadhi / tat-phala-upādāna-bhāva-lakṣita-svabhāvaṃ hi
09011 vastu dadhi iti / sa ca tādṛśaḥ svabhāvo anyatra na asti iti / pravṛtty-abhāvād
09012 arthinaḥ / tasmāt tan na ubhaya-rūpam ity ekānta-vādaḥ /
09013 api ca /
children.translated_text: Moreover:

children.text: 09014 sarvātmatve ca sarveṣāṃ bhinnau syātāṃ na dhī-dhvanī /
children.translated_text: And if everything had the nature of all, cognition and expression would not be differentiated;

children.text: 09015 bheda-saṃhāra-vādasya tad-abhāvād asambhavaḥ //184//
children.translated_text: the impossibility of the doctrine of the elimination of difference [follows] from the absence of that. //184//

But if there is some special distinction between these two, by virtue of which one thus instructed acts only with respect to the transformation of milk and not elsewhere—that very special distinction, which is the domain of activity of one desiring efficacious action, is the curd. For a real thing whose nature is characterized by its capacity to serve as the material cause of that effect is 'curd.' And that such nature does not exist elsewhere—therefore there is no activity of the purposeful agent [toward anything else]. Therefore, that is not of both forms—this is the absolutist position.

09105 na syāt uṣṇa-svabhāvo agnir na anuṣṇa ity api / svabhāva-antarasya
09106 asataḥ kathaṃcid avyavasthāpanāt / sarvathā apratipatter

09212 abhāvo na asti iti / yat punar etad artha-niṣedhe anarthaka-śabda-aprayogān
