09214 santy abhāveṣu śabdāḥ / teṣu kathaṃ svabhāva-bheda iti /
09215 tatra api /
children.translated_text: In that case too:

children.text: 09216 rūpa-abhāvād abhāvasya śabdā rūpa-abhidhāyinaḥ /
children.translated_text: Because absence has no form, words that express form

children.text: 09217 na āśaṅkyā eva siddhās te vyavacchedasya vācakāḥ //185//
children.translated_text: need not be suspected—they are established as denoting exclusion. //185//

This shameless one, not seeing anywhere a single form restricted [to a class], due to the absence of division among entities—how would he be convinced by a cognition having a form not conjoined with other [forms], or how would he designate objects? Therefore, due to non-apprehension of difference, the doctrine of their collection would not hold—[one could say] 'a camel would be curds' or 'it would not be.' But if, having apprehended two unconjoined forms, he were to collect [them]—since the cognition that conjoins a single form is sometimes restricted [to a particular], the difference of intrinsic nature of those two forms would also be produced by the difference of their appearances—because the determination of one and many belongs to the domain of appearance. And thus, one [thing] would not have both forms—so this is a false doctrine. It is established that there is no positive concomitance of intrinsic nature among entities; rather, the universal is characterized precisely by difference. And yet, by their nature, some produce a single cognition and similar effects, while others do not. Let the universal of entities be [their] difference of intrinsic nature. But for those [absences] which have no designation, which have no intrinsic nature at all—how can words, whose domain is the difference of intrinsic nature, [apply] there? Words must necessarily be applied to them [too]—because positive and negative injunction is not possible regarding what is not established in any way. And thus, this conventional practice, based on positive and negative concomitance, would not [apply] anywhere—even [the statement] 'fire has a hot nature, not a non-hot nature.' Because the other nature, being non-existent, cannot be established in any way—[there would be] complete non-comprehension, non-comprehension of the nature of fire—and the world would be deluded. [Objection:] It may be that nothing non-existent is negated there—rather, the non-hot, which exists as a different entity, is negated. [Reply:] How is what exists now called non-existent? We do not say that what is universally non-existent does not exist there—rather, the negation of place, time, and properties is made regarding all entities, not [the negation of] the property-bearer—because when that [property] is negated, there would be no application of the word referring to that [property-bearer], and because the negative particle cannot be used without a specified object. Then how is even that negation of place and so forth [possible]? Because there is no negation of place and the like there either, nor of the object. [Objection:] The connection is negated. [Reply:] But in the negation of that [connection] too, the same fault [applies]—because, [as you say,] the word does not apply to what is non-existent after negation, and so forth. Or if its negation when non-existent [is possible], then likewise the negation of the property-bearer too. Surely the negation of a connection is not 'it does not exist.' What then? In statements like 'not here is a pot,' 'not now,' 'not thus'—the cognition arises that 'this has no connection with that' or 'that is not its property.' And thus the connection is negated. But even so, how is it negated unless the cognition arises that 'this has no connection or no property'? And there is no possibility of this [cognition] arising in any way from absences, since [the cognition of absence] is itself of that nature. Therefore, the cognition of the absence of connection [arises] from the cognition 'this is not here' and so forth. That [cognition] would not arise in the absence of that [negation]. Or [alternatively], in the cognition [arising first], [the cognition of] its absence [follows]. If [cognitions] arising from that are the source of words, by what are they prevented? For precisely that which is not the object of conceptual thoughts is not the object of words either. If those [conceptual thoughts] have operated, who can prevent expression? For cognitions do not desire an inexpressible object. But it has been stated that the connection is not expressed in its own form—because when expressed, it appears in cognition as [something] connected. Non-comprehension is according to intention. Thus, even though cognized, this [connection], being precisely of the form of the connected [thing], is not expressed in its own form. Therefore, the absurd consequence [that applies] to absence does not apply to connection. Moreover—this [objector], responding to one who says that absence is expressible, if he does not speak [i.e., does not express absence], how would he respond? Or if he does speak, how is absence unexpressed? Or perhaps he simply does not accept absence—therefore he does not speak. But then how is it the case that absence does not exist? As for the response to [the argument that] the negative particle cannot be used without an object when the object is negated, since a word without meaning cannot be used—that will be stated. Therefore, words do exist regarding absences. How then is the difference of intrinsic nature [possible] in them?

children.text:
09218 vastu-vṛttīnāṃ śabdānāṃ kiṃ rūpam abhidheyam āhosvid bheda

09305 hetur iti / sa ca ayaṃ hetutvena apadiśyamānaḥ /
09306 upādhi-bheda-apekṣo vā svabhāvaḥ kevalo athavā /
children.translated_text: the intrinsic nature, either in dependence on a difference of limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>), or alone—

children.text: 09307 ucyate sādhya-siddhy-arthaṃ nāśe kāryatva-sattva-vat //186//
children.translated_text: is stated for the purpose of establishing what is to be proved—like produced-ness and existence [are stated] regarding destruction. //186//

The doubt might arise: do words that operate in reality denote form, or do they denote difference? But absence is characterized precisely as discrimination—because there is no form that could be made a ground, and because in the presence of a form, absence would be impossible—since an entity is characterized by the presence of that [form]. Therefore, this alone is the primary discrimination. Whether words that thus proclaim absence are about discrimination—there is no room for this doubt at all. Therefore it is established that all words and conceptual constructions have discrimination as their domain. Even though they depend on a single real thing, [they apply to] discriminations that, having been made to appear as if different through differences of limits fabricated for each [word], appear as different in cognition. Therefore, even when the intrinsic nature itself stands in the relation of what is to be proved and the means of proof, there is no conjunction of what is to be proved and the means of proof. Those two are not part of the thesis and the reason. And this [reason], being designated as a reason—

children.text:
09308 apekṣita-para-vyāpāro hi svabhāva-niṣpattau bhāvaḥ kṛtakaḥ /

children.translated_text: direction, other divisions of the intrinsic-nature reason should also be understood.

children.text: 09315 sattā-svabhāvo hetuś cen na sattā sādhyate katham /
children.translated_text: If the reason has the nature of existence—how is existence proved?

children.text: 09316 ananvayo hi bhedānāṃ vyāhato hetu-sādhyayoḥ //187//
children.translated_text: For the non-positive-concomitance of differences is contradictory between reason and what is to be proved. //187//

For an entity that requires the operation of another for the accomplishment of its intrinsic nature is 'produced' (<s>kṛtaka</s>). Therefore this term 'produced,' even while denoting intrinsic nature, implies the limiting condition of another. By this, 'being differentiated by the difference of conditions' and so forth are explained. Thus, the intrinsic nature is sometimes called a reason in dependence on a difference of limiting condition, sometimes without dependence—in general, as when existence [is predicated of] impermanence alone; sometimes by grasping a specific property that is part of the intrinsic nature, as when origination [is predicated] precisely there. In this

children.text:
09317 yadi sattvam anityatve anyatra vā hetuḥ syāt sādhyam api kasmāt
09318 na iṣyate / tat kila evaṃ prasādhyamānaṃ viśeṣībhavati /
09319 na ca viśeṣaḥ sādhāyituṃ śakyate ananvayāt / yathā āha pramāṇa-
09320 viśeṣayā ajñānād iti / so ayaṃ viśeṣo na sādhya eva vyāhanyate /
09321 kiṃ tarhi / hetāv api tulya-doṣatvāt / na hi hetur ananvayaḥ siddher
09322 aṅgaṃ tataḥ saṃśayāt / na eṣa doṣaḥ / yasmāt /
09401 bhāva-upādāna-mātre tu sādhye sāmānya-dharmiṇi /
children.translated_text: But when what is to be proved is merely the taking up of existence, [and] the property-bearer is general—

children.text: 09402 na kaścid arthaḥ siddhaḥ syād aniṣiddhaṃ ca tādṛśam //188//
children.translated_text: nothing [particular] would be established, and such [a proof] is not prohibited. //188//

If existence were a reason for impermanence or for something else, why would it not be accepted also as what is to be proved? It is claimed that what is being proved in this way becomes particularized. But a particular cannot be proved, because of non-positive-concomitance—as he says, 'because of ignorance through the particularization of the means of valid cognition.' This particularization is contradicted not only in what is to be proved, but also in the reason, because the fault is equal—for a reason without positive concomitance is not a component of proof, since doubt [arises] from that. This is not a fault, because:

children.text:
09403 na sarvathā sattā-sādhane viśeṣaḥ sādhito bhavati / bhāva-mātra-
09404 viśeṣaṇo asti kaścid dharmī iti prasādhayato anirdiṣṭa-svabhāva-viśeṣasya
09405 kasyacit sattā-mātre virodha-abhāvāt na iha sattā-sādhana-
09406 pratiṣedhaḥ kiṃ tu sa tathā asti kaścid iti kaṃcana asya bhedam
09407 aparāmṛśan bruvāṇaḥ kaṃ svārthaṃ puṣṇāti / tasmād anena upātta-
09408 bheda eva sādhyaḥ /
children.translated_text: a distinction is what is to be proved.

children.text: 09409 upātta-bhede sādhye asmin bhavad hetur ananvayaḥ /
children.translated_text: When what is to be proved in this case is the taken-up distinction, the reason has non-positive-concomitance;

children.text: 09410 sattāyāṃ tena sādhyāyāṃ viśeṣaḥ sādhito bhavet //189//
children.translated_text: therefore, when existence is what is to be proved, a particular would be proved. //189//

When proving existence, a particular is not proved in every respect. For one who is proving that there is some property-bearer qualified merely by existence—since there is no contradiction in the mere existence of something whose specific intrinsic nature is not indicated—the proving of existence is not prohibited here. But one who, saying 'it exists in some way,' without considering any distinction of it—what self-interest does he serve? Therefore, by this, precisely what has been taken up as

09507 sādhanād apākaroti / tathā ca āha /
09508 liṅgasya avyabhicāras tu dharmeṇa anyatra darśyate /
09509 tatra prasiddhaṃ tad-yuktaṃ dharmiṇaṃ gamayiṣyati /
children.translated_text: there, [the mark] well-known [as] connected with that [property] will indicate the property-bearer.'

children.text: 09510 tasmān na agny-ādi-sādhana-vat sattā-sādhanam apy anavadyam iti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, like the proof of fire and the like, the proof of existence too is not faultless.

children.text: 09511 aparāmṛṣṭa-tad-bhede vastu-mātre tu sādhane /
children.translated_text: But when what is proved is merely a real thing without considering that distinction—

children.text: 09512 tan-mātra-vyāpinaḥ sādhyasya anvayo na vihanyate //190//
children.translated_text: the positive concomitance of what is to be proved, pervading that alone, is not impaired. //190//

For that property-bearer—whether characterized as <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter), one, permanent, having the nature of pleasure and the like, or something else—being particularized in whatever way, its nature of that kind is being proved. And that does not have positive concomitance in that way. Even if mere existence has positive concomitance, nothing [is achieved] by what is [thus] established. [Objection:] But then the same absurd consequence would apply to fire and the like too. [Reply:] There too, there is no dispute about the mere existence of fire. But the non-establishment [arises] because of the non-positive-concomitance of the intended particular distinction of the distinguished substrate. It is not the substrate that particularizes it—it qualifies by the exclusion of what is not connected with that—this has been stated and will be stated. Therefore, there, the universal alone is proved through the exclusion of what is not connected with that. It is not the case that anywhere there is proof of existence in that way [i.e., as particularized]. Because the very object denoted by words like '<s>pradhāna</s>' and so forth does not exist anywhere—that [existence] is without qualification. [Objection:] How [can there be] absence? It is already established through being knowable, expressible, and provable. [Reply:] Then what—let it be established that 'the knowable exists.' Even so, what would be established? But elsewhere, that very universal of fire, being unestablished there, is [what is] proved. [Objection:] But even there, positive concomitance with a universal devoid of that non-connection is not established. [Reply:] Surely no one makes positive concomitance with what is of that [unreal] nature. For one who is demonstrating to another must show that 'smoke is inseparable from fire—where there is smoke, there is fire.' That [smoke], established as pervaded by fire alone, wherever it is itself seen, generates the cognition of fire precisely there. And there, the indication of what is to be proved [contributes] nothing—because the desired [conclusion] is achieved merely from the declaration of the observed connection. And without indicating that [specific fire], how could there be positive concomitance with what is qualified by that? Thus this [smoke] is established as inseparable from fire. It implicitly excludes the non-connection of fire with that location—and so [fire] is said to be proved in that way. But positive concomitance preceded by such a specification [of what is to be proved] does not [apply]—because the statement of what is to be proved is irrelevant here. Or if it were preceded by that, who separates the thesis from the proof? And so he says: 'The non-deviation of the logical mark is shown elsewhere through the property;

09513 sādhane punaḥ sattve svabhāva-viśeṣa-aparigraheṇa vastu-mātra-
09514 vyāpini sādhya-dharme na anvaya-vyāghātaḥ / na hi tatra avaśyaṃ

children.text: 09518 dharmo viruddho abhāvasya sā sattā sādhyate katham //191//
children.translated_text: a property contradictory to absence—how is that existence proved? //191//

But when what is proved is existence, without grasping a specific intrinsic nature, in the property to be proved that pervades merely a real thing, there is no impairment of positive concomitance. For it is not necessary to grasp a specific [nature] there—because of the capacity of the means of proof even when dependent on mere existence. [It is] not what is to be proved—because [that would be] fruitless. Moreover:

children.translated_text: [It is] to be stated. For a lamp that illuminates by being luminous does not perform its function if its own form is not cognized.

children.text: 09706 dharmo gamyaḥ /
children.translated_text: The pervader of that is ascertained—the essential nature that is to be understood,

children.text: 09707 tasya ayaṃ nivṛttau vā nivartakaḥ //192//
children.translated_text: [is what is to be understood] from the ascertainment of its property—the property of that property-bearer, ascertained as the pervader.

For when existence (<s>sattā</s>) is what is to be proved, every reason for it does not escape the three classes of faults: non-establishment, deviation, and contradiction. In that case, if a property of an existent is stated as the reason—how could it be present in [a subject] whose existence is unestablished? For one who accepts a property of an existent there—how could he not accept the existent [itself]? For the essential nature itself, with reference to some [aspect], is designated as a 'property' as if it were distinct from the property-bearer. For it has been stated that there is no distinction in what is expressed by the two words denoting 'property' and 'property-bearer.' Or, if one were to state a property of both [existent and non-existent]: since, for what does not depend on a real thing, even in the absence of mere exclusion through non-restrictive negation, there is no contradiction—just as 'it is not corporeal' [and so] incorporeality would apply even to what is entirely without designation. [Objection:] Since what is without designation does not exist, it cannot be the object of negation. [Reply:] Then let it be the object of positive assertion. If [one says] that too is not [the case]—then how is it not the object of negation, since negation has the form of the cessation of positive assertion? Thus this mere exclusion, being possible for both, how could it appropriate the indicative capacity obtained through the exclusion of the suspicion of occurrence in the dissimilar [class]? And one who himself states through his own words the property-hood of both [existent and non-existent], speaks of its occurrence even in what is other than the existent and [claims] non-deviation regarding existence—how is he not a madman? But for one who states as a reason for [proving] existence the exclusion of an object pervading mere existence, being a property of absence—his reason would be contradictory, because of its non-occurrence in some [cases where] that [existence] is present, and because of the existence of the exclusion of existence in [its] absence. Thus this threefold property does not possess the characteristics of a [valid] reason for proving existence, and there is no other alternative. Therefore, existence is not provable. But if it were to be proved, then with a universal pervading that alone, when the property-bearer, which is a property of a real thing, has established existence, there is no non-establishment. And if pervasion with that property to be proved is somehow ascertained, there is no contradiction or deviation—thus this unwanted consequence does not [arise]. But when pervasion is unascertained, or when relying on the property-bearer, no indicator indicates as being of that nature. For this very reason, pervaded by its own property, established—the essential nature is the indicator.

09806 ahetutvād vināśasya svabhāvād anubandhitā //193//
children.translated_text: Of that pervaded property, this is the excluder when it ceases, or the pervading property which itself ceases. For thus this is established as its pervader if it does not exist in the absence of that. By this, the characteristic of indicativeness for both types of proof-application should be understood. For the application is twofold: through similarity and through dissimilarity. As some say: 'positive' and 'negative.' There is no real difference between these two apart from the difference in application. For even in the application through similarity, the understanding of dissimilarity [follows] implicitly, because without that [dissimilar case], the positive concomitance of the reason with what is to be proved is absent. Likewise, in dissimilarity too, the understanding of positive concomitance [follows], because without that [positive case], there is doubt about the absence of the reason in the absence of what is to be proved—this we shall explain in detail. 'Just as an effect [proves] impermanence, or a non-effect [proves] the indestructible'— by this he shows an example of both. In the positive case: whatever is produced, all that is impermanent, like pots and so forth; and sound is produced—thus, having shown the pervasion of being-produced also by impermanence, [it follows that] sound, whose being-produced has been stated, is by its very capacity impermanent. Therefore, the statement of the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis) is not necessarily required here. This is the application of the positive [proof]. In the negative case too: in the absence of impermanence, there is no being-produced; and sound is produced—since it is established as being of that nature, in its absence, it does not exist. Since the existence of being-produced in sound and the existence of what is of its nature are established by capacity when existence is known, [there is] like the previous [case], no statement of the thesis. But the positive concomitance is established by implication (<s>arthāpatti</s>). For what is restricted to what is not of that nature does not cease when that ceases. Therefore, having established that restriction, the cessation should be stated. If that succeeds, it implies the restriction to what is of that nature—thus the positive concomitance is established. But how is it to be known that what is produced is necessarily impermanent, so that this can be said? Because: Due to the causelessness of destruction, there is invariable concomitance with essential nature. //193//

children.text: 10022 yatra nāma bhavaty asmād anyatra api svabhāvataḥ //196//

This is an intervening verse. Thus this entity, being independent regarding that state, is restricted to that state—like the complete aggregate of causes, as if with no possible obstruction, in the production of the effect. [Objection:] But even for some that are independent, there is not necessarily that state everywhere—because even in the aggregate of earth, seed, and water, sometimes the sprout does not arise. [Reply:] There too it is not [independent], because of dependence on the transformation of the continuum. There is no such dependence for an entity [regarding its destruction]. Even there, the final aggregate of causes that is uninterrupted from the production of the effect—that is fruitful. And that alone is the cause of the sprout there. The earlier transformation is for that [final aggregate's] sake. And nothing is capable of obstructing that [final aggregate] there—because of the non-arising of modification when there is unity, or the loss of unity when there is arising. And for one who has not lost its nature, since an obstructing cause that does not produce deficiency in the cause with respect to producing that is not an obstructer. [Objection:] But barley seeds and such are also not dependent regarding being caused for the rice sprout—because sometimes the conditions for its production are present there too. [Reply:] How are they not dependent? Since they do not have the very nature that produces that—[they lack] the nature of the rice seed—they are dependent on that nature. [Objection:] Then for some produced things or existents too, they do not have the very nature that is perishable; therefore, being dependent on that nature, they are not perishable. [Reply:] For rice seeds and so forth too, that nature is from their own cause—so what is not the cause of that would not have that nature. And that cause, having a restricted capacity, is understood precisely in its own form. And it is not reasonable that the restriction of the essential nature of things is accidental—because for what is independent, there would be no restriction of place, time, and substance. Likewise here too, a cause of restriction must be stated. Since these particular ones are born with a destructible nature—and here there is no restrictor of essential nature, because destruction is established for all born things. [Objection:] If the nature of the born is destructible—[Reply:] Indeed, birth is not the cause of a destructible nature; and without a cause, there is no restriction of essential nature. Therefore, there is here no differentiation of essential nature from a cause. And in its absence, neither would the result exist—[the cases] are not analogous. This independence of destruction, being contrary to existence anywhere and at any time, establishes non-existence by essential nature. For the essential nature that is independent—if it were to exist sometimes or somewhere, then it would be dependent on that time and substance, and thus would not be independent—as has been stated. [Objection:] Then would the perishable nature, being independent, be causeless? [Reply:] It is not causeless, because it exists from the cause of existence alone—because of arising as such. For of what is existent, it exists precisely as such. [Objection:] It is not necessary that what exists has existence from some [cause]. [Reply:] Then existence would be accidental, and it would not cease for anyone at any time or anywhere. For [otherwise] something would attach or not attach to something somewhere—bound or unbound. If this existence is without obstruction, it would not be restricted. Therefore it is not accidental anywhere. [Objection:] But how then is destruction said to be causeless? [Reply:] Because what has been born does not depend on anything else for being in that state. And it has been stated here: 'Destruction is not some other thing separate from existence; rather, destruction is essential nature itself—for it is born abiding for only a single moment.' [For] the dull understand its nature only afterward, not before, [even though it is visible], because of the absence of acuity in perception—thus it is established afterward through the observation of change, just as poison [is identified] by the unknowing.

children.text: 10023 so ayaṃ kvacid bhavan dṛṣṭo anapekṣatvāt svabhāvata eva bhavati /
children.translated_text: This, being observed to exist somewhere, exists by its essential nature alone, because of its independence.

children.text: 10024 tathā anyatra api svabhāva-bhāvī viśeṣa-abhāvād iti /
children.translated_text: Likewise, elsewhere too it exists by essential nature, because of the absence of distinction.

children.text: 10025 yā kācid bhāva-viṣayā dvidhā eva anumitis tataḥ /
children.translated_text: Whatever inference regarding an existent thing—that is only of two kinds; therefore,

children.text: 10026 sva-sādhye kārya-bhāvābhyāṃ sambandha-niyamāt tayoḥ //197//
children.translated_text: [it operates] through effect and essential nature in [proving] their respective <s>sādhyas</s> (what is to be proved), because of the restriction of the connection of those two [with their <s>sādhyas</s>]. //197//

children.text:
10028 tasmāt dviprakārā eva vastu-viṣaya-anumitiḥ kārya-liṅgā svabhāva-
10101 liṅgā ca / yathāsvaṃ vyāpini sādhye tayor eva pratibandhāt liṅgayor
10102 liṅgini / yathoktaṃ prāk /
10103 pravṛtter buddhi-pūrvatvāt tad-bhāva-anupalambhane /
children.translated_text: Because action is preceded by cognition, when there is non-apprehension of its [the object's] existence—

children.text: 10104 pravartitavyaṃ na ity ukta-anupalabdheḥ pramāṇatā //198//
children.translated_text: 'One should not engage [in action]'—thus the validity of non-apprehension as stated is [established as a <s>pramāṇa</s>]. //198//

Therefore, inference having a real thing as its object is of exactly two kinds: having an effect as the logical mark and having essential nature as the logical mark. Because of the connection of precisely those two marks with the pervading <s>sādhya</s>, as their respective <s>sādhya</s>. As was stated before.

children.text:
10105 tṛtīyas tu hetur anupalabdhir aviśeṣeṇa kvacid arthe gamaka ity
10106 ucyate / san-niścaya-śabda-vyavahāra-pratiṣedhe hi sarvā eva anupalabdhir
10107 liṅgam / san-niścayād hi śabda-vyavahārāḥ pravartante /
10108 te pravṛttir ity uktāḥ / tathā hy anupalabdhir eva asattvam
10109 ity uktam prāk / tac ca pratipattṛ-vaśān na vastu-vaśāt / tāvad hi
10110 sa bhāvo asya na asti yāvad atra apratipattiḥ / satā api te na tad-artha-akaraṇāt /
10111 vastutas tv anupalabhyamāno na san na asan / satām
10112 api svabhāva-ādi-viprakarṣāt kadācid anupalambhāt tasya asatsv api
10113 tulyatvāt / tad etat pratipattuḥ pramāṇa-abhāvān nivṛttaṃ sattvam
10114 anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaṃ sva-nimittān śabda-vyavahārān nivartayati /
10115 tena yā api iyam anupalabdhir upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptānāṃ
10116 vastuto apy asattva-rūpā apravṛtti-yogyatvāt / tasyā apy etat tulyaṃ
10117 prāmāṇyam atra viṣaye / asan-niścaya-phalā api sā / asattāyām api iyaṃ
10118 pramāṇam eva / na hy asti sambhavo yad upalabdhi-yogyaḥ
10119 sakaleṣv anyeṣu kāraṇeṣu san na upalabhyeta / na punaḥ pūrvā
10120 asattā-sādhānī / yasmāt
10121 śāstra-adhikāra-asambaddhā bahavo arthā atīndriyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Many objects unrelated to the scope of the treatise are beyond the senses,

children.text: 10122 aliṅgāś ca kathaṃ teṣām abhāvo anupalabdhitaḥ //199//
children.translated_text: and have no logical marks—how could their absence [be established] from non-apprehension? //199//

The third type of <s>hetu</s> (logical reason), <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension), is said to be an indicator of some object without distinction. For in the negation of the ascertainment, language, and conventional practice of what exists, every non-apprehension is a logical mark. For verbal conventions operate from the ascertainment of existence. Those are called 'operation.' For non-apprehension itself is non-existence, as was stated before. And that [is so] in dependence on the cognizer, not in dependence on the real thing. For to that extent that entity does not exist for him, so long as there is non-cognition of it here. Even for existing things, they [do not function for him] because of not performing their function for him. But in reality, what is not apprehended is neither existent nor non-existent—because even of existing things, due to the remoteness of essential nature and so forth, there is sometimes non-apprehension, and that [non-apprehension] is the same even regarding non-existent things. Therefore, this existence characterized by non-apprehension, which has ceased due to the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) for the cognizer, negates the verbal conventions that are its own occasions. Therefore, even this non-apprehension—of things that fulfill the conditions of apprehension—which in reality too has the nature of non-existence, because of its fitness for non-operation—even its validity in this domain is the same. It too has the fruit of ascertaining non-existence. Even regarding non-existence, this is indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For there is no possibility that what is fit for apprehension, when all other causal conditions are present, would not be apprehended. But the former [type of non-apprehension] does not establish non-existence. Because—

children.text:
10123 so ayam asattāṃ sādhayann anupalabdhi-mātreṇa sarva-arthānāṃ
10201 pramāṇa-traya-nivṛttyā sādhayet / tatra na śāstra-nivṛttir abhāva-sādhanī /
10202 tasya kvacid anadhikāre apravṛtteḥ / śāstraṃ hi pravartamānaṃ

10204 anyathā abaddha-pralāpasya aprāmāṇyāt / tatra ca prakaraṇe

10207 kāla-vyavahitā vā prakaraṇa-anupayogino dravya-viśeṣā na tān

10210 yena anumīyeran / na ca te pramāṇa-traya-nivṛttāv api
10211 na santi iti śakyante vyavasātum / tasmān na sarva-anupalabdhiḥ
10212 sādhanī nivṛtti-niścayasya / tad iyam /
10213 sad-asan-niścaya-phalā na iti syād vā apramāṇatā /
10214 na eva vā iyam anupalabdhiḥ pramāṇaṃ vyavasāya-phalatvāt pramāṇānām /
10215 na hi pravṛtti-niṣedhe api iyaṃ niḥśaṅka-paricchedaṃ
10216 cetaḥ karoti / saṃśayād api kvacil lokasya pravṛtteḥ / tathātve
10217 tan niravadyaṃ yadi niścaya-pūrvaṃ vyavahared iti sā iyam apravṛtti-
children.translated_text: would be faultless if it conducted conventional practice preceded by ascertainment—thus this is declared to have the fruit of non-operation.

children.text: 10218 phalā proktā /
children.translated_text: [This has been] stated.

children.text: 10219 pramāṇam api kācit syāl liṅga-atiśaya-bhāvinī //200//
children.translated_text: But some [non-apprehension] that possesses the excellence of a logical mark may also be a <s>pramāṇa</s>. //200//

This [person], establishing non-existence through mere non-apprehension, would establish it through the cessation of all three <s>pramāṇas</s> for all objects. In that case, the cessation of the treatise is not a proof of absence—because [the treatise] does not operate in [domains] where it has no scope. The treatise

children.text:
10220 atra na sarva-anupalabdhir apramāṇam / pramāṇam api kācil liṅga-
10221 viśeṣa-bhāvinī yathā-udāhṛtā prāk / yat punar uktam apramāṇam anupalabdhir iti
10223 svabhāva-jñāpaka-ajñānasya ayaṃ nyāya udāhṛtaḥ /
10301 yasya kasyacit svabhāvo na upalabhyate deśa-ādi-viprakarṣāt na
10302 sa tad-anupalambha-mātreṇa asan nāma yathoktaṃ prāk / yo api
10303 jñāpakasya liṅgasya abhāvād atīndriyaḥ pratikṣipyate arthaḥ svabhāva-
10304 viśeṣo vā yathā na asti viraktaṃ ceto devatā-viśeṣo vā
10305 na asti dāna-hiṃsā-virati-cetanānām abhyudaya-hetutā iti pratyakṣe
10306 apy arthe phalasya ānantarya-abhāvād atat-phala-sādharmyād viparyasto
10307 apavadeta api na tāvatā tad-abhāva eva vyavahitānām
10308 api hetoḥ phalānām utpatti-darśanāt mūṣika-alarka-viṣa-vikāra-vat /
10309 tad-bhāve virodha-abhāvād atra anupalabdhi-mātram apramāṇam /
10310 bhāve kiṃ pramāṇam iti cet / ata eva saṃśayo astu bhaved
10311 vā pramāṇam ity apratikṣepaḥ / tad atra keṣāṃcid arthānāṃ
10312 svabhāvānāṃ vā darśana-pāṭava-abhāvāt kāraṇānāṃ kārya-utpādana-
10313 niyama-abhāvāc ca bhavej jñāpaka-asiddhiḥ / neyatā tad-abhāvaḥ /
10314 punaḥ paryāyeṇa keṣāṃcid abhivyakteḥ /
children.translated_text: Because of the manifestation of some [things] again in turn.

children.text: 10315 kārye tu kāraka-ajñānam abhāvasya eva sādhakam //201//
children.translated_text: But in the case of an effect, the non-cognition of the cause is a proof of absence alone. //201//

Here, not every non-apprehension is a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>. Some [non-apprehension] that possesses a specific logical mark is also a <s>pramāṇa</s>, as exemplified before. But what was stated [is that] non-apprehension is a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>—
This principle is illustrated for the non-cognition of what indicates essential nature.
When the essential nature of something is not apprehended due to remoteness of location and so forth, that [thing] is not called 'non-existent' merely from its non-apprehension, as was stated before. Also, an object that is beyond the senses—rejected because of the absence of an indicative logical mark—or a specific essential nature—as [in the argument] 'a dispassionate mind does not exist,' or 'a specific deity does not exist,' or 'the mental acts of giving, non-violence, and abstinence do not have the property of being causes of prosperity'—even regarding a perceptible object, because of the absence of immediacy of the result, one might wrongly deny [it] due to its similarity with what does not have that result; but not merely from that [denial] is there [proof of] the absence of that, because even for delayed effects that are remote from their causes, production is observed—like the effects of rat and rabid-dog poison. Because there is no contradiction with its existence, mere non-apprehension here is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. [Objection:] What is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for its existence? [Reply:] For that very reason, let there be doubt; or there may be a <s>pramāṇa</s>—hence non-rejection. Therefore, regarding some objects and essential natures, there may be non-establishment of their indicator due to the lack of skill in observation, and because there is no restriction on causes producing effects—[but] the absence of that [indicator] should not be taken [as proof of non-existence].

children.text:
10316 svabhāva-abhāve sādhye tad-anupalambha eva apramāṇam ucyate /
10317 kāraka-anupalambhas tu pramāṇam eva / na hy asti sambhavo yad
10318 asati kāraṇe kāryaṃ syāt / nanu kadācit kāraṇa-nāśe api kārya-sthitir
10319 dṛṣṭā / na brūmaḥ kāraṇa-sthiti-kāla-bhāvī kāryam iti / hetu-rahitā
10320 tu bhāva-utpattir na asti ity ucyate / na ca tathā sthāyī bhāvas tad-upādānaḥ /
10321 pāraṃparyeṇa tu santāna-upakārāt tat-kārya-vyapadeśaḥ /
10322 yady asya kathaṃcid abhāvaḥ sidhyet tat-phalaṃ na asti iti niścīyate /
10323 svabhāva-anupalambhaś ca svabhāve arthasya liṅgini /
10324 svabhāva-abhāva eva liṅgini svabhāva-anupalambho api kaścit pramāṇam eva /
10325 eva yady anupalabhyamāno vyāpakaḥ svabhāvo asya
10326 siddhiḥ syāt / yathā vṛkṣatvaṃ śiṃśapāyāḥ /
10327 tad-abhāvaḥ pratīyeta hetunā yadi kenacit //202//
children.translated_text:
When the absence of an essential nature is to be proved, the mere non-apprehension of that is said to be a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>. But the non-apprehension of a cause is indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For there is no possibility that an effect would exist when the cause is absent. [Objection:] But sometimes the persistence of an effect is observed even when the cause has perished. [Reply:] We do not say that the effect exists [only] at the time of the cause's persistence. Rather, it is said that the arising of an entity without a cause does not exist. Nor is a persistent entity such a material cause [at every moment]. But through succession, because of the assistance to the continuum, it is called 'its effect.' If its absence could somehow be established, then [the conclusion] 'its result does not exist' is ascertained.
And the non-apprehension of essential nature, in [proving the absence of] the object that has [that nature as] a logical mark—
Even the non-apprehension of essential nature is in some cases indeed a <s>pramāṇa</s> for [establishing] the absence of essential nature, provided the pervading essential nature that is not apprehended could be established—
just as tree-hood [is the pervading nature] of the <s>śiṃśapā</s>.
The absence of that would be cognized if by some reason— //202//

children.text:
10401 yady asya kāraṇasya svabhāvasya vyāpakasya vā abhāvaḥ kutaścid
10402 gamakād hetoḥ sidhyet / so ayaṃ asan eva sva-kāryaṃ
10403 vyāpyaṃ vā nivartayati / tad-abhāva-asiddhau nivartye api saṃśayāt /
10404 katham idānīṃ bhāvasya svayam anupalabdher abhāva-
children.translated_text: How then, from the non-apprehension of an entity by itself, is the establishment of absence

children.text: 10405 siddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: [achieved]?

children.text: 10406 dṛśyasya darśana-abhāva-kāraṇa-asambhave sati /
children.translated_text: When there is the impossibility of a cause for the non-observation of what is visible,

children.text: 10407 bhāvasya anupalabdhasya bhāva-abhāvaḥ pratīyate //203//
children.translated_text: the non-existence of an entity that is not apprehended is cognized. //203//

If the absence of this cause, essential nature, or pervader could be established from some indicating reason, then this very [thing], being non-existent, negates its own effect or what is pervaded. But when the absence of that is not established, even regarding what is to be negated, there is doubt.

children.text:
10408 bhāvo hi yadi bhaved yathāsvaṃ grāhakeṇa karaṇena upalabhya
10409 eva bhavet / sa darśana-pratibandhiṣu vyavadhāna-ādiṣv asatsu upalabhya
10410 eva / anupalabdhas tv asann iti niścīyate / tādṛśaḥ sata
10411 upalambha-avyabhicārāt / ayam eva hetur hetu-vyāpakayor abhāve
10412 api veditavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: should be understood also in the case of the absence of the <s>hetu</s> and its pervader.

children.text: 10413 viruddhasya ca bhāvasya bhāve tad-bhāva-bādhanāt /
children.translated_text: And in the presence of a contrary entity, because of the obstruction of the existence of that,

children.text: 10414 tad-viruddha-upalabdhau syād asattāyā viniścayaḥ //204//
children.translated_text: from the apprehension of what is contradictory to it, there would be the ascertainment of non-existence. //204//

For if an entity were to exist, it would exist only as apprehended by its own appropriate means of cognition. When the obstacles to observation such as intervening barriers and so forth are absent, it would [exist] only as apprehended. But when not apprehended, it is ascertained as non-existent—because of such [a thing's] non-deviation from the apprehension of what exists. This very reason

children.text:

10418 na pṛthag vyavasthāpyate / tata eva virodha-gater virodhāc ca abhāva-
10419 sādhanāt / bhavatu nāma evaṃvidhāyā anupalabdher abhāva-

10421 dṛṣṭānta-anapekṣaṇāt / na hy asyāṃ kaścid dṛṣṭānto asti / kiṃ
10422 na nirupākhyaṃ vyomakusuma-ādi dṛṣṭāntaḥ / tad asat katham
10423 avagantavyaṃ yena evaṃ syāt / anupalabdher eva iti cet / tatra
10424 katham adṛṣṭāntikā asattā-siddhiḥ sadṛṣṭāntatve vā anavasthā-prasaṅgaḥ /
10425 tathā ca apratipattiḥ / tasmān nirupākhya-abhāva-siddhi-vad

10427 na avadhāraṇa-paṭuḥ / nimittaṃ hy asac-śabda-vyavahārāṇām
10428 upalabhya-anupalabdhiḥ / sā sva-saṃnidhānāt sva-nimittān

10501 dṛṣṭāntaḥ / asattā punar atra anupalabdhir eva / ata eva iyaṃ kāraṇāt

10505 nirupākhye api iyam eva pravṛttir niṣidhyate / anupalabdhi-
