12510 vedam adhyayanam adhyayana-pūrvatā-sādhanam /
children.translated_text: Vedic study be the means of proving being preceded by [prior] study.

children.text: 12511 sarvathā anāditā sidhyed evaṃ na apuruṣa-āśrayaḥ /
children.translated_text: In every way, beginninglessness would be established thus, not dependence on a non-person.

children.text: 12512 tasmād apauruṣeyatve syād anyo apy anara-āśrayaḥ //244//
children.translated_text: Therefore, if [the <s>Veda</s> is] non-authored, there would be something else too that is not dependent on humans. //244//

Just as even the first fire made by a traveler is preceded by another flame, not by the churning of fire-sticks—because it is a traveler's fire, like the subsequent fire. But how is there deviation for the traveler's fire? For relying on the capacity to produce flame, an alternative cause for combustion is excluded: 'if it could exist without a flame, it would exist elsewhere too.' There, if the two births—from flame and from something else—are not mutually exclusive, then [one might suspect] that not being produced from a flame could also hold otherwise, since both properties are possible in a single object; thus it is suspected that the traveler's fire or any other object would not be restricted to one [origin]—this is the deviation. That [deviation] too—the descent of two mutually exclusive properties—is said to be non-contradictory in the universal of a real thing, but not in a particular that differentiates states, because of the contradiction of being and not being that in a partless self. And there is no mutual exclusion between birth from flame and birth from something else in the traveler's fire, because there is no impossibility other than [being] excluded from origination from flame. Such a traveler's fire may be produced from flame, but not every [fire]. Because the exclusion of a particular cannot be effected there, and because a possible particular is not necessarily restricted to [one] condition. As for 'if it could exist without a flame, it would exist elsewhere too'—indeed it does [exist elsewhere]. If the aggregate by which it comes into being existed—one would show the possibility of that [aggregate] or show the absence of that, or the flame there—that would [settle it]. Therefore, the learning of one [person] preceded by another does not establish that all are in that same condition, because of the non-impossibility of it being otherwise. But for one of such a kind, lacking the appearance of that activity, it might be so. What is of such a nature should be stated thus—but [an argument] stated without distinction, while a distinguishing particular is possible, does not bear fruit. [Objection:] How is the particular possible, since those persons too are simply incapable, just like present-day persons? [Reply:] Here too, no contradiction is observed between capability and personhood—therefore a positive assertion of what is non-contradictory, [using] non-apprehension, is not indicative. For it has been stated that there is no knowledge of contradiction regarding what is beyond the senses. And this does not differ from the previous argument: 'if persons were capable, even present-day [persons would be capable].' This would [only prove] the impossibility of the particular, and that is difficult to establish. 'Where one is incapable, all persons [are incapable] there'—this too is deviant, as in the previous [argument], because of the establishment of capability for someone in the <s>Bhārata</s> and so forth, even though present-day [persons] are incapable. Therefore, for those who discriminate causes, even in objects that have the appearance of being that or not that, the difference of essential nature should be shown. In its absence, either everything is of that nature or nothing is. And here we do not see an essential difference between the worldly and the Vedic. In the absence of that, since both are perceived only as a universal, one who discriminates a property of one, suspecting that [property] as possible given that essential nature—the argument of suspected deviation is made. [Objection:] But between Vedic and non-Vedic, there is indeed a particular distinguished by [its revelation of] truth. [Reply:] True, there is. Not only of those two. What then? Of the <s>Ḍiṇḍika Purāṇa</s> and its counterpart too. And a difference of name that illuminates the difference of one's own procedure does not refute being person-made, because of the unwanted consequence [applying] elsewhere too. If persons were unable to compose such a composition, or if one without established convention could discriminate [a divinely] composed one, then clearly the <s>Veda</s> would be non-authored (<s>apauruṣeya</s>). [Objection:] But persons are simply unable to compose <s>mantras</s>. [Reply:] We shall examine this later. Moreover, a <s>mantra</s> is not some entirely different thing. What then? It is a statement that accomplishes the desired purpose of those who possess the power of truth and austerity. And that is seen even in present-day persons, from the observation of the arrest of poison, fire, and so forth through the power of truthful resolve, according to each [person's capacity]. And because certain <s>Śabaras</s> (tribals) even today compose <s>mantras</s>. And because non-Vedic <s>mantra</s>-rituals are observed among Buddhists and others. And those are person-made. If those too are non-authored, then how is non-authored [synonymous with] non-erroneous? For in the <s>mantra</s>-rituals of Buddhists and others, violence, sexual union, the view of a self, and such—which are causes of non-prosperity—are described differently [from Vedic mantras]. How could both, stating contradictory things about a single [matter], be true? In positing a different meaning there, the same [applies] elsewhere too—hence from the non-determination of meaning, there is non-cognition in some [cases]. And thus even what is [actually] valid is useless if non-authored. If [one says] Buddhists and others have no [real] <s>mantras</s>—then one should also have to take poison in other [non-Buddhist cases]. Buddhists too are observed to be engaged in poison-rituals. So the absence of <s>mantras</s> [for them] is also contradicted. Rituals are also performed by non-verbal means such as <s>mudrās</s> (hand gestures), <s>maṇḍalas</s>, and <s>dhyānas</s> (meditations). And it is not reasonable that those are non-authored and eternal. When those can accomplish ritual actions, what obstacle is there for persons in composing verbal formulas? Therefore, there is nothing these [persons] are incapable of doing. [Objection:] But how can both <s>mantra</s>-rituals, being born of truth, be mutually contradictory? [Reply:] Indeed, they are not everywhere born of truth. They may also be characterized by the declarations of persons possessed of power. And that power may come from special attainments of movement and so forth too. [Objection:] If <s>mantras</s> are person-made, why don't all persons compose <s>mantras</s>? [Reply:] Because of the deficiency of the means for composing them. If [they] were endowed with such [qualities as] truth, austerity, and so forth, they would indeed compose [them]. Moreover, a person composes poems—[does it follow that] every person would be a poet? Or if not, then no one at all [is a poet]—[such would be] an unprecedented verbal reasoning! Truly, those who lack the means for composing <s>mantras</s> do not compose <s>mantras</s>. But we do not see that completeness [of means] in anyone, because of the uniformity of nature among persons. It has been stated here: 'A <s>mantra</s> is not some entirely different thing—[it is merely] the convention of speech of those possessing truth and so forth.' And those [qualities] are seen in some persons. That all persons lack them—since there is no contradiction to the possibility of that [occurring], this is indeterminate. And non-apprehension is not a cause of certainty regarding what is beyond the senses by nature. And the powers of memory, intellect, penetration, and truth are not [necessarily] present in all. There may be means for attaining other qualities, just as there are different traditions of means for accomplishing that. Nor can everything that exists be observed. For this very reason, what has not been observed cannot be denied. Nor is there anything that prevents any quality that wishes to arise in persons, because when the exclusion [of that quality] is unobserved, the excluder-excluded relationship is unestablished. By this, the denial of omniscience and so forth are also given their answer. There too, the principle that 'such a tradition of means for accomplishing that, which is of this kind, does not exist' [does not hold]. Nor [does the principle] that 'what is not observed does not indicate what is not of that nature'—because even existing [things] may fail to initiate their effects, and because of the inability to observe due to the extreme subtlety of essential nature. Therefore, 'study [of the <s>Veda</s>] is preceded by other study, [and this is known] from study'—this deviates even in the study of the <s>Bhārata</s>, because it is present [there too]. [Objection:] But there is no fault because of the qualifier 'Vedic.' [Reply:] But what excellence does the study of the <s>Veda</s> have, such that it cannot be studied otherwise? For a qualifier that is not contradicted by the dissimilar [class] does not exclude the reason from this [dissimilar class], because of the possibility of non-contradictory [properties] in a single [subject]. [Objection:] Because of [the study] of present-day [persons]. [Reply:] This has been answered. [Objection:] Because of non-observation. [Reply:] This too has been refuted. Nor does mere non-observation indicate absence—[this is] simply deviation. Therefore, the qualifier is not superior [to what is unqualified]—[this is] the same as what has not been taken up. The pervasion 'whatever Vedic study there is, all that is preceded by another [prior] study' is also not established, because being in that condition is not established for all. But what has been observed as the cause of that—that is indeed so. When a particular has been observed, grasping the universal by abandoning that particular as the cause—that is simply deviant, like the yellow color of substances in the proof of fire.  By this, [arguments from] statement and so forth for proving attachment and so forth are also answered. Let

children.translated_text: Of the practices of <s>mlecchas</s> (barbarians) and so forth, and of atheistic statements too—

children.text: 12522 anāditvāt tathābhāvaḥ pūrva-saṃskāra-santateḥ //245//
children.translated_text: because of beginninglessness, such is the condition, due to the continuity of prior impressions. //245//

For a person himself, having reflected, or [learning] from another, studies. It is not the case that sounds resonate by themselves for those whose faculties are not engaged, so that [the <s>Vedas</s>] would be non-authored. [The <s>Vedas</s>] might be non-authored if there were a beginning of persons. But even then, [study] preceded by another is not established, because of the absence of a teacher. Therefore, the first student would be the author himself. So this beginningless human activity—proceeding from the observation of each preceding [generation], like children's play in the sand and so forth—would be [merely] human convention, not non-authored. If non-authorship [follows] from beginninglessness, there would be even more that is non-authored now. For thus:

children.translated_text: what [is the use] of non-authorship?

children.text: 12606 sati vā veda-vākyānām eva apauruṣeyatve /
children.translated_text: Or, if the non-authorship belongs to Vedic statements alone—

children.text: 12607 artha-saṃskāra-bhedānāṃ darśanāt saṃśayaḥ punaḥ //246//
children.translated_text: from the observation of differences in meaning and impressions, doubt [arises] again. //246//

Some practices of <s>mlecchas</s>—such as marriage with one's mother, festivals of <s>Madana</s> (the love god), and so forth—are also beginningless. And atheistic statements too deny what is unprecedented, the next world, and so forth. For those who have not had impressions instilled [in them] do not initiate those [practices] through others. Even for those whose conventions are fashioned by their own intuition—because their activity [proceeds] precisely through the gathering of conceptual constructions of meanings not [previously] heard. That something comes from somewhere—since there is no continuous [chain traceable to] a single teacher, it is said to be 'preceded by another.' Previously, [there were] worldly conventions, proceeding in accordance with observation—activities both correct and incorrect. [Objection:] But in those posited as primordial, conventions not previously observed are accepted as having subsequently arisen. [Reply:] No, because even those, having been deposited by the impressions of others, awaken in accordance with their conditions. [Objection:] Let everything be non-authored. [Reply:] In such a [definition of] non-authorship, what virtue would there be even if it is established? Certainly, non-authorship is intended [to mean] 'non-deceptive.' But since that [non-deceptiveness] exists for some beginningless [traditions] that are deceptive too—

children.translated_text: What result would there be in establishing the [authorlessness] of phonemes, since there is no difference from other [phonemes]? For the phonemes of worldly [speech] and the <s>Veda</s> are not different. And even if they were different, since there is no difference in recognition, there would be the absurd consequence of non-establishment of their identity from that [recognition]; and because of the non-perception of difference, the Vedic phonemes are not established [as distinct]—because from [the same] recognition, there would be the consequence of non-apprehension [of any difference]. And because [this is] not accepted [by anyone]. And in establishing the authorlessness of those [phonemes], since they are the same everywhere—what is left out by this [argument]? And thus all conventional usage would be authorless. But not all [conventional usage] is truthful—so the effort is pointless. Now, if the sentence

children.text: 12701 vākyaṃ na bhinnaṃ varṇebhyo vidyate anupalambhanāt //247//
children.translated_text: is desired [to be] authorless—

Even if [the <s>Veda</s> were] authorless, if it generated a determinate cognition of its meaning, there would be confidence. But the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> (etymologists), <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, and others are seen to dissect Vedic sentences through arbitrary superimposition and denial. Nor do those meanings cohere for them—because of the primacy of convention in the assignment of meaning, and because multiple interpretations are possible even for a single sentence; because of the multiple meanings listed for roots and suffixes; because even established usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>) is not unconditionally accepted; because of the abundance of words without established usage; because the meaning of those [words] requires instruction by a person; and because that instruction follows that [person's] desire—there is simply no determination regarding the meanings of Vedic sentences. Moreover, this person establishing authorlessness would establish it either for the phonemes or for the sentence. Therein:

a sentence is not something different from the phonemes, because of non-perception. //247// For in the words and sentences like '<s>Devadatta</s>' and the like, apart from the appearance of the 'da' sound and the like, we do not see any other appearance in cognition—unlike the appearance of a second phoneme. Nor can it be determined that something not appearing [in cognition] exists as an object of apprehension or as something else—like some other aspect. [Objection:] An effect that cannot arise from anything else is indicative [of the sentence]. [Reply:] This might be so, if even when those phonemes are present, that effect would not occur. [Objection:] It does not occur in a different word or sentence even though they [the phonemes] are undifferentiated. [Reply:] No—because the non-differentiation [of phonemes across different words] is not established. [Objection:] Non-differentiation is established from recognition. [Reply:] No—because that [recognition] deviates and is not demonstrative. Even with non-differentiation of phonemes, the difference of understanding from the difference of sentences could be the difference of effects. And that [understanding comes] from the sentence. And how would that [sentence] be beyond the senses? If it were generated by mere proximity [of phonemes], even one who has not learned [the language] would [understand]. Therefore, there is nothing called a 'sentence' that is a separate entity from the phonemes, whose authorlessness could be established. Since that does not exist, the authorlessness of the phonemes, which are undifferentiated from those of the <s>Veda</s>, has been refuted in the first alternative. Moreover, let the sentence be a separate entity.

children.text: 12823 ekatve api hy abhinnasya kramaśo gaty-asambhavāt //250//
children.translated_text: even if one, since sequential apprehension of what is undivided is impossible— //250//

For a sentence is a verbal form whose meaning is complete. And if those components are individually of that kind, then each of them is [itself] a sentence. And thus the sentence does not have many components. And since the sentence-meaning would be understood through the apprehension of a single component, there would be no dependence on other components, and no expenditure of time. Because when that [sentence], whose nature is without parts, is apprehended in an instant, upon the arising of a single cognition there is complete understanding. And otherwise, [having parts] would contradict [its] oneness. And when heard all at once, temporal difference [in apprehension] is not reasonable. But, lest the sentence lose its many-componented nature because the sentence-meaning is established from a single component alone without expecting any other component, [one might say] all components are heard at once. Even then, temporal delay is simply not reasonable—because all [components] are heard in the very time of apprehending a single component. And in sequential hearing, since the sentence-meaning is established from a single one of the individually meaningful [components], the others would be pointless. And when heard all at once, the meaningfulness of those that individually have separate meanings is not established through any observed capacity. [Objection:] There is no fault because of seeing meaning in the combined [components]. [Reply:] No—because a form that does not exist separately cannot exist in combination either. And because no other entity arises [from the combination]. For the proponents of sound-origination, this is indeed not a fault—because even though individually incapable, the components have a special function of mutual assistance, and being thus endowed with excellence, they serve a special effect. But when each component is individually capable, the imagining of another [component] would be pointless. But if the sentence is one and without components—

children.translated_text: temporal difference is simply not reasonable. For the sequential apprehension of one [thing] is not reasonable—because the grasped and the ungrasped would be undifferentiated. But sequential apprehension of a sentence is observed—because the time of uttering, hearing, and remembering any sentence is completed through the sequence of many moments and eye-blinks. And because no sound-essence that does not partake of the phoneme-form [yet] appears in a single cognition is [ever] perceived. Because of the sequential apprehension of phonemes. Even when those [phonemes] are undifferentiated, since the difference of sentences is due to sequence, the apprehension of a sentence involves sequence. If the assistance of the phoneme-sequence were not needed, then even with the phonemes arranged in any random way, any sentence whatsoever would be apprehended—or even without phonemes [at all]. Because what lacks sequence cannot assist what has sequence. And because it is impossible to utter without sequence. And because there is no other possibility. [Objection:] Phonemes do not [truly] exist in the sentence—that one sound-form alone, due to the sequence of its manifestors, appears as if having sequence and as if divided into phonemes. [Reply:] The manifestation of what is without sequence by a sequential manifestor has been refuted. Because of the contradiction of the manifested and the unmanifested. And in a sentence that is without a phoneme-portion, one who has not heard the whole [sentence] would not apprehend the whole sentence—because one [partless sentence] cannot have a portion; nor would anyone hear it whole. Even the [claim] that the sentence is determined by the final cognition which has the impressions of all phonemes is false—because that [sentence], not partaking of a phoneme-form, is never apprehended by anyone. And because, since phonemes cannot be apprehended without sequence, whence is there a sentence called [something] without sequence, graspable by a single cognition? Nor do we perceive any other unpartitioned sound-essence beyond the apprehension of the final phoneme. Nor does even the speaker himself discern [such a thing]. It is merely the confused mind, deluded by the desire for something good, that dreams: 'if it were so, it would be good for me'—that 'the sound, whose parts are completed in the final cognition, shines forth.' For even in the words and sentences that are being recalled, the phonemes are not discerned without a particular sequence. Because in a cognition without sequence, there is no before and after. [And] the difference of words and sentences, which is caused by that [sequence], would not exist. Nor do we see any other sound-form apart from the phoneme-sequence—as stated. And if it does exist, it would be either impermanent or permanent. If impermanent—produced by effort, how would that not be of human origin? For what is impermanent must necessarily originate from something. For as stated, if [it arose] spontaneously, there would be no restriction of place and the like of its existence. And that [origination] is observed [only] in unimpaired instruments impelled by effort, and not otherwise. From observing the property of the cause, human effort alone is the cause. Therefore, it would be of human origin. Even if it were permanent, perception [of it] would always [occur], since there would be no possibility of obstruction. //251//

children.text: 13115 kāmam anya-pratīkṣā astu niyamas tu virudhyate //252//
children.translated_text: Let there be dependence on another; but restriction is contradicted. //252//

Now, if that sound-form were eternal and had the nature of being perceivable—then that nature, never departing from it, would be perpetually perceived. For thus it would be eternal if it were not dislodged from its capacity by anything, because the capacity to produce cognition is of its very nature, and because otherness has already been refuted. Nor is any obstruction of perception possible for what is of perceivable nature—because even in the presence of that [obstruction], since it does not break up its nature, the setting aside of capacity is impossible. For what does not produce a surplus in it has no effect whatsoever. And what has no effect—how is it an obstruction of anything, or anything else?—this has been mostly examined. What surplus do walls and so forth produce or destroy in pots and so forth, that they are considered obstructions? We do not say they produce any surplus. Rather, not all moments of the pot are the causes of sense-cognition for everyone; but the object, sense, and light, taken together, are causes of cognition through the production of a distinguished subsequent moment from each other, because what is not benefited cannot reasonably be dependent [on another]. It has been stated that for what has a capable nature, there would be perpetual generation or perpetual non-generation [of cognition] by another. And those [factors], being uninterrupted, assist each other through another that obstructs—because of the cooperating [factor of] fitness for the uninterrupted location, because of the arising of a mutual surplus from them. But when there is interruption, due to the absence of the cause, because a capable subsequent moment does not arise, cognition does not arise. Therefore, due to the cessation of the previously arisen capable [moment], when there is a wall, because of the non-arising of another [moment] that wishes to arise through the absence of its cause, cognition does not arise due to the deficiency of the cause—thus walls and so forth are called 'obstructions.' Not because what was previously fit is blocked, since it does not lose its essential nature. Alternatively, even mutual assistance among momentary entities is possible, because the capacity of causes and conditions is inconceivable to one who is not omniscient. Therefore, what stands between the sense and the object as an obstruction might produce a surplus in those two through differences in the degree of deficiency in the production of cognition. When there is a difference in obstruction, from the observation of dullness and sharpness of hearing in sound and so forth. Otherwise, since the proximity of something that has no effect anywhere would be equal to non-proximity, the correlation 'this belongs to that' would be merely a conceptual construction, not based on reality. And causal functions do not conform to superimposition. For a boy is not hired for cooking from the [mere] designation of 'burner.' Therefore, even when there is conceptual construction, entities that are not changed by that would operate according to their own nature. So even with the obstruction, the senses and so forth would [still] inform. But they do not. Therefore it is understood that [the obstruction] confers a modification upon them. But for eternal sounds, there is neither loss nor gain of surplus when something [else] is present. So if their nature is to produce cognition, they would all produce all cognitions of their respective objects for everyone, all at once. If not, then never for anyone any [cognition at all]—this is an absolute [dilemma]. [Objection:] Absence of hearing is due to the incompleteness of some cooperating [factor]. [Reply:] This might be so—[one might say:] not because of obstruction are all sounds not always heard, but rather some cooperating [factor] for their cognition is specifically restricted; it exists for some

children.translated_text: We do not reject that causes have cooperating [factors]. But causes, while depending [on cooperating factors], [depend on them as] assisting that condition. Because the surplus obtained from that serves the effect. Likewise, if sound too were to produce its effect depending on something—let it do so. But the restriction to its prior essential nature would not hold, because of [its] dislodgment from it. And because from what is depended upon, another essential nature is obtained. For it has been stated that what does not assist is not depended upon. And when the assistance of that is something different, the absence of connection and so forth of that have been stated. And its unknowability—because cognition arises precisely from the assistance. Therefore, sound does not depend on the sense, the contact, itself, or anything else as the basis for the production of cognition in producing its own cognition—because everything there has no effect. Moreover: these sounds would be either pervasive or non-pervasive. If they are non-pervasive, there would be non-perception everywhere. How would something located in one place be perceived by someone situated in a place devoid of it? [Objection:] In the view that accepts perception without contact, there is no fault. [Reply:] No, because even there, different degrees of being in a fit location are required, like a magnet and so forth. Otherwise, there would be no distinction of clear and unclear hearing. And if the condition for perception is present, they would be perceived equally in every location. Therefore, they are not non-pervasive. If they are pervasive, there would be the perception of all [sounds] simultaneously. //253//

children.translated_text: It might be [objected:] Those conditionings of sounds are specifically restricted. Among them, a sense conditioned by a certain [conditioning] is the perceiver of only a certain [sound]—thus there is no simultaneous hearing of all sounds. [Reply:] If hearing of the senses is restricted due to the specificity of conditioning, then there would be no hearing of a conglomerate of many sounds—a din. For a din is not a single sound. Because of the simultaneous hearing of things of different essential natures. And because the establishment of difference is based on difference of essential nature. [Objection:] Hearing at once is due to the brevity [of the sounds], and is an error. [Reply:] Then in the stream of sounds of a flute and so forth, the cognition would be confused because of the gathering of meaningful components. And the refutation of this will be stated here. Therefore, because of the restriction of the sense to a single object of cognition, the manifold din would not be heard.  [Objection:] If only sounds (<s>dhvanis</s>) are heard there, then they are not meaningful [sounds]. [Reply:] In a din, phonemes, words, and sentences are not heard—because only bare sounds are heard. And the sense, whose capacity is restricted to the meaningful [sound], is not [restricted] to the [bare] sounds. In that case: 'That [a meaningful sound] exists as distinct from sounds—this faith is excessive!' //256//

children.translated_text: For we do not observe sound (<s>dhvani</s>) and meaningful sound (<s>śabda</s>) as having distinct forms. We determine the nature of the [meaningful] sound as one single thing when hearing the sequence of phonemes. How then do we, without determining, engage in conventional practice that presupposes determination? Therefore, this is just a specific kind of sound named 'phoneme' and so forth. Moreover: 'When other sounds exist [simultaneously], how is the meaningful sound heard?' Neither is the sound different from the [bare] sound, nor [heard] separately together with it. For instruction from another is not weightier regarding a directly perceived object. So this [person], hearing sound alone when other speakers are present, understands the absence of capacity of those conditions for perceiving it to produce something other than that. For if they were capable, what is accomplished by that [capability] would be perceived. But the conditions, being of precisely that nature—how would they initiate something different in a din? For it is not reasonable that there be a difference of effect when there is no difference of cause, because difference would be causeless—as has been stated. And it is not the case that the meaningful sound is not heard in a din, because of the observation of the division of words and sentences. Or how, due to the restriction of capacity, would there be a different course of [bare] sounds? //257//

children.text: 13415 dhvanibhir vyajyamāne asmin vācake api kathaṃ na te //258//
children.translated_text: how are those [faults] not [present] even in this meaningful [sound] that is manifested by sounds? //258//

Even those senses with restricted capacities hear the various sounds that are specific to each sound—but not [meaningful] sounds in the same way. So what aversion do they have to [meaningful] sounds? As for what was said—'sounds are not established as different from meaningful sounds'—how are they not established? Because of the cognition of meaning from speech. For there is no cognition of word-meaning from a lesser portion of the sound. And that [portion] is not equal to another. So this cognition of the meaning to be accomplished in the complete form of words and sentences is not possible in the incomplete portions of sounds—thus the existence of a sound-form that is without sequence is established. And the sound is a sequential part. [Reply:] No, because what is without sequence, being distinct from what is sequential, has already been refuted. And there would be overextension in this way. Since in the parts of an action, the earlier [parts] are not connected with the later, and since from a single part there is no cognition [of the whole], in hand-signals and such, which are causes of understanding meaning, a complete form that is the nature of action, distinct from that [sequence], would have to be accepted—just like sound. [The truth is:] it is reasonable that the different phoneme-parts or action-parts, being sequential, arising from the use of their respective instruments, become the objects of conceptual thought and produce the cognition of meaning exactly in accordance with convention. Moreover:

children.translated_text: And there can be no fixed arrangement of them, due to the contradiction with an alternative sequence. //259//

The meaningful sound, manifested by sequential sound-portions, supposedly speaks. But they too do not illuminate it all at once, because of being sequential. Nor does a single portion alone manifest the [complete meaningful] sound, because of the unwanted consequence of the purposelessness of others. And at the time of a single phoneme-portion, the complete form is not observed. So how would this, whose complete perception is not assembled, establish [anything] for the purpose of the assemblage of complete perception—just like the sounds? For what distinction is there, in utter non-perception, between the existent and the non-existent regarding objects that are to be established through perception? Nor is mere proximity a means of proof, because [the meaningful sound] requires manifestation. And this [manifestation], being sequential, is of equal use for the existent and the non-existent—thus what is to be accomplished through sounds cannot be accomplished. There too it is the same—enough with the rest. Therefore, there is no non-authorship in phonemes or in sentences. [Objection:] If the sentence is the sequence of phonemes—[Reply:] it is not, because of the non-difference of phonemes. The sentence is not some other thing that is the sound-form, which is non-authored. Rather, what we call a 'sentence' is characterized by the sequence of phonemes. [Objection:] That [sequence] is what is to be proved as non-authored. [Reply:] No, because the sequence of phonemes is not different [from them]. This [sequence] is not something other than the phonemes—when it is visible, because the division is observed; when it is invisible, because there is no cognition of it from that, due to the absence of a mark. And if the sequence, which possesses difference, is absent—

children.text: 13607 anitya-avyāpitāyāṃ ca doṣaḥ prāg eva kīrtitaḥ //260//
children.translated_text: And in the case of impermanent and non-pervasive [phonemes], the fault has already been stated. //260//

If the sequence of phonemes (<s>varṇas</s>) is uncreated, and they are not many of the same class — so that some would have a fixed sequence while others would have their order reversed at will — but rather there is only one <s>akāra</s> in the triple world, and likewise one <s>gakāra</s>, then only '<s>agni</s>' (fire) would [result], not '<s>gagana</s>' (sky), since the prior-and-posterior relationship of <s>akāra</s> and <s>gakāra</s> is fixed. Even for created things that are subject to the regularity of causal transformation, the reversal of sequence cannot be accomplished — as in the case of seed, sprout, leaf, and so forth, and seasons, years, and the like. How much more so for uncreated things whose nature is an unchanging state, established in some particular way, since without abandoning their prior state there is no possibility of being otherwise — or, if there were such abandonment, the undesirable consequence of destruction [would follow]. Especially when the sequence is permanent. This variation of sequence at each step would arise either from the difference of phonemes [requiring] the production of something new, or from the multiplicity of phonemes — and neither is accepted.
Moreover:
The absence of spatial and temporal sequence [follows] from the description of [their] pervasiveness and permanence.
Furthermore, this sequence of phonemes would be either produced by spatial position — as in a row of ants — or produced by temporal position — as in the case of seed, sprout, and the like. Neither of these two kinds is possible for [permanent] phonemes, because of their pervasiveness and permanence. For spatial priority-and-posteriority consists in functioning while mutually excluding each other's positions; this is not possible for phonemes, since all [phonemes] occupy the same position as every other — like wind and sunshine, or like the self (<s>ātman</s>) and the like. Similarly, temporal priority-and-posteriority consists in functioning while excluding each other's times — when one does not exist, the other exists. This too is not possible for permanent [entities], since all exist at all times. And there is no other possibility. Therefore, how could the priority-and-posteriority of phonemes

The sequence of manifestations (<s>vyaktis</s>) too cannot constitute the sentence, since permanent manifestations have been refuted.
It is not the form-sequence of the phonemes [themselves] that is the sentence. What then? [It is the sentence] of their manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>). [The idea is that] this [manifestation], arising from the sequence of cognitive factors that manifest each respective phoneme, possesses sequential order, and therefore 'the sequence [of manifestations] is the sentence' — this too is false. For that [permanent manifestation] has already been rejected for permanent [entities]. The particular effect-nature itself, through the direct imposition of potency upon the causes of cognition,

children.text: 13713 yathā dīpo anyathā vā api ko viśeṣo asya kārakāt //262//
children.translated_text: like a lamp. Or is it otherwise? What distinction does it have from a producer (<s>kāraka</s>)? //262//

Indeed, the world designates as 'effect-nature' that form which is perceived only from a certain [source], relying on the perception that is inseparable from that [source's] perceivability. And this [effect-nature] exists for phonemes too. And the same is the basis [for effect-nature] elsewhere as well — there is no distinction. Then how, when the ground for acceptance is the same, are phonemes not effects?
Nor is the establishment of effect-nature based on perception [alone]. What then? It is based on existence — [the principle] 'it exists when [its cause] exists.' From where is that existence established, such that it would not establish effect-nature? For when this [existence] is not established, it does not follow that 'it exists thus.' Therefore, the proof of existence is that which establishes it. And that is perception alone.
True, this would be so if its existence were not already established prior [to perception]. For that proof of existence is one which is preceded by non-establishment. But is not that form [already] unestablished which is useful for an uninterrupted cognition of that kind? If [one says:] 'It is already established, but not utilized due to the deficiency of other [conditions]' — how then is there non-difference between the utilized and the non-utilized? Nor is there a difference [in the phoneme itself] that is untouched by the nature of the word — since the superiority [i.e. the additional factor] that is established as [producing] the utilization is itself the cause. For it is only that whose presence accomplishes the thing to be accomplished that is reasonably useful therein. If one [says] this very superiority is useful, the same problem applies to it.
Therefore, [what is] superior is precisely the operation of unmediated capacity — the difference of state; everything else is not. And the dependence on what is not superior has already been rejected.
Furthermore, that [capacity], being established from the operation of the instruments alone, is of the same nature as all effects. Whether everything expressible is expressed in the manifestation of such [a capacity], or nothing at all — there is no distinction. For thus:

children.translated_text: being invariably [connected with that operation], the effect-nature [of phonemes is established]; for in a [mere] manifester, that [invariable connection] is impossible. //263//

If that which is established in the world as a 'manifester' — one that causes the cognition of another through the medium of its own cognition, like a lamp and the like — if it were already established [prior to manifestation], that is established from the moment the homogeneous material cause [exists]. That very cognitive superiority is not [itself caused by the manifester], since it is conditioned by the totality of [its own] causal factors.
Those, however, who are 'producers' (<s>kārakas</s>) through the perception of what was not [previously] established — like a potter and the like with respect to a pot — even recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) and other alleged proofs of establishment do not support the definition of [a mere] cause.
Furthermore, the claim that a later cognition of '<s>a</s>' has the same object as a prior cognition of '<s>a</s>' and is 'like it' and so forth — this too is not capable of proving the non-difference of the two particulars (<s>svalakṣaṇas</s>), since [non-difference] is established [only] from their own natures. When speaking in general terms, there is no contradiction even with having different objects. And for two cognitions that have a single object, their being prior and posterior is untenable — since [things] arise or do not arise depending on whether or not their causes are present; and since even when [causes are] present, what has not arisen is not caused by that — the two [cognitions] have entirely different sets of causes. In that case, even if one [object] is non-different, since what is capable does not wait [for another], it is logically contradictory that the prior and posterior cognitions have a single object. Even if there is a difference in the nature of the appearances of the cognitions, it is also unjustified [to claim] single-objectness merely from the sameness of name — since the same would follow for pots and the like. If [one says] that in the case [of pots], [the argument] is not probative because of observed contradiction — here too, by what is the absence of contradiction established? As long as the pervasion — that [the same name] is pervaded by a difference of denotable meaning — is not established, the exclusion [of sameness] remains doubtful. And when a word of different nature entering into hearing at each production is established as 'one,' why not pots and the like too? In that case too,

children.text: 13905 tad-rūpa-āvaraṇānāṃ ca vyaktis te vigamo yadi /
children.translated_text: And if the 'manifestation' of those [words] is the removal of obstructions to their form,

children.text: 13906 abhāve karaṇa-grāma-sāmarthyaṃ kiṃ nu tad bhavet //264//
children.translated_text: in the absence [of obstruction], what would be the capacity of the collection of instruments? //264//

For there is never a non-perception of a word when the instruments are operative. But the operation of a manifester does not necessarily make the object perceived — since sometimes, even in the presence of light, pots and the like are not perceived. This invariable perception from their operation would obtain for a word only if it arises [from that operation]. Since for what is not produced, there is no possibility of its being established through the operation [of instruments that do not produce it].
If [one objects:] 'Perception [is possible] because [the word] is pervasive and permanent' — what then is the assurance regarding pots and the like? If [one says:] 'Because that [pervasiveness and permanence] is not desired for them' — is the word desired as having the same properties? And it has been stated that there is no superiority in it. And when pervasiveness and permanence have been refuted [for words] — [the objection that] 'there is no fault because other manifesters are possible for pots and the like' [does not apply]. For light is established as their manifester. If potters and the like were manifesters, they would be exactly like [light]. But they surpass [light]. Therefore, from the superiority of the manifester, they are actually producers.
Since there is no other explanation for a subsidiary [cause]. And this is the same for words too — since there too, the instruments have a superiority based on [the word's being in a] location fit for the sense-organ and so forth. And since the property of being a producer of pots and the like is observed in the instruments. And since for that very lamp and the like, and for some other object, there is no other manifester — therefore their causes would be their manifesters.
Therefore, there is no [mere] manifestation of the word. Or rather, [if there is] manifestation, it is either the superiority [arising] from the instruments, or the removal of an obstruction, or cognition — since there is no other alternative. Of these, the arising of a superiority is not [acceptable], because of the undesirable consequence of impermanence — since that [superiority] is characterized by the loss of a prior form and the arising of [a new one].

children.translated_text: Since there is no distinction among words [in being permanent], the manifestation of other [entities] too would follow;

children.text: 13914 tathā abhyupagame sarva-kāraṇānāṃ nirarthatā //265//
children.translated_text: and if that is accepted, all causes would become purposeless. //265//

For the instruments are certainly not capable of doing nothing to an obstruction. And removal is [a type of] absence. And it has been stated that absence is not an effect. Nor has any obstruction been [shown to exist] for a permanent word, due to the impossibility [of anything obstructing a permanent entity] — this too has been said.
Therefore, there is no attribution of instruments to [the removal of] an obstruction. Nor are these [instruments] without capacity — since in the absence of their operation, the word is not perceived. Therefore it is fitting that they produce the words. Otherwise:

children.translated_text: And if the word is permanent:

children.translated_text: The proof [for permanence] — recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>), correct usage, and the like — that is considered [valid],

children.text: 13925 anudāharaṇaṃ sarva-bhāvānāṃ kṣaṇa-bhaṅgataḥ //266//
children.translated_text: is a non-example for all entities, due to the momentariness [of all things]. //266//

If instruments, despite having properties common to all causes, are [merely] manifesters, then nothing whatsoever would be an effect. And this is not tenable, since it would entail the purposelessness of all causes — because no additional property can be conferred upon an [already existing] entity, because the absence of obstruction is not an effect, because cognition too is established just like [any other] entity, and because if some [cause] were a producer with respect to cognition, then, by the same reasoning, others of the same kind would also be so, entailing that everything would be an effect.
Therefore, this collection of things considered to be producers would be useless — neither in manifestation nor in action. And thus this world would be without benefit to what needs no benefit, and without purposive activity.

14001 For all entities are momentarily perishing (<s>kṣaṇa-bhaṅgin</s>), since destruction requires no cause—this has been stated 14002 and will be stated further. And [all entities] that arise do so from other [causes]. Because existence cannot be uncaused. 14003 Therefore, this recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>), the application of 'existent' and the like, does not anywhere apply 14004 to what is stable and of uniform nature. It is observed only in things like lamps and the like, which undergo transformation into successive natures— 14005 hence it is contradictory. No. Because in things like lamps, whose births are undifferentiated, it arises from error, through deception by similarity. 14006 'Undifferentiated birth'—on what basis is this said? Because the very non-difference [you assert] is to be examined everywhere 14007 in terms of temporal sequence. [Objection:] Likewise for difference too. [Reply:] Then let there be doubt about that very matter. And there is no proof from what is doubted. 14008 14009 [Objection:] Unity [is established] because no distinction is perceived. [Reply:] No. Because existence and non-existence are established through the temporal sequence of cognitions—because there is a real distinction of natures. 14010 14011 For if later cognitions, whose causes were present earlier, had arisen just like the earlier cognition, [they would be identical]. 14012 But those that do not arise indicate a deficiency of causes. Because from a capable [cause] production [occurs], but the incapable does not again acquire capability; 14013 14014 or if it does acquire [capability], stability is impossible. Therefore, even this application of 'existent' is nothing but production, 14015 due to the capacity of the agent. For one that is itself capable has no use for that [agent]. 14016 'Application' too is described as nothing but the production of what is capable of accomplishing the desired end— 14017 either dependent on a similar-class material cause or independent—like the application of an axe and the like, 14018 or the application of <s>karma</s> (action) and the like. As for one who thinks that recognition in direct experience 14019 is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) itself, and that therefore stability is established from perception alone— 14020 we shall refute that too later on. 14021 Other fallacious reasons [for permanence] are also to be refuted. 14022 There is no property whatsoever that accompanies what is of the same class. Because all <s>dharmas</s> (properties) are in this condition [of momentariness]. And as for the thesis of universal stability, just as stated,

For it is indeed perceptually evident that these cognitions 14103 arise from mental effort (<s>manaskāra</s>) and the like, which are counted among persons or are qualities of persons. 14104 And being an effect (<s>kāryatā</s>) is nothing other than the specific presence and absence [of something]. 14105 That presence is perceptible, and we shall state that absence too, characterized by non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>), is 14106 established through the capacity of perception. From that very [fact], the cognitions' being effects of persons 14107 is to be inferred, since [this thesis] has the character of a logical mark through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). 14110 The sequential arrangement (<s>ānupūrvī</s>) that is distinct from the phonemes has been dealt with precisely through the examination of <s>sphoṭa</s>. 14111 Nor is it of the nature of phonemes. Because the real nature of a thing does not transcend these alternatives [of being either identical or different]. 14112 This error would be one of cognition that manifests the superimposition of one form upon things lacking that form— 14113 [giving rise to the appearance of] 'sequential arrangement.' And how could that be non-personal (<s>apauruṣeyī</s>)? Because it is presented as 14114 a fabrication of cognition (<s>buddhi-viṭhapana</s>). Furthermore, since there is no absolutely permanent 14115 nature of anything, the sound (<s>dhvani</s>) must be non-eternal. 14116 And being either uncaused or caused by something else, it would be permanent—but not [produced] from 14117 human activity (<s>puruṣa-vyāpāra</s>). Therefore it is not non-personal. How is it known that 14118 sound is non-eternal, or that there is another entity [distinct from it]? 14119 Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound (<s>dhvani</s>) is impermanent. 14120 For the destruction of entities does not arise from anything [external]. It would be the very nature of the entity itself, 14121 because a thing with that property arises from its own causes. Nor is [destruction] of the nature of a specific entity, 14122 because that will be refuted [below]. Therefore it would be of the nature of mere existence. 14123 Hence, sound or any other entity that partakes of existence— 14124 every entity whatsoever is non-eternal: this is established. [Objection:] It is not established, because the arising of destruction itself 14125 from something else is not proven. For fire [destroys] wood, a stick [destroys] 14201 a pot—thus causes of destruction of entities are observed. The defining mark of cause and effect, they say, 14202 is conformity with positive and negative concomitance. [Reply:] No. Because when the earlier [entity] ceases by its own nature, 14203 another arises in a modified form dependent on a distinctive assemblage of conditions. 14204 Or let fire be a cause of the destruction of wood. Is that destruction, born from fire, the wood itself,

children.translated_text: 14207 because it has not been destroyed. 14208 Why, when a different entity arises from a different entity, is the wood said to have ceased to exist, 14209 or is it not perceived? For an overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>) would follow thus. 14210 [Objection:] 'That itself is its destruction.' 14211 If the very entity born from fire is the absence [of wood], then this [statement] 'it is not perceived because it has ceased to exist'— 14212 [fine,] let that be called its 'absence.' Even so, 14213 how [can there be] 14214 the destruction of one thing by another? For it is not reasonable that merely by naming some entity, 14215 the wood is not perceived. Nor is one thing the destruction of another, 14216 because of overextension—because of the absence of any distinguishing feature of that [destruction], being a real different entity, 14217 from other [entities]. [Objection:] The destruction produced by fire in the wood is not all [destruction]. 14218 [Reply:] What is the connection with 'wood'? [Objection:] The relation of substratum and dependent. [Reply:] 14219 No. Because that will be refuted. [Objection:] The relation of product and producer. [Reply:] Why 'from fire'? 14220 Because it arises from the wood itself. [Objection:] There is no fault, since it arises dependent on that [fire]. [Reply:] 14221 What dependence is there for what gains no enhancement? Or if it does gain [enhancement], another piece of wood would arise. 14222 But the earlier [state] is the cause of non-departure [from its nature]. That is exactly what is observed. [Objection:] Therefore, from fire, the earlier [wood's] destruction. 14223 [Reply:] What is this [fire's] connection with the earlier [state]? The same problem arises, and there is no terminus. 14224 Therefore, necessarily, fire, conferring an enhancement suitable for connection with destruction, produces something entirely new— 14225 14226 and the earlier [wood] should be perceived in its same condition. And 'destruction of wood' means 14301 the absence of wood. But absence is not a product. And what would produce it is a non-producer indeed—hence [it is] not to be considered, 14302 as stated. And when the absence of a nature is different from that [entity], the very nature of the entity 14303 that ceases from that [cause] would have been established—so how 14304 can it be said to have 'ceased to exist'? Therefore, 14305 let not one thing be the destruction of another—why is the wood not perceived? //270//
