14411 eva / tathā ananyatve / tasmāt sato rūpasya tattvānyattva-avyatikramāt /
14412 upakāra-utpādanasya ca rūpa-niṣpādana-lakṣaṇatvāt /
14413 tad-atat-kriyā-vikalo na kartā eva iti na kasyacid hetur ahetuś ca
14414 na apekṣate / tasmāt svayam ayaṃ bhāvas tat-svabhāva iti siddham /
14415 ahetutve api nāśasya nityatvād bhāva-nāśayoḥ//
children.translated_text: 14322 And even upon the destruction of destruction, the entity would return. [Objection:] For even when the killer is slain, 14323 the one [killed] by him does not come back to life. [Reply:] No. Because the killer is a cause of the slaying of that [person]. 14324 We do not say that upon the cessation of the cause of destruction—fire, stick, and the like—the entity must [return to] existence. 14325 Rather, [we speak of] the absence of the entity, characterized by absolute non-apprehension (<s>atyanta-anupalabdhi</s>). 14326 Upon the cessation of that [destruction], what other course is there besides remaining in [the entity's] own nature? For the killer is not like the death 14327 of <s>Caitra</s>. Rather, [the killer] is like a stick and the like. Death 14401 is [<s>Caitra</s>'s] destruction. And upon the cessation of that [death], there would indeed be his re-existence. 14402 Even when destruction is not a different entity, there would be destruction, but the wood itself [would remain]. 14403 Because of its existence, [destruction] is without a cause—there is no other course than this. //273// 14404 Destruction that is not a different entity from the wood—that [wood] itself becomes that [destruction]. And that 14405 already exists previously—so what is the efficacy of fire and the like here? Therefore, 14406 because they contribute nothing to that, they are in no way required. Nor does it merit 14407 the relation 'this belongs to this,' since that [relation] is grounded in contribution. Otherwise, there would be overextension. 14408 Even in indirect contribution, this dilemma necessarily follows: 14409 is the contribution a different entity or that very [thing] itself? If it is a different entity, 14410 then the question of its being a contribution and so forth is raised again—the same situation 14411 applies. Likewise if it is not different. Therefore, since the form of what exists does not transgress being either identical or different, 14412 and since the production of a contribution has the character of producing a form, 14413 [fire,] being incapable of either identical or different action, is simply not an agent—hence it is not a cause of anything, and being causeless, 14414 [destruction] requires nothing [external]. Therefore it is established that this entity is by its own nature of that character [i.e., self-destroying]. 14415 Even though destruction is without a cause, because of the permanence of both entity and destruction,

children.text: 14416 sahabhāva-prasaṅgaś ced asato nityatā kutaḥ //274//
children.translated_text: 14416 the unwanted consequence of simultaneous existence [of entity and its destruction]—[you may ask:] whence is permanence for what is non-existent? //274//

children.text:
14417 syād etad yasya api vināśo ahetukaḥ so avaśyaṃ nitya iti bhāvas
14418 tad-abhāva-lakṣaṇo vināśaś ca saha syātām iti / na / tasya nitya-anitya-
14419 dharma-ayogāt / na hy asaty ayaṃ vikalpaḥ sambhavati /
14420 tayor vastu-dharmatvāt / vināśasya ca akiṃcitvāt / bhavato hi
14421 kenacit sahabhāvaḥ syāt / na ca vināśo bhavati / tasmād adoṣaḥ /
14422 asattve abhāva-nāśitva-prasaṅgo api na yujyate /
children.translated_text: 14422 The unwanted consequence that non-existence would be destroyed by absence is also not tenable,

children.text: 14423 yasmād bhāvasya nāśena na vināśanam iṣyate //275//
children.translated_text: 14423 because the destruction of an entity by [its own] destruction is not accepted [as requiring an external cause]. //275//

14417 It might be thought: even for one whose destruction is without a cause, the entity, being necessarily permanent, 14418 and destruction—characterized by the absence of that [entity]—would coexist simultaneously. [Reply:] No. Because it is incompatible with 14419 the properties of being permanent and impermanent. For this dilemma is impossible with respect to what is non-existent. 14420 Because both [permanence and impermanence] are properties of real things. And because destruction is nothing [real]. For simultaneous existence 14421 would belong to something that exists. But destruction does not exist [as a real entity]. Therefore there is no fault.

children.text:
14424 katham asan vināśo bhāvaṃ nāśayet / ato avināśī bhāvaḥ syād
14425 ity aprasaṅga eva / vināśād bhāva-nāśa-anabhyupagamāt / yo hi
14501 vināśa iti kiṃcin na ity āha sa kathaṃ tato bhāva-nāśam icchet /
14502 katham idānīm asati vināśe bhāvo naṣṭo nāma / na hy asad-vināśā
14503 naṣṭā gaṇyante pratyutpanna-avasthāyām / na hi yo yena atadvān
14504 sa tena tathā vyapadiśyate pratīyate vā / yathā aśvo viṣāṇena /
14505 na vai vināśo na asty eva / sa tu na asti yo bhāvasya bhavanti / bhāva
14506 eva tu kṣaṇa-sthiti-dharmā vināśaḥ / tam asya svabhāvam uttara-
14507 kālaṃ vibhāvayanto vināśo asya bhūta iti yathā-pratīti vyapadiśanti
14508 ity uktam / na hi bhāvasya kiṃcit kadācid bhavati / sa eva
14509 kevalaṃ sva-hetubhyas tathābhūto bhavati / tan na kenacid bhavatā
14510 sa naṣṭaḥ / kiṃ tarhi / svabhāva eva asya yena sa naṣṭo nāma /
14511 kathaṃ tarhi idānīm ahetuko vināśo bhavati ity ucyate /
children.translated_text: How then is it said that destruction is without a cause?

children.text: 14512 naśyan bhāvo apara-apekṣa iti taj-jñāpanāya sā /
children.translated_text: A perishing entity does not depend on another—to convey this,

children.text: 14513 avasthā ahetur uktā asyā bhedam āropya cetasā //276//
children.translated_text: that state is called causeless, by mentally superimposing a distinction upon it. //276//

How could a non-existent destruction destroy an entity? Therefore, the entity would be indestructible—this unwanted consequence simply [follows]. Because destruction of an entity through destruction is not accepted. For one who says that destruction is nothing at all—how could he desire the destruction of an entity from that? How indeed, when destruction does not exist, is an entity said to be destroyed? For those devoid of non-existent destruction are not counted as destroyed in the present state. For one who does not possess something is not designated or cognized by that [thing]—just as a horse [is not designated] by a horn. It is not that destruction does not exist at all. But that [destruction] which [opponents claim] belongs to an entity does not exist. Rather, the entity itself, whose nature is to endure for a moment, is destruction. Those who discern this intrinsic nature of it at a subsequent time designate it according to common understanding as 'its destruction has occurred'—so it has been said. For nothing ever comes into being for an entity. It simply arises in that manner from its own causes. Therefore it is not destroyed by anything that comes into being. What then? It is its very own nature by which it is said to be destroyed.

children.text:
14514 na bhāvo jāto aparasmān nāśaṃ pratilabhate tathābhūtasya eva
14515 svayaṃ jāter ity apara-apekṣa-dharma-antara-pratiṣedha-arthaṃ tat-
14516 svabhāva-jñāpanena artha-antaram iva dharmiṇo dharmaṃ cetasā
14517 vibhajya tan-mātra-jijñāsāyāṃ svabhāva eva tathā ucyate / tad etan
14518 manda-buddhayaḥ kvacit tathā darśanād ghoṣa-mātra-vipralabdhā
14519 nāśaṃ guṇaṃ tasya ca bhāvam āropya sahetukam ahetukaṃ
14520 vā apratiṣṭhita-tattvayā bhāva-cintayā ātmānam ākulayanti /
14521 svato api bhāve abhāvasya vikalpaś ced ayaṃ samaḥ /
14522 nanv aparabhāvitve api vināśasya svata eva bhāvasya bhavato
14523 ayaṃ tattvānyattva-vikalpas tulyaḥ / tadā kim artha-antara-bhāve
14524 bhāvo na dṛśyate anarthāntaratve api tad eva tad bhavati /
14525 tan na kiṃcid asya jātam iti kathaṃ vinaṣṭo nāma / nanv atra /
14526 na tasya kiṃcid bhavati na bhavaty eva kevalam //277//
children.translated_text: An entity that has arisen does not obtain destruction from another, since its very arising is of that nature—to negate a separate property that depends on another, by conveying its intrinsic nature, one mentally distinguishes a property of the property-bearer as though it were something separate, and when there is inquiry into just that, its intrinsic nature itself is so expressed. Those of dull intellect, seeing it thus in some cases, deceived by mere words, superimposing destruction as a quality and the entity [as its bearer], with a view of entities that has not ascertained the truth, confuse themselves [thinking it is] with or without a cause. Even from the entity's own [nature]—

children.text:
14527 ity uktam / na hy ayaṃ vināśo anyo vā kaścid bhāvasya bhavati ity
14528 āha / kiṃ tarhi / sa eva bhāvo na bhavati iti / yadi hi kasyacid bhāvaṃ
14529 brūyāt na bhāvo anena nivartitaḥ syāt / tathā ca bhāva-nivṛttau
14530 prastutāyām aprastutam eva uktaṃ syāt / na hi kasyacid
14531 bhāvena bhāvo na bhūto nāma / tadā na bhūto yadi svayaṃ na
14601 bhavet / na bhavati iti ca prasajyapratiṣedha eṣa na paryudāsaḥ /
14602 anyathā iha api kasyacid bhāve na pratiṣedha-paryudāsayo rūpa-
14603 bhedaḥ syād ubhayatra vidheḥ prādhānyāt / evaṃ ca apratiṣedhāt
14604 kasyacit paryudāso api kvacin na syāt / yadi hi kiṃcit kutaścin
14605 nivarteta tadā tad-vyatireki saṃspṛśyeta / tat-paryudāsena / tac
14606 ca na asti / sarvatra nivṛttir bhavati ity ukte kasyacid bhāvasya eva
14607 pratītiḥ / tathā ca anena artha-antara-bhāva eva uktaḥ syāt / na tayoḥ
14608 parasparaṃ vivekaḥ / aviveke ca na paryudāsaḥ / tad evaṃ vyatireka-
14609 abhāvād anvayo api na syāt / tasya eka-svabhāva-sthiti-lakṣaṇatvāt /
14610 tat-sthitiś ca tad-anya-vyatireke sati syāt / sa ca na asti ity apravṛtti-
14611 nivṛttikaṃ jagat syāt / tasmād yasya nāśo bhavati ity ucyate sa
14612 svayam eva na bhavati ity uktaṃ syāt / na vai ghoṣa-sāmyād viṣaya-
14613 antara-dṛṣṭo vidhiḥ sarvatra yojanām arhati / na hi gardabha iti
14614 nāma-karaṇād bāleya-dharmā manuṣye api saṃyojyāḥ / tathā na
14615 caitrasya putro bhavati ity atra dṛṣṭo vidhir nāśe api virodhāt /
14616 evaṃ ca abhidhāne api prayojanam āveditam eva / ataḥ
14617 bhāve hy eṣa vikalpaḥ syād vidher vastv-anurodhataḥ /
14618 bhāvo avaśyaṃ bhavantam apekṣate / sa ca svabhāva eva / niḥsvabhāvasya
14619 kvacid vyāpāre samāveśa-abhāvāt / vyāpāra iti hi
14620 tathābhūta-svabhāva-utpattiḥ / sā niḥsvabhāvasya kathaṃ syāt /
14621 katham idānīṃ bhavaty abhāvaḥ śaśa-viṣāṇam ity ādi-vyavahāraḥ /
14622 na vai śaśa-viṣāṇaṃ kiṃcid bhavati ity ucyate / api tv evam
14623 asya na bhavati iti bhāva-pratiṣedha eva kriyate / api ca / vyavahartāra
14624 eva etad evaṃ vyāpāra-vad iva samāropya ādarśayanti
14625 prakaraṇena kenacit / na tu tat tathā / sarva-artha-vivecanaṃ hi
14626 tatra tattvaṃ na kasyacit samāveśaḥ / na khalv evaṃ vināśo vastuni
14627 tad-bhāvāt / asāv api yadi vaktṛbhir evaṃ khyāpyate na
14628 tu svayaṃ tathā tadā na kiṃcid bhavati iti iṣṭam eva / tasmāt svayaṃ
14701 bhavan svabhāvo vikalpa-dvayaṃ na ativartate tattvam anyattvam
14702 iti / atattvam eva svabhāvasya anyattvam / na hi rūpa-rasayor
14703 apy anyad eva parasparam anyattvam / svabhāva-apratibandho
14704 anyattvam iti cet / ko ayaṃ pratibandho nāma yena sa ca na
14705 syāt / na anya-svabhāvaś ca / janma iti cet / sarva-kāraṇānāṃ parasparam
14706 avācyatā syāt / tathā ca sarvaḥ sarvasya kathaṃcid upayogi
14707 iti na kaścit kutaścid anyaḥ syāt / evaṃ ca avācyatā ity api kāryakāraṇabhāva
14708 eva śabda-antareṇa uktaḥ syāt / na artha-bhedaḥ / svabhāva-ananugamanaṃ
14709 tv anyattvaṃ brūmaḥ / sa ca svabhāvavatāṃ parasparam
14710 asty eva ity anyattvam eva / na ca taj-janma-lakṣaṇāt
14711 svabhāvapratibandhād anyaḥ pratibandho nāma / anāyattasya
14712 vyabhicāra-avirodhāt / tato dharma-bhedāc ca anyattvam / jñāna-kṛtaḥ
14713 pratibandha iti cet / syād etat / yat-pratipatti-nāntarīyakaṃ
14714 yaj-jñānaṃ tad-gatau niyamena tat-pratibhāsanāt tad atad-rūpam
14715 apy avācyam iti / na / tasya niḥsvabhāvatvāt svayam / sa eva hi
14716 tasya svabhāvo yaḥ pratibhāti / svabhāvavattve asya tadvat pratibhāsa-
14717 prasaṅgāt / apratibhāsamānasya ca dṛśya-abhāvāt / adṛśyatve
14718 api na tad-rūpaṃ jñānam iti kasya kim āyattā pratipattiḥ / na
14719 ca yad yad āyattā-pratītikaṃ tasya svabhāva-pratibhāsa eva naśyati /
14720 prakāśa-āyatta-pratītīnām iva nīla-ādīnām / kā vā tasya pratyāsattiḥ /
14721 tatra yat tasminn anātma-rūpe pratīyamāne sa svayaṃ
14722 pratyupatiṣṭhate / atiprasaṅgo hy evaṃ syāt / pratīyamānasya
14723 tad-upādānatā iti cet / ko ayam upādāna-arthaḥ / na kāryakāraṇabhāvo
14724 anabhyupagamāt / abhyupagame vā na kārya-kāraṇe anyonya-
14725 pratīti-pratyupasthāpane / pratīter eva tan-nāntarīyakatā
14726 pratyāsattir iti cet / nanu sa eva asati pratibandhe na yuktā ity ucyate /
14801 na akārya-kāraṇayoḥ kaścit pratibandha iti ca uktam / yat -pratipatti-
14802 nāntarīyakaṃ yaj-jñānam ity api taj-jñāne sati syāt / na hi yo
14803 vijñāne svarūpeṇa asvarūpa-asaṃsargeṇa na pratibhāsate tasya kiṃcij
14804 jñānam / tad-abhāvān na sidhyati avācyatā-lakṣaṇam artha-
14805 rūpasya / tad bhavatā vastutas tattvānyattva-bhājā bhavitavyam /
14806 yasya tu vinaśyato bhāvasya na kiṃcid bhavati / tena
14807 na bhāvo bhavati ity uktam abhāvo bhavati ity api //278//
children.translated_text: —so it has been said. For neither this destruction nor anything else comes into being for an entity—thus he says. What then? That very entity simply does not come into being. For if one were to speak of the coming into being of something, the entity would not be eliminated by it. And thus, when the cessation of the entity is under discussion, something irrelevant would have been stated. For an entity is not said to have not come into being by the coming into being of something. It has not come into being only if it itself does not come into being. And 'does not come into being' is a <s>prasajya-pratiṣedha</s> (simple negation), not a <s>paryudāsa</s> (implicative negation). Otherwise, here too, in the coming into being of something, there would be no formal difference between negation and implicative negation—

children.text:
14808 yad apy ayaṃ bhāvasya abhāvo bhavati ity āha / tad api bhāvo
14809 na bhavati ity eva uktaṃ bhavati / evaṃ hi sa nivartito bhavati /
14810 pratiṣedhe vidher asambhavāt / tata eva asya vināśe na kaścid hetuḥ /
14811 tathā hi /
children.translated_text: For indeed:

children.text: 14812 apekṣyeta paraḥ kāryaṃ yadi vidyata kiṃcana /
children.translated_text: Another [cause] would be required if something were to be an effect;

children.text: 14813 yad akiṃcitkaraṃ vastu kiṃ kenacid apekṣyate //279//
children.translated_text: but what need has a thing that produces nothing for anything else? //279//

As for the statement that non-existence of the entity comes into being—that too amounts to saying that the entity does not come into being. For thus it is negated. Because a positive injunction is impossible in [mere] negation. Therefore, for this reason, there is no cause whatsoever for its destruction.

children.text:
14814 sati hi kārye kāraṇaṃ bhavati / na ca naśyato bhāvasya kiṃcit
14815 kāryam ity uktam / tasmād yo nāma nāśa-hetuḥ sa bhāve na
14816 kiṃcit karoti ity akiṃcitkaro na apekṣyaṇīyaḥ / tat kathaṃ idānīm
14817 anutpanna-atiśayas tad-avastha eva bhāvo naṣṭo nāma /
14818 nanv atiśaya-utpattāv api sa eva tasya atiśaya utpanna iti kathaṃ
14819 sa naṣṭo nāma / tena na ayaṃ tad-avastho naṣṭo nāma / yena svayaṃ
14820 na bhavati tena naṣṭaḥ / na artha-antara-utpādād ity uktam / na hy
14821 atiśaya-utpattyā svayaṃ na bhūto nāma / abhāvasya sarva-atiśaya-upākhyā-
14822 nivṛttyā sarva-bhāva-dharma-viveka-lakṣaṇatvāt / bhāvasya
14823 ca utpatti-samāveśa-lakṣaṇatvāt / tasmān na abhāve kasyacid bhāva-upakṣepo
14824 anyasya /
children.translated_text: —of another.

children.text: 14825 etena ahetukatve api hy abhūtvā nāśa-bhāvataḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, even if [destruction is] without a cause, from the fact of destruction's never having existed before,

children.text: 14826 sattā-nāśitva-doṣasya pratyākhyātaṃ prasañjanam //280//
children.translated_text: the objection that existence would be destroyed is refuted. //280//

For a cause exists [only] when there is an effect. And it has been said that a perishing entity has no effect whatsoever. Therefore, that which is supposedly a cause of destruction does nothing to the entity and, being ineffectual, need not be postulated. How then is an entity said to be destroyed when it is in the very same state, with no new quality having arisen? But even if a new quality were to arise, that very quality would be its own [new arising]—so how is it [the original entity] said to be destroyed? Therefore, it is not destroyed by being in the same state, but because it itself does not come into being—it is [said to be] destroyed. Not by the arising of something else—so it has been said. For the arising of a new quality—

children.text:
14827 yo api manyate ahetuke api vināśe abhūtvā asya bhāvāt sattā-anityatvaṃ
14901 ca durnivāram / abhūtvā bhavann ahetuko bhavati ity api
14902 viruddham iti / so apy anena eva pratyākhyātaḥ / kasyacid bhāvān abhyupagamāt /
14904 yathā keṣāṃcid eva iṣṭaḥ pratigho janmināṃ tathā /
children.translated_text: Just as for some, resistance is accepted as the nature of produced things, so too—

children.text: 14905 nāśaḥ svabhāvo bhāvānāṃ na anutpattimatāṃ yadi //281//
children.translated_text: destruction is the intrinsic nature of entities, but not of those that are unproduced. //281//

One who thinks that even if destruction is without a cause, since it [destruction] comes into being having not existed before, the impermanence of existence is unavoidable, and that it is also contradictory to say it is without a cause while coming into being having not existed before—he too is refuted by this very [argument], because the coming into being of something [separate] is accepted.

children.text:
14906 atha api syād / bhavatu nāma svabhāva eṣa bhāvānāṃ ya ime kṣaṇa-
14907 sthiti-dharmāṇāḥ / sa tu utpattimatām eva bhaviṣyati / na hi svabhāva
14908 iti sarvaḥ sarvasya svabhāvo bhavati pratigha-ātmatā-vat /
14909 satyam etat / tathā api /
14910 svabhāva-niyamād hetoḥ svabhāva-niyamaḥ phale /
children.translated_text: From the restriction of the nature of the cause, there is restriction of the nature in the effect;

children.text: 14911 na anitye rūpa-bhedo asti bhedakānām abhāvataḥ //282//
children.translated_text: there is no formal difference among impermanent things, due to the absence of differentiating [factors]. //282//

Even if it be [conceded]: let this indeed be the intrinsic nature of entities that are momentary by nature. But it will belong only to those that are produced. For not every nature belongs to everything—like the nature of resistance. True, this is so. Nevertheless:

children.text:
14912 na vai pratigho anyo vā svabhāvo akasmāt pratiniyamavān / yādṛśī
14913 tu sva-hetoḥ śakti-sthitis tādṛśaṃ phalaṃ bhavati iti hetu-svabhāva-
14914 niyamāt phala-svabhāva-niyamaḥ / ākasmikatve apy asya ukto
14915 doṣaḥ / pratighāta-ātmatā-hetu-svabhāva-pratiniyamavan na naśvara-
14916 janana-pratiniyata-svabhāvaṃ bhāvaṃ paśyāmaḥ / yena taj-janmā
14917 tathā syān na anyaḥ / sarva-ākāra-janmanāṃ vināśa-darśanāt /
14918 nanv idam apy aniśceyam eva sarva-ākāra-janmāno naśyanti iti /
14919 tāsām aniḥśeṣa-darśanāt / vicitra-śaktayo hi sāmagryo dṛśyante /
14920 tatra kācit syād api yā anaśvara-ātmānaṃ janayet / na / jñeya-adhikārāt /
14921 ye kadācit kvacit kenacij jñātāḥ santo na jñāyante
14922 teṣāṃ sattā-anubandhī nāśa iti brūmaḥ / ta eva kṛtakā anityāḥ
14923 sādhyante / na hy ayaṃ sambhavo asti yat te jñāna-janana-
14924 svabhāvāḥ punar anaṣṭā na janayeyur apekṣeran vā param /
14925 taj-janana-svabhāvasya niṣpatteḥ / na ca teṣv anapekṣeṣu kasyacit
14926 kadācit kiṃcij jñānaṃ nivarteta / na ca evaṃbhūtaṃ kiṃcid asti /
14927 sarvasya kenacit kadācit jñānāt / jñāna-mātra-arthakriyāyām apy
15001 asāmarthye vastv eva na syāt / tathā hi tal-lakṣaṇaṃ vastv iti
15002 vakṣyāmaḥ / tasya ca vināśa-avyabhicārāt sa sattā-anubandhī /
15003 pratyākhyeyā ata eva eṣāṃ sambandhasya api nityatā /
15004 ata eva yathā uktād vastu-mātra-anubandhād vināśasya śabda-vat
15005 sambandha-nityatā api pratyākhyeyā / yā ca śabda-śaktir yogyatā-ākhyā
15006 artha-pratipattyā āśrayo jaiminīyair varṇyate sa artha-antaram
15007 eva na bhavati / tathā hi / yogyatā iti rūpa-atiśaya eva bhāvānām ity
15008 āveditaṃ prāk / astu vā artha-antaram / tathā api
15009 sambandha-doṣaiḥ prāg uktaiḥ śabda-śaktiś ca dūṣitā //283//
children.translated_text: Indeed, neither obstruction (<s>pratigha</s>) nor any other nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) is restricted without a cause. Rather, the result (<s>phala</s>) occurs in accordance with the capacity-disposition (<s>śakti-sthiti</s>) of its own cause—thus from the restriction of the cause's nature follows the restriction of the result's nature. The fault of causelessness (<s>ākasmikatva</s>) has already been stated. We do not observe any entity whose nature is restricted to producing perishable things that possesses a nature restricted by the cause of having the character of obstruction, such that from its birth alone it would be so and not otherwise—because destruction is observed in all kinds of produced things. But [the opponent objects:] even this cannot be determined—that all kinds of produced things perish—because not all of them have been exhaustively observed. For assemblages of diverse capacities are seen. Among those, there might be one that produces an imperishable entity. No—because of the domain of the knowable. Those which, having been known at some time, somewhere, by someone, are no longer known—of those we say that destruction is concomitant with existence (<s>sattā-anubandhī nāśa</s>). Those very things that are produced (<s>kṛtaka</s>) are established as impermanent (<s>anitya</s>). For there is no possibility that those whose nature is to produce cognition, not having perished, would fail to produce it or would depend on something else, since their nature of producing that has been accomplished. And when those are independent, no one's cognition of anything would ever cease. But nothing of this sort exists, since everything is known by someone at some time. Even in the case of the capacity for cognition alone as causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>), if there were no capacity, it would not be a real thing (<s>vastu</s>) at all. For we shall say that a real thing is defined by that. And because destruction never deviates from that, it is concomitant with existence. Therefore the permanence of the relation of these is also to be rejected. For this very reason, just as stated, since destruction is invariably connected with mere real things, the permanence of the relation, like that of sound, is also to be rejected. And the capacity of sound (<s>śabda-śakti</s>), called fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>), which the <s>Jaiminīya</s>s describe as the basis through understanding of meaning—that is not a separate thing at all. For thus: fitness is merely an excellence of form of entities—this was explained before. Or let it be a separate thing; even so, the capacity of sound is refuted by the faults in the relation previously stated. //283//

children.text:
15010 ukto hi sambandha-artha-antara-vāde aneka-prakāro doṣaḥ / tena eva
15011 sā śabda-śaktir dūṣitā iti na punar ucyate / api ca /
15012 na apauruṣeyam ity eva yathā artha-jñāna-sādhanam /
children.translated_text: It is not the case that merely being authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>) makes [Vedic words] a means of knowing objects as they are;

children.text: 15013 dṛṣṭo anyathā api vahny-ādir aduṣṭaḥ puruṣa-āgasā //284//
children.translated_text: for fire and such are observed otherwise [i.e., as erroneous causes of cognition], undamaged by any human fault. //284//
For the fault of multiple kinds has been stated in the discussion of relation as a separate category. By that very [argument] the capacity of sound is refuted, so it need not be repeated. Moreover—

children.text:
15014 bhavantu nāma apauruṣeyā vaidikāḥ śabdāḥ tathā api sambhāvyam
15015 eva eṣām ayathārtha-jñāna-hetutvam / na hi puruṣa-doṣa-upadhānād
15016 eva artheṣu jñāna-vibhramaḥ / tad-rahitānām api pradīpa-ādīnāṃ nīla-utpala-
15017 ādiṣu vitatha-jñāna-jananāt / tad ime śabdāḥ saṃskāra-nirapekṣāḥ
15018 prakṛtyā ca artheṣu pratibhāna-hetavaḥ syuḥ / svabhāva-viśeṣād
15019 vahny-ādi-vat / vitatha-vyaktayaś ca niyamena eva niyama-
15020 kāraṇa-abhāvād ayuktam iti cet / avitatha-vyakti-niyame kiṃ
15021 kāraṇam / tasmād yathārtha-vyakti-niyama-vat prakṛtyā ayathārtha-
15022 vyakti-niyamaḥ kiṃ na kalpyate / athavā vahny-ādi-vad eva artheṣu
15023 ubhaya-jñāna-hetutvaṃ syāt / na hy apauruṣeyā api vahny-ādaya
15024 ekatra yathārtha-jñāna-hetavo api sarvatra tathā bhavanti iti /
15025 tathā śabdānām apy apauruṣeyatve apy ubhayaṃ syād iti / bhavatu
15026 vahny-ādīnām kṛtakatvād yathā-pratyayam anyatra anyathātvam
15027 na punar nityeṣu śabdeṣv etad asti / nanv evaṃvidho anyatra
15028 apy asty eva dharmas teṣām api saṃketa-balād anyathā-vṛtteḥ
15029 kārya-janana-svabhāva-sthitau ca eṣāṃ samaya-āder apekṣaṇīyasya abhāvāt /
15101 tataḥ pratītir artheṣu sarvasya sarvadā syāt / na ca asti
15102 tasmān na śabdāḥ sthita-svabhāvā iti / api ca /
15103 na jñāna-hetutā eva syāt tasminn akṛtake mate /
children.translated_text: There would be no capacity to cause cognition (<s>jñāna-hetutā</s>) at all in that [sound], if it is held to be uncreated (<s>akṛtaka</s>);

children.text: 15104 nityebhyo avastu-sāmarthyān na hi janma asti kasyacit //285//
children.translated_text: for from permanent things, due to the incapacity of non-real things, there is no production of anything whatsoever. //285//

Let the Vedic words be authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>); even so, it is entirely possible that they cause cognition of objects not as they are. For erroneous cognition regarding objects does not arise only from the imposition of human faults. Because even things free of such [human faults], like lamps and the like, produce false cognition regarding blue lotuses and such. So these words, without depending on mental impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), would by their very nature be causes of apprehension regarding objects, due to a particular nature (<s>svabhāva-viśeṣa</s>), like fire and such. And if their manifestations are necessarily false, [the opponent says] this is wrong because there is no cause for such restriction—then what would be the cause for the restriction to non-false manifestations?

children.text:
15105 yady akṛtakaḥ śabdo na tasmād artheṣu pratītir eva syāt / pratīti-
15106 janma-itara-kālayos tulya-rūpasya pratīti-janmani sāmarthya-
15107 sambhāvanā-ayogāt / evam ayaṃ janako na evam iti vivecanīyasya
15108 rūpa-bhedasya abhāvāt / na yādṛśo asya ajanakas tādṛśa eva janako
15109 yuktaḥ / anya-apekṣā api niṣiddhā eva / tasmān na nityānāṃ kvacid
15110 vijñāna-janana-sāmarthyam / kadācid ajanane nityam ajanana- prasaṅgāt /
15111 kārya-sātatya-adarśanāc ca na te kathaṃcit kartāra ity
15112 ukta-prāyam / yā apy etā nitya-abhimateṣv ākāśa-ādiṣu pratipattayas
15113 tā api na tat-svabhāva-bhāvinyaḥ / tathā hi /
15114 vikalpa-vāsanā-udbhūtāḥ samāropita-gocarāḥ /
children.translated_text: Cognitions arisen from the impressions of conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa-vāsanā</s>), having superimposed objects,

children.text: 15115 jāyante buddhayas tatra kevalaṃ na artha-gocarāḥ //286//
children.translated_text: arise there [in relation to permanent things] merely without having real objects as their domain. //286//

If sound is uncreated (<s>akṛtaka</s>), then there would be no cognition of objects from it at all. Because there is no reason to suppose capacity at the time of producing cognition rather than at other times, since its form is identical [at all times]. Because there is no difference of form to be discriminated—such that 'in this way it produces, and not in that way.' It is not reasonable that what is of such a nature as to be non-productive should be productive in the same form. Dependence on something else is also prohibited. Therefore permanent things have no capacity to produce cognition anywhere. Because if they fail to produce at any time, there follows perpetual non-production. And because continuity of effects is not observed, they are in no way agents—this has been stated.

children.text:
15116 svalakṣaṇa-viṣayā hi buddhir niyamena tad-yogyatā-upasthāpana-anuvidhāyinī
15117 iti tasmin saty asyāḥ kāraṇe yogye sā bhavaty eva /
15118 tad yadi nityānāṃ padārthānāṃ svalakṣaṇe kasyacit jñānaṃ syāt
15119 sarvasya sarvadā syāt / kārya-viśeṣā hi vyaktayaḥ kathaṃcit
15120 kvacid upayujyamānās tad-upajanana-yogya-atiśaya-pratilambha-hetum
15121 vastu-viśeṣam apekṣanta iti yuktam / tathā akārya-viśeṣo nityo
15122 bhāvaḥ kenacid gṛhyamāṇas tat-kāraṇa-apekṣo yadi grahaṇam asya
15123 janayet yuktaṃ yat tena eva gṛhyeta / tac ca sthita-svabhāvatvān
15124 na sambhavati iti / sarveṇa samaṃ gṛhyeta na vā kenacid iti
15125 san kenacid dṛṣṭo na nityaḥ kaścid atīndriyaḥ syāt / na ca etad asti /
15126 tasmād artha-sāmarthya-anapekṣāḥ samāropita-gocarā āntaram eva upādānaṃ
15127 vikalpa-vāsanā-prabodham āśritya bāhya-artha-śūnyā bhrāntaya
15128 eva ākāśa-ādiṣu sarvasya sambhavanti iti / tasmān na aparāvṛtti-
15201 dharmāḥ śabdāḥ / tattve vā kuta etad avitatha-artha-pratītaya
15202 eva iti / na hy agnir himasya bheṣajam ity ādiṣu śīta-pratighāta-
15203 sāmarthyaṃ loka-prasiddhaṃ agneḥ khyāpyata iti sarvaṃ tathā
15204 bhavati / lokasya sva-icchā-kṛta-saṃketa-anuvyavahārāt kim ayaṃ
15205 lokaḥ sva-saṃketam anuvidadhad evaṃ pratyeti āhosvic śabda-
15206 svabhāva-sthiter iti sandehaḥ / loka-icchayā api parāvartyamānāḥ
15207 śabdāḥ punar anyatra anyathā dṛśyanta iti loka-prasiddhy-anuvidhāne
15208 api sambhavaty eṣām anyathābhāvaḥ / tasmāt kasyacid avaiparītya-
15209 darśane api sarveṣāṃ tathābhāvo na sidhyati / akṛtaka-svabhāvatve
15210 api hy eṣāṃ kaścin mithyā-artha-niyato api syād iti svabhāva-
children.translated_text: for even among these, some might be restricted to false objects—and due to

children.text: 15211 aparijñānāt sarvatra saṃśayaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: non-comprehension of [their] nature, there would be doubt everywhere.

children.text: 15212 mithyātvaṃ kṛtakeṣv eva dṛṣṭam ity akṛtaṃ vacaḥ /
children.translated_text: Falsity is observed only in produced things, [so] uncreated speech

children.text: 15213 satya-arthaṃ vyatirekasya virodhi-vyāpanād yadi //287//
children.translated_text: has true objects, if the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) pervades the opposite. //287//

For cognition that has a particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) as its object necessarily conforms to the presentation of fitness for that [particular]. Therefore, when the suitable cause is present, that [cognition] necessarily arises. So if anyone were to have cognition of the particular of permanent entities, everyone would have it at all times. For manifestations, being specific effects, being utilized somehow somewhere, require a particular real thing as the cause for obtaining the excellence suitable for producing that [cognition]—this is reasonable. But a permanent entity, not being a specific effect, if grasped by someone, would, if it were to produce apprehension depending on a cause [for that],

children.text:
15214 atha yan mithyā-arthaṃ vacanaṃ tad akhilaṃ kṛtakam iti hetu-vyatirekeṇa
15215 sādhya-vyatirekasya vyāpter anyatra asambhavād akṛtakaṃ
15216 satya-artham iti syād vinā apy anvayena / yo hi yena avyāptas
15217 tatra tad-vyatirekaḥ śaṅkyeta / na ca viruddhayor ekatra sambhavo
15218 asti / asambhave ca vijātīyasya gaty-antara-abhāvād iṣṭa-artha-siddhes
15219 tat-sādhanatvāc ca liṅgasya vyartham anvaya-darśanaṃ
15220 vyatireka-mātreṇa eva siddher iti / satyam etat yadi vipakṣayor
15221 vyāpyavyāpakabhāvaḥ sidhyet / sa tu na siddhaḥ / yasmāt
15222 hetāv asambhave anukte bhāvas tasya api śaṅkyate /
children.translated_text: When the impossibility of the reason [in the opposite locus] is not stated, the existence of that [reason there] may also be suspected,

children.text: 15223 viruddhānāṃ padārthānām api vyāpaka-darśanāt //288//
children.translated_text: because even contradictory things are observed to have a common pervader. //288//

Now, if all speech that has false objects is entirely produced, then because the absence of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) is pervaded by the absence of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) through negative concomitance, it might follow that the uncreated is true in its objects, even without positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>). For where [the reason] is not pervaded by [something], the absence of that in that [locus] might be suspected. But there is no co-occurrence of contradictories in one locus. And when there is no occurrence of the dissimilar, since there is no other recourse, the desired conclusion is established; and since the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is the means of establishing that, observation of positive concomitance is redundant, since the conclusion is established by negative concomitance alone. This is true—if the mutual pervasion of the two opposed [properties were established].

children.text:
15224 yadi hetoḥ sādhya-vipakṣe abhāvaḥ sidhyet tadā sādhya-vyatirekaṃ
15225 hetu-vyatireko vyāpnuyāt / na ca tatra tasya asambhave
15226 pramāṇaṃ paśyāmaḥ / na ca aviruddha-vidhiḥ pratiṣedha-sādhano
15227 yuktaḥ / atiprasaṅgāt / na ca ekatra dṛṣṭasya anyatra asambhava
15228 eva pṛthag viruddha-sahabhāvinām api darśanāt / anityatva-vat
15229 prayatnānantarīyaka-itarayor / na ca tathāvidhasya adarśanād asattvam
15230 eva / yasmāt /
15301 na asattā-siddhir ity uktaṃ sarvato anupalambhanāt /
children.translated_text: Non-existence is not established, as has been said, from non-apprehension of everything.

children.text: 15302 asiddhāyām asattāyāṃ sandigdhā vyatirekitā //289//
children.translated_text: When non-existence is not established, the negative concomitance (<s>vyatirekitā</s>) is doubtful. //289//

If the absence of the reason in the opposite of the provable (<s>sādhya-vipakṣa</s>) were established, then the absence of the reason would pervade the absence of the provable. But we do not see a proof for the impossibility [of the reason] there. Nor is it proper that the assertion of something non-contradictory proves a negation—due to overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>). Nor is it the case that what is observed in one place necessarily does not occur elsewhere, since even things coexisting with contradictories are observed separately—like impermanence and [being] immediately preceded by effort, with respect to their contraries. And from the non-observation of such [a pervasion], one cannot infer non-existence. Because—

children.text:
15303 na hy ayaṃ puruṣa-mātrakaḥ sarvaṃ draṣṭuṃ samartho yena asya
15304 darśana-nivṛttyā na tathā syāt / yasya hi jñānaṃ jñeya-sattāṃ
15305 na vyabhicarati sa evaṃ bruvāṇaḥ śobheta adarśanān na asti iti /
15306 tad ime svabhāva-deśa-kāla-viprakarṣeṇa santo apy anupalakṣyāḥ
15307 syuḥ / tathā hi / ko atyantaparokṣe arthe saṃvādanam itarad
15308 vā sarva-darśī vacanasya akṛtakasya itarasya vā vibhāvayituṃ samarthaḥ /
15309 pratipāditaṃ ca etat kvacit tathā dṛṣṭānām apy arthānāṃ
15310 punaḥ kathaṃcid anyathābhāvaḥ yathā kvacid deśe madhurāṇi
15311 nimba-phalāni saṃskāra-viśeṣād āmalakī-phalāni ca na
15312 ca idānīm atad-darśinā tāni pratikṣeptavyāny eva iti / tasmād akṛtakaṃ
15313 ca syād syān mithyā-arthaṃ ca iti na virodhaṃ paśyāmaḥ / na
15314 hi iyam anupalabdhir adṛśya-ātmasv abhāva-sādhikā ity uktam / tena
15315 yat kiṃcin mithyā-arthaṃ tat sarvaṃ pauruṣeyam ity aniścayād
15316 avyāptiḥ / tathā hi /
15317 anvayo vyatireko vā sattvaṃ vā sādhya-dharmiṇi /
children.translated_text: Positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), or the existence [of the property to be proven] in the subject (<s>sādhya-dharmin</s>)—

children.text: 15318 tan-niścaya-phalair jñānaiḥ sidhyanti yadi sādhanam //290//
children.translated_text: if these are established by cognitions whose result is the determination of those [relations], then that is the means of proof (<s>sādhana</s>). //290//

For this mere human being is not capable of seeing everything, such that by the cessation of his seeing, [something] would not exist. Only one whose cognition never deviates from the existence of the knowable would look good saying 'it does not exist because it is not seen.' These [things], though existing, might be unperceivable due to remoteness of nature, place, or time. For who is capable of determining agreement or otherwise regarding completely remote objects, being an all-seer, whether speech is uncreated or otherwise? And this has been demonstrated: even regarding objects that have been observed in some way, how then [can there be certainty]?

children.text:
15319 tathā ca uktam / ya eva tu ubhaya-niścita-vācī sa sādhanam dūṣaṇam
15320 vā na anyatara-prasiddha-sandigdha-vācī punaḥ sādhana-apekṣatvād
15321 iti / ko hy adṛṣṭa-virodhasya sambhavaṃ pratyācakṣīta / tad ayaṃ
15322 vyatirekaḥ saṃśayād asādhanam / api ca /
15323 yatra sādhya-vipakṣasya varṇyate vyatirekitā /
children.translated_text: Where the negative concomitance of the opposite of the provable (<s>sādhya-vipakṣa</s>) is described,

children.text: 15324 sa eva asya sapakṣaḥ syāt sarvo hetur ato anvayī //291//
children.translated_text: that very [locus] would be a similar case (<s>sapakṣa</s>) for it; therefore every reason involves positive concomitance (<s>anvayī</s>). //291//

And thus it has been said: Only that which expresses what is ascertained in both ways is a proof or refutation—not that which expresses what is established on only one side or is doubtful, because it still requires proof. For who would deny the possibility of an unobserved contradiction? Therefore this negative concomitance, being doubtful, is not a means of proof. Moreover—

children.text:
15401 yat kiṃcin mithyā-arthaṃ tat sarvaṃ pauruṣeyam iti hetu-vipakṣeṇa
15402 sādhya-vipakṣasya vyāptis tad-abhāve abhāva-siddhau syāt / tad-abhāve
15403 bhavatas tena vyāpty-ayogāt / yā eva ca vijātīyayor vyāvṛtti-siddhiḥ
15404 sā eva anvaya-sthitir vipakṣa-vyavaccheda-lakṣaṇatvāt sādhyasya /
15405 pratiṣedha-dvayāc ca vidhi-siddhir iti kā ananvaya-avyatireka-vyāpti-
15406 siddhiḥ / tan na kaścid hetur ananvayo nāma / eka-vyavacchedasya
15407 tad-vijātīya-siddhi-nāntarīyakatvāt / anitya-nirātmatā-ādi-vyavacchede
15408 api tathā syāt / na / vyatireka-vyavacchedasya bhāva-rūpatvāt /
15409 na bhāva-rūpa-vyavacchede bhāva-anuṣaṅgaḥ / abhāva-vyavacchedas
15410 tu niyamena bhāva-upasthāpanaḥ / bhāva-abhāvayor anyonya-viveka-
15411 rūpatvāt / abhāva-rūpas tu vyatirekaḥ sa ca vyatiricyamāno
15412 bhāvam upasthāpayati na evaṃ nairātmya-ādayaḥ svabhāva-viśeṣāt /
15413 kriyā-bhoga-adhiṣṭhāna-asvatantro hy ātmā nirātmā / tat-svātantrya-
15414 lakṣaṇatvād ātmanaḥ / tad rūpaṃ nairātmyaṃ na ātma-nivṛtti-
15415 mātram anyathā nirupākhye kṛtakatva-ādy-ayogān na tato nairātmya-
15416 siddhiḥ syāt / ātma-vyavacchedena nirātmano bhāvasya parāmarśād
15417 adoṣa iti cet / paryudāsena vastu-saṃsparśād tad eva
15418 vastu-rūpaṃ nairātmyam āyātam / yasya api na abhāva-rūpo vyatirekas
15419 tasya bhāva-rūpa-vyavacchede na bhāva-siddhiḥ syād iti
15420 na anvaya-anuṣaṅgaḥ / tathā anairātmye api na bhāva-siddhiḥ / yathā
15421 na idaṃ nirātmakaṃ jīvaccharīraṃ prāṇa-ādimattvād iti vipakṣayor
15422 vyāpyavyāpakabhāva-cintāyām aprāṇa-ādimattva eva nairātmyaṃ
15423 dṛṣṭam / tad-abhāve ca na asti iti svayaṃ na bhavad api prāṇa-ādīnāṃ
15424 na ātmani siddhim upasthāpayati / tathā sādhye api prāṇa-ādibhir
15425 vyudasyamānaṃ syāt kevalam / nairātmye abhāvāt prāṇa-
15426 ādayas tan-nirasanā na ātma-upasthāpanāḥ / tatra bhāva-asiddheḥ /
15427 na ca nairātmya-nivṛttyā ātma-siddhiḥ syāt / vipakṣa-vyatireka-darśane
15428 api prasaṅgāt / tan na viparyaya-vyāptir vyatireka-asiddhau /
15429 tat-siddhir eva ca anvaya-siddhiḥ / asiddhau vā tad-vyatireka-nivṛtti-
15430 siddhāv api tad-asiddhir iti sādhye api prasaṅgaḥ / tan na ananvayā
15431 vyatireka-vyāptiḥ / mithyā-arthatāyās tu pauruṣeyatvena vyāptyā
15501 apauruṣeyān nivṛttāv api na satya-arthatvam / prakāra-antara-sambhavāt /
15502 dvairāśye tu śabdānām etat syād eka-nivṛttau gaty-antara-
15503 abhāvāt / te tv anarthakā api syur iti na iṣṭasiddhiḥ / artha-pratīter
15504 na anarthakā iti cet / eṣa puruṣa-vyāpāraḥ syāt / artha-antara-vikalpa-vat /

children.text: 15526 atha api bhāva-śaktiḥ syād anyatra apy aviśeṣataḥ //292//
children.translated_text: But even if there were an inherent power (<s>bhāva-śakti</s>), it would apply equally elsewhere as well. //292//

The <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of the counter-instance of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) by the counter-instance of the <s>hetu</s> (reason), namely 'whatever has a false meaning, all that is of human origin (<s>pauruṣeya</s>),' would hold when absence is established in the absence of that. But for you there is no pervasion by that in its absence. And indeed, the very establishment of exclusion from both dissimilar classes is itself the positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), since the <s>sādhya</s> is characterized by exclusion from the counter-instance. And from the double negation comes the establishment of the positive rule—so what is this establishment of pervasion without positive or negative concomitance? Therefore there is no reason called 'without positive concomitance,' because a single exclusion necessarily entails the establishment of the dissimilar class. [Objection:] The same would apply in the exclusion of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth. [Reply:] No, because the exclusion by negative concomitance has a positive nature. In the exclusion of what has a positive nature, there is no entailment of a positive entity. But the exclusion of absence necessarily presents a positive entity, because existence and non-existence have the nature of mutual distinction. Negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) has the nature of absence, and when it differentiates, it presents a positive entity—but <s>nairātmya</s> (selflessness) and the like do not, due to the distinctive nature [of those concepts]. For the self (<s>ātman</s>) that is not independent as the basis for action and experience is 'selfless' (<s>nirātman</s>), because the self is characterized by that independence. That form is <s>nairātmya</s>—it is not mere cessation of the self; otherwise, since there would be no applicability of being produced and so forth to what is without designation, the establishment of selflessness would not follow therefrom. [Objection:] If it is said there is no fault, because of the apprehension of a positive entity that is selfless through the exclusion of the self—[Reply:] Through the implicative negation (<s>paryudāsa</s>), due to contact with a real entity, that very entity-natured selflessness has been arrived at. For one whose negative concomitance does not have the nature of absence, in the exclusion of what has a positive nature there would be no establishment of a positive entity—thus there is no entailment of positive concomitance. Similarly, in the case of non-selflessness too, there would be no establishment of a positive entity. Just as 'this living body is not selfless because it possesses breath and so forth'—when considering the pervader-pervaded relationship between the two counter-instances, selflessness is seen only in the absence of possessing breath and so forth. And in the absence of that it does not exist—thus it itself does not present the establishment of breath and so forth in the self. Likewise, even in the case of the <s>sādhya</s>, what is being excluded by breath and the like would remain alone. Because of their absence in selflessness, breath and the like negate that—they do not present the self. Because of the non-establishment of a positive entity there. Nor would the establishment of the self follow from the cessation of selflessness, because of the unwanted consequence even when observing negative concomitance from the counter-instance. Therefore there is no converse pervasion when negative concomitance is not established. And the establishment of that is itself the establishment of positive concomitance. Or, if it is not established, even when the cessation of its negative concomitance is established, there is non-establishment of that—thus the unwanted consequence applies to the <s>sādhya</s> as well. Therefore, without positive concomitance there is no pervasion by negative concomitance. But by the pervasion of having-false-meaning with being-of-human-origin, even when <s>apauruṣeya</s> (non-human-originated) [texts] are excluded, there is no truth of meaning, because of the possibility of another mode. But this would apply if words were of two classes only—in the exclusion of one, there being no other possibility. But they could also be meaningless, so the desired conclusion is not achieved. [Objection:] They are not meaningless because of the cognition of meaning. [Reply:] This would be a human activity, like the alternative meaning. Just as, even when not having that meaning, others interpret the stories of <s>Bharata</s>, <s>Urvaśī</s>, and so forth differently, and some have cognition following that interpretation—similarly, this attribution of meaning to meaningless [words] is human-made, not made by the nature of the words, because it depends on human instruction, just like alternative meanings. For things that illuminate by nature, such as fire and the like, do not depend on that [instruction]. But it is reasonable that a person teaches by declaring the activity of his own convention. Since there is no difference in depending on instruction between what is established by human convention and what is established by nature, and since there is no other distinguishing feature, it is difficult to conclude that one is natural and the other is of human origin. [Objection:] There is a distinguishing feature—agreement with valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). [Reply:] We will refute this later, [showing] that there is no operation of other valid means of knowledge regarding objects that are entirely beyond perception. By the mere distinguishing feature of agreement with <s>pramāṇa</s> between two objects having similar properties, if one is <s>apauruṣeya</s>, then even more would now be <s>apauruṣeya</s>. There are also some human-made statements of this kind—the unwanted consequence extends to those as well. Just like those, these too would have the desired meaningfulness, be of human origin, and be in accord with <s>pramāṇa</s>. Moreover, we see this as contradictory—that mantras are <s>apauruṣeya</s>. For: If the mantras are someone's convention, accomplishment of a purpose is

children.text: 15618 asāmarthyam apekṣaṇe //293//
children.translated_text: [Reply:] There is incapacity in [what requires] dependence. //293//

The accomplishment of a purpose from mantras is certainly not from human convention. What then? This is the inherent nature of existence (<s>bhāva-svabhāva</s>)—that these, however employed, are fruit-giving. But then, since the form of the syllables (<s>varṇa</s>) is undifferentiated everywhere, even from any kind of application there should be a result. For the mantra is nothing but syllables. [Objection:] The sequence (<s>krama</s>) is the mantra. [Reply:] That the sequence is something different has already been refuted. It has been stated that there is no sequence other than the syllables. And if they are non-different, then the syllables alone are the mantra. And since they are undifferentiated everywhere, they would always be fruit-giving. But disruption is observed even from the slightest deviation of sequence—from someone's [faulty] performance, from the incompleteness of the deity's presence, and from improper worship. But in total disruption, because of the non-performance of someone's convention, and because of the absence [of the deity], there is neither purpose nor harm. Moreover, whether the sequence is something different or not, since the mantra—whether having the nature of syllables or the nature of that sequence—is the cause of the purpose and is uncreated, being eternal it would always be present, and thus there would be perpetual accomplishment of that purpose. For the production of results from inherent power (<s>bhāva-śakti</s>) would be unimpaired, so there should be no deficiency of results. For it is not reasonable that there be deficiency of effect when the cause is complete—because of the unwanted consequence of its being a non-cause. The desired result is not achieved from the mere application of mantras alone,

children.text: 15624 prayoktṛ-bheda-apekṣā ca na asaṃskāryasya yujyate //294//
children.translated_text: And dependence on the difference of the performer is not fitting for what cannot be conditioned. //294//

If mantras were to acquire some excellence of nature from the ritual procedure or from something else, that capable [factor] would be what is required there. But it has been said that this does not exist for eternal things. Therefore, why is this incapable [factor] required? Thus, being independent [of ritual],

If mantras bestow accomplishment solely by inherent power (<s>bhāva-śakti</s>), they would not exclude any sacrificer (<s>yajamāna</s>) or anyone else. For one's own nature does not become otherwise toward another. Because it is not diminished by one nor enhanced by another, because there is no causal relation with anyone, and because of the absence of proximity and distance. For this very reason, because of its being unconditionable, there is no performer either. Therefore,

children.translated_text: what does the performer do for those upon which no particular [modification] can be superimposed,

children.text: 15728 yena tataḥ kaścit phalam aśnute anyo na /

children.text: 15729 prayogo yady abhivyaktiḥ sā prāg eva nirākṛtā //296//
children.translated_text: If the application is manifestation, that has already been refuted. //296//

For impermanent entities have superimposed particularities. Due to the difference of nature caused by that, having acquired excellence therefrom, they would be otherwise elsewhere. But not when there is no difference—because of the non-difference of effect when there is non-difference of cause; and because of the unwanted consequence of the particular [effect] being uncaused when there is a particular [difference]—this has mostly been stated already. Therefore, these mantras, being fruit-giving due to an excellence of nature, even though they are products, would not be otherwise even when employed by a <s>śūdra</s> and the like, because there is no difference in the nature of persons designated as <s>śūdra</s> or <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. For things whose real difference depends on difference of nature are not altered by the difference of nominal designation that follows human desire. [Objection:] There is a difference of <s>jāti</s> (class/caste) between them. [Reply:] That is observed where there is difference of form, quality, and capacity—like between cows and horses. And the world recognizes this without instruction. We do not see any specific quality restricted [to either caste] in the same way. And not seeing [such a quality], how would we recognize a difference? And this difference of cognition in the world that follows the difference of name would exist even without a difference of <s>jāti</s>, from the performance of specific activities and from convention—like the designations of physician, merchant, and so forth. Therefore, these mantras, being employed by an undifferentiated [person], acquire a nature that is equally undifferentiated from that, and would thus be equally fruit-giving. But when the result comes from these [mantras] by convention, this is not a fault—because of the restriction of the production of results to the taste of the convention-maker. For entities that operate by their nature merit the unwanted consequence through that [nature]. But those that operate by human will do not, since they operate in whatever way [the person wills]. And as for the performer enjoying the result, we understand 'application' as the production of what is suitable for the desired purpose, or the transformation of a [mental] continuum. Both of these would apply when a particular [modification] arises. Otherwise,

children.text: 15801 na hi nityānāṃ kācid abhivyaktir ity uktam yato abhivyañjakaḥ
children.translated_text: For it has been said that there is no manifestation of eternal things, such that the performer

children.text: 15825 manojapo vā vyarthaḥ syāc śabdo hi śrotra-gocaraḥ //298//
children.translated_text: Or else mental recitation (<s>manojapa</s>) would be purposeless, for sound is the domain of the ear. //298//

For there is no manifestation of sound through something else as a transformation of its own nature, nor is there a removal of a covering. Rather, a cognition directed toward that [sound] is [what is meant by 'manifestation'], since what is unheard is designated as 'unmanifest.' In that case, if the speaker were the cause of cognition, the same would apply to the hearer as well—he too would enjoy the result just as the speaker does. For there is no one other than the speaker who has that nature [of causing cognition] elsewhere, since [the speaker] is the cause of cognition of that [sound]. [Objection:] The difference is that the hearer's cognition is conditioned by another (<s>para-upādhi</s>), not the speaker's. [Reply:] But what use does the speaker serve for the hearer such that a conditioning factor is accepted? [Objection:] From that comes the hearing of sound. [Reply:] But this is precisely what is being questioned—how [does it come] from that?—since there is no connection. [The speaker] would be a 'causer of hearing' for him by bringing the object near. But that is not possible, because [sound] is in no way transformed [by the speaker]. Sense-organ conditioning and the like have also been discussed. [Objection:] From the cognition of both 'he makes me hear' and 'I make [him] hear,' there is a distinction between speaker and hearer. [Reply:] Since there is no actual beneficiary and benefactor, it is mere delusion (<s>bhrānti</s>); if [the distinction] existed [on that basis], there would be an unwanted over-extension. Because even elsewhere delusion-based cognition is observed. And when there is no benefit whatsoever, such cognition is not justified, since this would extend to everyone mutually. Even delusion arises elsewhere [only] when there is some benefit and some proximity—it too would not arise when there is absolutely no benefit. Therefore, since there is no distinction between the speaker and hearer in being the cause of manifestation, the connection with the result would be equal [for both]. Moreover:

too

children.text: 15910 tathā syus tad-arthā ced asiddhaṃ kalpanā-anvayāt //299//
children.translated_text: would be so if they were directed toward that [sound]—but this is unestablished, because of [their] connection with conceptual construction. //299//

Sound is characterized by being grasped by the ear. If [this characterization] is overstepped, there would be an unwanted over-extension. [Objection:] In this way, there would be the same problem even for universals. [Reply:] We do not say [it must be] sound alone. But sound is necessarily of that character, because there is no other defining mark for it. In that case, if the performer is the cause of manifestation of <s>mantras</s> whose nature is sound, [then] the performer—the reciter—of instruments (<s>karaṇas</s>) whose hearing is not manifested is not connected with the result of the <s>mantra</s>, nor is one who recites mentally. For at that time we do not apprehend any object through the ear. And a <s>mantra</s> is not non-verbal in nature. [Objection:] If you think that even that [mental cognition] is a manifestation of sound, because it arises indirectly from that— [Reply:] For even one who meditates with the mind does not have a cognition resembling a <s>mantra</s> without the hearing of sound. Therefore, since that [mental cognition] too originates from sound, it is itself a manifestation of sound. [Objection:] In this way there would be an infinite regress—for even mental conceptualizations of word-meanings are produced in a series.

15923 sarvathā śabda-svabhāvānāṃ mantrāṇāṃ prayogāt phala-avāptau
children.translated_text: In every way, since the result is obtained through the employment of <s>mantras</s> whose nature is sound,

children.text: 15924 vyartho manojapo vikalpasya śabda-rūpa-asaṃsparśāt /
children.translated_text: mental recitation is purposeless, because conceptual construction has no contact with the nature of sound.

children.text: 15925 sva-sāmānya-svabhāvānām eka-bhāva-vivakṣayā /
children.translated_text: Because of the statement that treats what has its own particular nature and what has a universal nature as identical,

children.text: 15926 ukteḥ samayakārāṇām avirodho na vastuni //300//
children.translated_text: there is no contradiction for convention-makers—not in reality. //300//

We do not say that every cognition arising from sound is a manifestation of it. Rather, that which has it [sound] as its object is a manifestation of it. The having-it-as-object of mental conceptualization (<s>mano-vikalpa</s>) is unestablished. For we shall explain that conceptual constructions do not operate upon particulars (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). For they arise from the internal awakening of conceptual impressions (<s>vikalpa-vāsanā</s>), independently of the presentation of an external object, since they exist even when the external [object] departs and arrives. For that which does not depend on the positing of the existence of something is not a cause of it. And how can what is not a cause be an object? Therefore, mental conceptualization is not a manifestation of sound such that one possessing it would be a performer. [Rather,] a cognition that is produced from it [sound] and has it as its object is a manifestation of it. The performer is one who has recourse to that [manifestation]. Here too it has been said that the same problem applies to the hearer as well. And when one applies [sound] for the sake of knowledge, the sound acts upon the person—because it generates cognition in him. The person does not [act upon] the sound—because of his not benefiting it in its own nature. Yet the person is [called] the 'performer' of sounds—this is an extra-ordinary convention.

16009 kārya-bhedo yuktaḥ / tasmād asti sā bhedavatī yato ayam
16010 pratīti-bhedaḥ / satyam
16011 asti sā puruṣa-āśrayā //301//
children.translated_text: But the convention-maker, combining according to convention the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>)—which is the domain of the sense-faculties—and the universal character (<s>sāmānya-lakṣaṇa</s>)—which appears in conceptual construction—as they are used in ordinary discourse, announces the convention and produces meaning in accordance with that convention. Therefore there is no fault in mental recitation and the like. But when results are obtained from the real nature of things, they would not arise from contact with what does not have that nature. As for what was said—'there is no sequence (<s>ānupūrvī</s>) other than the phonemes'—regarding that: [Objection:] If the sequence did not exist, then in hearing 'lake' (<s>saras</s>) and 'taste/juice' (<s>rasa</s>), there would be no difference of effect. [Reply:] For in the syllables of <s>saras</s> and <s>rasa</s> and the like, there is no difference of phonemes, nor is there anything other than the phonemes from which there could be a difference of effect. Yet we observe different cognitions for the two, and the sequence alone is dissimilar. And a difference of effect is not justified when there is no difference of cause. Therefore that [sequence] exists as possessing differentiation, from which there is this difference of cognition. True—

children.text: 16012 tathā hi /
children.translated_text: That [sequence] exists as dependent on the person. //301//

children.text: 16013 yo yad-varṇa-samutthāna-jñānajāj jñānato dhvaniḥ /
children.translated_text: For thus:

children.text: 16014 jāyate tad-upādhiḥ sa śrutyā samavasīyate //302//
children.translated_text: Whatever sound (<s>dhvani</s>) arises from the cognition born from the production of a particular phoneme—

children.text: 16015 taj-jñāna-janita-jñānaḥ sa śrutāv apaṭu-śrutiḥ /
children.translated_text: that [sound] is conditioned by it and is ascertained through hearing.

children.text: 16016 apekṣya tat-smṛtiṃ paścād ādhatte smṛtim ātmani //303//
children.translated_text: One whose cognition is generated by that cognition, being of unclear audition, after attending to the memory of that, deposits memory within himself. //303//

children.text: 16017 ity eṣā pauruṣeyy eva tad-hetu-grāhi-cetasām /
children.translated_text: Thus this [sequence] is entirely person-made (<s>pauruṣeyī</s>)—for the minds that grasp its cause,

children.text: 16018 kāryakāraṇatā varṇeṣv ānupūrvī iti kathyat //304//
children.translated_text: the causal relation among phonemes is called 'sequence' (<s>ānupūrvī</s>). //304//

children.text: 16107 anyad eva tato rūpaṃ tad varṇānāṃ padaṃ padam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the nature of phonemes in words is something different from [the phonemes themselves]—that is the word (<s>pada</s>); each word, being differentiated by the producer's impressions, when combined, produces a difference of effect. //305//

children.text: 16108 kartṛ-saṃskārato bhinnaṃ sahitaṃ kārya-bheda-kṛt //305//

children.translated_text: For vocal expression (<s>vāg-vijñapti</s>) arises from mind and is designated as phonemes, words, and sentences. There, the thought that produces the <s>sa</s>-phoneme, as the immediately preceding condition, gives rise to the thought that produces the <s>a</s>-phoneme. Likewise, the thoughts producing the <s>ra</s>-phoneme, the <s>ā</s>-phoneme, and the <s>visarjanīya</s> are each caused by the preceding one. Thus these phonemes, being mutually caused, are born from the sequence of their own causes. Even at the time of hearing, when slow-moving [phonemes], requiring the cooperative condition of the cognition of the preceding phoneme, generate their own cognition, they depend upon the memory of the preceding phoneme and merge into memory. This is the nature of phonemes—characterized by the production of conditions through differentiated causal relations,

children.text:
16109 tasmān na khalv eka eva padeṣu varṇānāṃ svabhāvaḥ kartṛ-citta-

children.text: 16112 sā ca ānupūrvī varṇānāṃ pravṛttā racana-ākṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: And that sequence of phonemes proceeds from the form of arrangement—

children.text: 16113 icchā aviruddha-siddhīnāṃ sthita-krama-virodhataḥ //306//
children.translated_text: because there is a contradiction between the established sequence and the accomplishment of [results] not contrary to one's wish. //306//

Therefore, the nature of phonemes in words is certainly not singular, because of differentiation through the difference of the producer's mental impressions. And that [nature], when combined with the others,

children.text: 16121 kāryakāraṇatā-siddheḥ puṃsāṃ varṇa-kramasya ca /
children.translated_text: Since the causal relation and the sequence of phonemes among persons is established,

children.text: 16122 sarvo varṇa-kramaḥ pumbhyo dahana-indhana-yukti-vat //307//
children.translated_text: all phoneme-sequence is [derived] from persons—like the relation of fire and fuel. //307//

It has been said that the particular nature produced by cognitions that are in a causal relation is the sequence (<s>ānupūrvī</s>) of phonemes. And since that is made by the deliberation and reflection of a person, the phonemes do not have a fixed sequence—because of the sequence being one in which accomplishment is not contrary to one's wish. Like the conformity to a particular sequence. For it is not possible to rearrange at will the sequence of things that have a fixed spatial and temporal order—such as the <s>Himavat</s>, <s>Vindhya</s>, and <s>Malaya</s> [mountains], or seeds and sprouts. From this very fact, when there is a sequence of conceptual constructions reckoned as a property of persons,

16212 asādhāraṇatā siddhā mantra-ākhya-krama-kāriṇām /
children.translated_text: The uniqueness of persons who create the sequence of <s>mantras</s> and names is established

children.text: 16213 puṃsāṃ jñāna-prabhāvābhyām anyeṣāṃ tad-abhāvataḥ //308//
children.translated_text: through [their] knowledge and power; for others, because of the absence of that [knowledge and power]. //308//

When fuel is present, combustion occurs; when absent, it does not—yet fire that has no visible fuel is not without fuel, because there is no restriction of [fire] to [particular] place and time. And if there were restriction, it would be to that very fuel, since fuel is defined as the material cause of combustion. Similarly, if this phoneme-sequence did not depend on a person's conceptualization, it would manifest by itself without any support; [and yet] even with effort it could not [be produced]—since it does not originate from that [i.e., from nothing]. If [any cause] were capable [of producing sequence] anywhere, then everything would be so—because of the absence of distinction. And when something arises only when its [cause] is present, then if what is not distinguished from that [cause] were not responsible for it, causal relation everywhere would be refuted—since [causal relation] is characterized by co-presence and co-absence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). Or else another defining mark would have to be stated. All entities such as pots and the like—both artificial and natural—would [then] be equally [problematic]. For even there, conceptualization is possible in the same way, and there is no distinguishing factor. For those [artifacts] too are made by someone only after observing another's activity, and some whose makers are unknown [also exist]—so let there be a denial of [human] creation for all or some. Therefore, this entire phoneme-sequence is person-made, because it does not transgress the nature of things with an established causal relation. For this very reason:

children.text: 16323 ye api tantravidaḥ kecin mantrān kāṃścana kurvate /

children.text: 16324 prabhu-prabhāvas teṣāṃ sa tad-ukta-nyāya-vṛttitaḥ //309//
children.translated_text: their power belongs to that [original] master, since they operate according to the principles stated by him. //309//

"This sequence of syllables is capable of neutralizing poison and the like, and no other"—if another person also knew this, he would understand it in the same way. But this is not the case. Therefore, this sequence is productive of effects by its very nature, and is known only by certain [extraordinary] persons—thus there exists a person who sees hidden meanings. For this meaning—"this is capable, this is not"—cannot be

For they, observing his prescriptions and proceeding according to his instructions, are capable. Those who violate his prescriptions

children.text: 16410 pratipāditā hi puruṣa-kṛtās tad-adhiṣṭhānāc ca phaladā mantrāḥ /
children.translated_text: For <s>mantras</s> have been established as person-made, and they give results through his empowerment.
